# Getting Started

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/

<div class="dox-hero" markdown>

<div class="dox-hero__text" markdown>

<img class="dox-hero__mascot" src="assets/mascot.png" alt="Doxie, the Dox mascot" width="140" height="137">

# Fast backends<br>in Dart

<p class="dox-hero__lead"><strong>Everything your Dart backend needs.</strong></p>

<p class="dox-hero__lead">
Dox is a web backend framework for Dart.
Routing, an ORM, migrations, validation, auth and a CLI come in one place.
It runs one isolate per CPU core and builds to a small native binary.
</p>

<p class="dox-hero__actions" markdown>
[Build your first API](tutorial/index.md){ .md-button .md-button--primary }
[GitHub](https://github.com/dartondox/dox){ .md-button }
[Blog](/blog/){ .md-button }
</p>

</div>

<div class="dox-hero__code" markdown>

```dart
Route.get('/blogs', BlogController.index); // (1)!

enum Status { active, draft }

@Dto() // (2)!
class BlogFilter {
  final Status status; // ?status=active, else 422
  const BlogFilter({required this.status});
  static const DtoSchema<BlogFilter> schema =
      $BlogFilterDto; // (3)!
}

class BlogController {
  static Future<List<Blog>> index(
    BlogFilter query, // (4)!
  ) async {
    return Blog()
        .where('status', query.status.name)
        .get(); // (5)!
  }
}
```

1.  A route points at a static method. No reflection, no controller registry.
2.  `@Dto()` marks an input class. `build_runner` generates the checks from the fields and their types.
3.  The generated schema. The same schema feeds the OpenAPI docs.
4.  Ask for the DTO as a parameter. Dox reads the query (or the body), checks it, and gives you a typed object. Bad input gets a `422` before your code runs.
5.  The ORM. The same code runs on Postgres, MySQL and SQLite. Postgres and MySQL use native drivers.

</div>

</div>

Your code is plain Dart. The speed comes from the native server: it runs
on the isolate's own thread, so a request never waits for another thread.
See [Performance](digging-deeper/performance.md) for every route and how
it was run.

## Run it in two minutes

You need [Dart](https://dart.dev/get-dart) 3.13 or newer. Nothing else: the
starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install.

```bash
dart pub global activate dox             # install the CLI
dox create my_app                            # download the starter project
cd my_app
dart pub get
dox s                                        # start the server
```

Open a second terminal and call the first route:

```bash
curl localhost:3000/ping
```

```text
pong
```

That is a Dox app. Keep going with the [tutorial](tutorial/index.md): it adds a
model, a database table, validation, login and a Docker image, one short step
at a time.

!!! note "The CLI is not found?"
    `dart pub global activate` puts `dox` in `$HOME/.pub-cache/bin`.
    Add that folder to your `PATH`. See [Installation](getting-started/installation.md).

## What you get

<div class="grid cards" markdown>

-   :material-lightning-bolt: **Fast by default**

    A native HTTP server, one isolate per CPU core and streamed bodies.
    `dox build` makes one native binary. See [Performance](digging-deeper/performance.md).

-   :material-database-outline: **ORM and query builder**

    Models, relations, migrations and transactions for Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB and SQLite.
    Postgres and MySQL use native drivers. See [Database](database/index.md).

-   :material-check-decagram-outline: **Typed validation**

    Write a `@Dto` class. Dox checks the input and gives your controller a typed object.
    See [Validation](the-basic/validation.md).

-   :material-file-document-outline: **OpenAPI**

    OpenAPI 3.1 docs and a Scalar docs page, made from your routes and DTOs.
    See [`dox_openapi`](packages/openapi.md).

-   :material-folder-outline: **File storage**

    Local disk and S3 behind one API, with signed URLs. See [`dox_storage`](packages/storage.md).

-   :material-cached: **Cache**

    Memory, file and Redis cache with tags and locks. See [`dox_cache`](packages/cache.md).

-   :material-access-point: **Real time**

    [Socket.IO](packages/socketio.md), with Redis for many servers.

-   :material-shield-lock-outline: **Security**

    JWT [authentication](security/authentication.md), [CORS](security/cors.md),
    [encryption](security/encryption.md) and [hashing](security/hashing.md).

-   :material-console: **CLI**

    Create projects, controllers, models and migrations. Run, build and migrate.
    See [CLI reference](reference/cli.md).

</div>

# Installation

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/getting-started/installation/

# Installation

This page shows how to install the Dox CLI, make a new project and start the server.

Dox needs **Dart 3.13** or newer.

## Install the CLI

```bash
dart pub global activate dox
```

Check that it works:

```bash
dox version
```

!!! warning "`dox: command not found`"
    The shell can not find the CLI when the pub `bin` folder is not in your `PATH`.
    Add this line to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`, then open a new terminal:

    ```bash
    export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"
    ```

## Create a new project

```bash
dox create new_blog
```

`dox create` downloads the newest release of
[dox-sample](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-sample), the starter project.
To get one exact release, add `--version` with a release tag of dox-sample.

It also makes your `.env` file from `.env.example`, with a new random `APP_KEY`.
Then get the packages:

```bash
cd new_blog
dart pub get
```

The starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install.
The file `db/dox.sqlite` is created at the first start.
To use Postgres or MySQL instead, change `DB_CONNECTION` and the `DB_*`
values in `.env`. See [Database](../database/index.md).

!!! info "Add Dox to an existing Dart project"
    Add the packages you need with `dart pub add`:

    ```bash
    dart pub add dox_core dox_orm dox_migration
    dart pub add dev:dox_builder dev:build_runner
    ```

## Start the server

```bash
dox s
```

`dox s` does two things:

- It runs `dart run bin/server.dart`. When you change a file in `lib/app/`, it hot reloads the new code. No restart is needed. For routes, providers, config and other start-up code, it restarts the server.
- It runs `dart run build_runner watch`, so generated files stay up to date.

To skip the builder, use `dox s --ignore-build-runner`.
To turn hot reload off, use `dox s --no-reload`.
To start the server without the CLI, run `dart run bin/server.dart`.

At each start it also runs the new migrations in `db/migration`.
The server uses the port in `APP_PORT` in the `.env` file (`3000` by default).
Check it:

```bash
curl localhost:3000/ping
```

```text
pong
```

## Start the server with Docker

```bash
docker compose up -d --build
```

This starts the app, a queue worker and a Postgres database.
The app and the worker always use the Postgres service. They set `DB_CONNECTION` and `DB_NAME` themselves.
The database port is open on this machine only (`127.0.0.1`), not on the network.
To start only the database and run the app with `dox s`, use `docker compose up -d postgres`.
Then set `DB_CONNECTION=postgres` and `DB_NAME=dox` in `.env`.

!!! tip "Production"
    Do not use `dox s` or `dart run` in production.
    Build a native binary with `dox build`. See [Deployment](../digging-deeper/deployment.md).

## Run the code generator

Dox makes code for models and DTOs with `build_runner`.
`dox s` already runs it. To run it alone:

```bash
dox build_runner:watch   # runs again on every file change
dox build_runner:build   # runs once
```

## AI agents

The Dox packages ship skills for AI coding agents.
A skill tells the agent how to use the real API of a package.
Install them in your app, after `dart pub get`:

```bash
dart run skills@ get
```

It finds the skills of your dependencies and installs them for your agent.
It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and others.
Run it again after you add a package or update one.
It only reads the packages listed in your own `pubspec.yaml`. To get the skill of a package that comes in through another one (like `ioredis`), add it to `pubspec.yaml`.
See [skills](https://pub.dev/packages/skills) for the options.

The starter project also has an `AGENTS.md` file with the rules of the project.

## Packages

| Package | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `dox` | the CLI |
| `dox_core` | HTTP server, routing, requests, responses, validation |
| `dox_orm` | query builder and models |
| `dox_migration` | database migrations |
| `dox_auth` | Login with access tokens, JWT or sessions |
| `dox_builder`, `dox_annotation` | code generation for models, DTOs and the container |
| `dox_validation` | [typed validation schemas](../packages/validation.md) |
| `dox_openapi` | [OpenAPI docs](../packages/openapi.md) |
| `dox_storage` | [file storage: local, S3](../packages/storage.md) |
| `dox_cache` | [cache: memory, file, Redis](../packages/cache.md) |
| `dox_cache_database` | [cache in a database table](../packages/cache.md#database-store) |
| `dox_socketio` | [Socket.IO server](../packages/socketio.md) |
| `dox_queue` | [background jobs](../digging-deeper/queue.md) |
| `dox_queue_database` | [queue in a database table](../digging-deeper/queue.md#database-driver) |
| `dox_scheduler` | [scheduled tasks](../digging-deeper/scheduler.md) |
| `dox_mailer` | [send email](../digging-deeper/mail.md) |
| `dox_view` | [HTML views](../the-basic/views.md) |
| `dox_inertia` | [Inertia.js pages](../the-basic/inertia.md) |
| `dox_http_native` | [native HTTP server](../digging-deeper/native-server.md) (Rust) |
| `dox_postgres_native`, `dox_mysql_native` | native drivers for [Postgres](../database/postgres-native.md) and [MySQL/MariaDB](../database/mysql-native.md) |

# Add a package

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/getting-started/add-a-package/

# Add a package

`dox add` adds a Dox package to your app and sets it up.

```bash
dox add orm
```

## What it does

1. Runs `dart pub add dox_orm`. `orm` is short for `dox_orm`. The full name works too.
2. Runs `dart pub get`.
3. Runs the setup command of the package, `dox orm:install`.

The setup command writes the config files, adds the keys to `.env` and `.env.example`, and runs `build_runner` when the package needs it.
At the end it prints what it did and the next steps.

A package with no setup command is only added. `dox add` then says so.

## Options

Words after the name go to the setup command:

```bash
dox add orm --driver=postgres
```

`--dev` adds the package as a dev dependency.

## Safe to run twice

The setup command never overwrites a file and never changes a `.env` key that is already there.
So you can run `dox add` again. It only adds what is missing.

## Packages with a setup command

| Command | What it sets up |
| --- | --- |
| `dox add orm [--driver=sqlite\|postgres\|mysql]` | The ORM and migrations. See [Database](../database/index.md). |
| `dox add queue [--driver=database\|redis\|sync]` | Queued jobs and `bin/queue.dart`. `database` is the default and needs `dox add orm` first. See [Queue](../digging-deeper/queue.md). |
| `dox add scheduler` | Scheduled tasks and `bin/schedule.dart`. See [Scheduler](../digging-deeper/scheduler.md). |
| `dox add mailer [--transport=log\|smtp\|resend\|mailgun\|postmark\|ses]` | Mail. `log` is the default. See [Mail](../digging-deeper/mail.md). |
| `dox add cache [--store=file\|redis\|memory\|database]` | Cache stores. `database` needs `dox add orm` first. See [Cache](../digging-deeper/cache.md). |
| `dox add auth` | Access token auth. Needs `dox add orm` and a `User` model first. See [Authentication](../security/authentication.md). |
| `dox add storage [--disk=local\|s3]` | File storage. See [File storage](../digging-deeper/file-storage.md). |
| `dox add socketio [--broadcasting]` | Socket.IO, and broadcasting with the flag. See [Socket.IO](../packages/socketio.md). |
| `dox add view` | Views and `resources/views/`. See [Views](../the-basic/views.md). |
| `dox add inertia` | The server side of Inertia. It prints the Vite steps. See [Inertia](../the-basic/inertia.md). |
| `dox add mcp` | An MCP server with a sample tool. See [MCP](../packages/mcp.md). |

The first `dox add orm` can download (or build) the Postgres and MySQL drivers once, also the one you do not use. After it, `pubspec.yaml` skips the unused drivers, so later builds do not get them.

To add a setup command to your own package, see [Package commands](../digging-deeper/package-commands.md#ship-an-install-command).

# Build a blog API

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/

# Build a blog API

This tutorial takes you from an empty folder to a small blog API that runs as one native binary.

Every step has the full code and a `curl` command to check it.

The finished project is on GitHub: [examples/blog-api](https://github.com/dartondox/dox/tree/main/examples/blog-api).
CI builds it and runs its tests on every push, so the code on these pages keeps working.

## What you will build

A JSON API for blog posts.

| Method | Path | Who | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/posts` | anyone | list all posts |
| `GET` | `/api/posts/{id}` | anyone | one post, or `404` |
| `POST` | `/api/posts` | logged in user | make a post (`201`, or `422` on bad input) |
| `PUT` | `/api/posts/{id}` | logged in user | change a post |
| `POST` | `/api/auth/register` | anyone | make an account, get a token |
| `POST` | `/api/auth/login` | anyone | log in, get a token |
| `GET` | `/api/auth/user` | logged in user | the user of the token |

## What you need

- Dart **3.13** or newer: `dart --version`.
- `curl`, to call the API.
- About 15 minutes.

You do not need Docker or a database server. The app uses SQLite, which is one file in your project.

## The steps

1. [Create the project](01-create-project.md)
2. [Model and migration](02-model-and-migration.md)
3. [Routes and controller](03-routes-and-controller.md)
4. [Validation](04-validation.md)
5. [Login with dox_auth](05-auth.md)
6. [Test](06-test.md)
7. [Build and deploy](07-build-and-deploy.md)

## The finished project

Files that you make or change in this tutorial are marked with `*`.
The template has more files (queue, scheduler, storage). This tree shows the ones that matter here.

```text
blog/
├── bin/
│   ├── migrate.dart              runs the dox migration:* commands
│   ├── server.dart               runs the migrations, starts the server
│   └── queue.dart, schedule.dart, seed.dart
├── db/migration/
│   ├── ..._create_posts_table.dart   *
│   ├── ..._create_users_table.dart
│   └── migrations.dart           the list of migrations (Dox writes it)
├── lib/
│   ├── app/http/controllers/
│   │   ├── auth.controller.dart  *
│   │   └── post.controller.dart  *
│   ├── app/dtos/
│   │   ├── login_user/login_user.dto.dart   *
│   │   ├── register_user/register_user.dto.dart *
│   │   └── save_post/save_post.dto.dart    *
│   ├── app/models/
│   │   ├── post/post.model.dart  *
│   │   └── user/user.model.dart
│   ├── config/
│   │   ├── app.dart              * adds the DTO list
│   │   ├── database.dart
│   │   └── env.dart              the .env keys, typed
│   ├── routes/api.dart           *
│   ├── providers/
│   │   ├── auth_provider.dart    *
│   │   └── orm_provider.dart
│   └── generated/
│       ├── container.g.dart      * generated
│       └── dtos.g.dart           * generated
├── test/http_test.dart           *
├── .env                          made by dox create
├── Dockerfile
└── pubspec.yaml                  * adds dox_auth
```

Start with [step 1: create the project](01-create-project.md).

# Step 1: Create the project

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/01-create-project/

# Step 1: Create the project

This step makes a new Dox project, points it at SQLite, starts the dev server and calls the first route.

## 1. Install the CLI and make the project

```bash
dart pub global activate dox
dox create blog
cd blog
dart pub get
```

`dox create` downloads the [dox-sample](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-sample) template from GitHub and names the package `blog`.
So every import in this tutorial starts with `package:blog/`.


## 2. Use SQLite

`dox create` already made `.env` with a new random `APP_KEY`. The template already uses SQLite:

```ini title=".env"
APP_PORT=3000
APP_KEY=<your new random key>

DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=db/dox.sqlite
```

Dox makes the file `db/dox.sqlite` at the first start. SQLite does not read the other `DB_*` lines.
The app reads these keys through the typed class in `lib/config/env.dart`. See [Environment variables](../digging-deeper/env.md).

!!! note "The folder must exist"
    Dox makes the database file when it is missing, but not its folder.
    If you set `DB_NAME=storage/blog.sqlite`, run `mkdir storage` first.

## 3. Start the server

```bash
dox s
```

`dox s` runs the code generator and the server. It hot reloads your code when you save a file in `lib/app/`. It restarts the server for routes, config and other start-up code.
The first start is slower, because it compiles the SQLite library.
At the first start it also runs the migrations of the template.
The last line is a JSON log line with this message:

```text
Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 8 isolate (native)
```

Open it at `http://localhost:3000`. The number of isolates is the number of CPU cores.

## Check it

In a second terminal:

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/ping
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
...

pong
```

The route is in `lib/routes/api.dart`. The `ApiRouter` has the prefix `api`, so `/ping` is served at `/api/ping`.

## Next

[Step 2: Model and migration](02-model-and-migration.md)

# Step 2: Model and migration

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/02-model-and-migration/

# Step 2: Model and migration

This step makes the `posts` table with a Dart migration and a `Post` model for it.

## 1. Make the model and the migration

Stop `dox s` first with `Ctrl+C`.
`dox s` restarts the server when a new file appears, and the server runs new migrations at start.
So it would run the new migration before you add the columns.

```bash
dox make:model Post -m
```

This makes two files and updates one:

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart` | the model (new) |
| `db/migration/<date>_create_posts_table.dart` | the migration (new) |
| `db/migration/migrations.dart` | the list of all Dart migrations. Dox writes it. Do not edit it. |

The template already has `bin/migrate.dart`. The `dox migration:*` commands run it.

## 2. Add the columns to the migration

Open the new file in `db/migration`. Add `title` and `body`:

```dart title="db/migration/2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table.dart"
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreatePostsTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('posts', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('title');
      table.text('body');
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('posts');
  }
}
```

- `table.id()` makes an auto increment primary key on every database.
- `table.timestamps()` makes `created_at` and `updated_at`. The model fills them.

## 3. Add the fields to the model

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'post.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'posts')
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>[];

  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? body;
}
```

Every column field is nullable. A new `Post()` has no values yet.
`id`, `createdAt` and `updatedAt` come from `PostGenerator`. You do not declare them.

## 4. Run the migrations on server start

Nothing to change here. The template's `bin/server.dart` already runs the migrations before the server starts:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() async {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);

  await Migrator(
    migrations: migrations,
    config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
  ).migrate();

  await Dox().startServer();
}
```

This also works in the native binary of [step 7](07-build-and-deploy.md).

## 5. Run the migration and the generator

```bash
dox migration:run
```

```text
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
```

!!! tip "The migration ran too early?"
    If `dox s` was still running, the `posts` table may already exist without `title` and `body`.
    Run `dox migration:rollback`, then `dox migration:run` again.

The model needs its generated file `post.model.g.dart`.
`dox s` makes it while it runs. If `dox s` is not running, run the generator once:

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

## Check it

```bash
dox migration:status
```

```text
Migration                                 Batch  Status
2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table   1      Ran
2026_10_25_000000000_create_queue_tables  1      Ran
2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table      2      Ran
```

The first two come with the template. The server ran them at the first start in step 1.

Now start the server again with `dox s`.

# Step 3: Routes and controller

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/03-routes-and-controller/

# Step 3: Routes and controller

This step adds a resource controller and the routes to list, create and show posts.

## 1. Make the controller

```bash
dox make:controller Post -r
```

`-r` makes a resource controller with the seven CRUD methods.
Replace the file with this. It keeps only `index`, `store` and `show`:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class PostController {
  /// GET /api/posts
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  /// POST /api/posts
  Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = req.input('title')
      ..body = req.input('body');
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// GET /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> show(int id) async {
    Post? post = await Post().find(id);
    if (post == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return post;
  }
}
```

How it works:

- `@Inject()` puts the controller in the container. Dox makes it for you. `dox s` runs `build_runner`, which adds it to `lib/generated/container.g.dart`.
  A new project already has `container: registerContainer` in `lib/config/app.dart`, so you change nothing there.
- A controller returns a model or a list of models. Dox sends it as JSON.
- `response(post).statusCode(201)` sets the status code.
- `show(int id)` gets the `{id}` from the URL. `/api/posts/abc` answers `404`, because `abc` is not an `int`.
- `req.input('title')` reads the body as it is. It is not checked yet. [Step 4](04-validation.md) fixes that.

## 2. Add the routes

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (ApiController c) => c.pong);

    Route.resource('posts', PostController);
  }
}
```

`PostController` is the class. Dox gets the controller from the container.
You do not add the router to a list. Dox finds every `Router` class by itself.

`Route.resource` makes one route for each method the controller has:

| Method | Path | Controller method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/posts` | `index` |
| `POST` | `/api/posts` | `store` |
| `GET` | `/api/posts/{id}` | `show` |

The controller has no `update` or `destroy`, so those routes are not made.

## 3. Start the server

```bash
dox s
```

If it is already running, it restarts by itself when you save a file.

## Check it

Make a post:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post."}'
```

```text

content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...

{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z"}
```

List the posts:

```bash

```

```json

```

Show one post:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/posts/1
```

```json

```

A post that does not exist:

```bash

```

```text

...

```

# Step 4: Validation

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/04-validation/

# Step 4: Validation

This step checks the input of create and update with a `@Dto` class.

Bad input gets a `422` answer, and the controller does not run.

## 1. Make the DTO

```bash
dox make:dto SavePost
```

One class is enough for create and update, because both need the same fields.
Replace the file with this:

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'save_post.dto.g.dart';

/// Typed, checked input. Run `dox build_runner:build` after a change.
@Dto()
class SavePost {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;

  const SavePost({required this.title, required this.body});

  static const DtoSchema<SavePost> schema = $SavePostDto;
}
```

- A field that is not nullable and has no default is required.
- The rules run from top to bottom. `@Trim()` removes spaces first. An empty string then counts as missing.
- See [Validation](../the-basic/validation.md) for all rules.

## 2. Give the DTO list to the app

The generator writes a list of all DTOs to `lib/generated/dtos.g.dart`.
Dox needs this list, because it does not use reflection.
Add two lines to `lib/config/app.dart`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:blog/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  /// DTOs (generated list in lib/generated/dtos.g.dart)
  dtos: dtos,

  // ... the rest stays the same
);
```

## 3. Use the DTO in the controller

Ask for `SavePost` as a parameter. Dox checks the body and gives you a typed object.
This also adds `update`, so `PUT /api/posts/{id}` works:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class PostController {
  /// GET /api/posts
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  /// POST /api/posts
  Future<DoxResponse> store(SavePost body) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// GET /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> show(int id) async {
    return _find(id);
  }

  /// PUT /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> update(int id, SavePost body) async {
    Post post = await _find(id);
    post
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return post;
  }

  Future<Post> _find(int id) async {
    Post? post = await Post().find(id);
    if (post == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return post;
  }
}
```

`Route.resource` in `lib/routes/api.dart` sees the new `update` method and adds `PUT` and `PATCH /api/posts/{id}`. You change nothing there.

## 4. Run the generator

`dox s` runs it for you. Without `dox s`:

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

It writes `lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.g.dart` and `lib/generated/dtos.g.dart`.

## Check it

A title that is too short, and a body that is too short:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hi","body":"Short"}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...

{"title":"The title must be between 3 and 100 characters","body":"The body must be at least 10 characters"}
```

An empty body:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
```

```json
{"title":"The title is required","body":"The body is required"}
```

Good input still gives `201`:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Second post","body":"Validation works now."}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
```

Update the first post:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:3000/api/posts/1 \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hello Dox (edited)","body":"My first post, edited."}'
```

```json
{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox (edited)","body":"My first post, edited.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:59:13.539886Z"}
```

# Step 5: Login with dox_auth

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/05-auth/

# Step 5: Login with dox_auth

This step adds register and login with a JWT token, and only lets a logged in user create or change posts.

## 1. Add the package

```bash
dart pub add dox_auth
```

## 2. Make the users table

The template already has a `User` model in `lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart`:

```dart title="lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users', softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}
```

`password` is in `hidden`, so it is never in the JSON. This matters: the token holds the user as JSON, and anyone can read a JWT.

The `users` table already exists. The template has its migration, and the
server ran it at the first start in [step 1](01-create-project.md):

```dart title="db/migration/2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table.dart"
class CreateUsersTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('name');
      table.string('email').unique();
      table.string('password');
      table.softDeletes();
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }
  // ...
}
```

`table.softDeletes()` makes the `deleted_at` column that `softDelete: true` needs.
`email` is unique, so a second register with the same email fails.

## 3. Make the DTOs

```bash
dox make:dto RegisterUser
dox make:dto LoginUser
```

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

part 'register_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class RegisterUser {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 2, max: 50)
  final String name;

  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  @Unique('users', column: 'email')
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  const RegisterUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<RegisterUser> schema = $RegisterUserDto;
}
```

`@Unique` comes from `dox_orm`. It reads the database, so it runs after the other rules.
`dox_orm` also has a class named `Schema`, so the import hides it.

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'login_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class LoginUser {
  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  final String email;

  final String password;

  const LoginUser({required this.email, required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<LoginUser> schema = $LoginUserDto;
}
```

## 4. Set up the auth provider

A provider runs once in every isolate at start. This one tells `dox_auth` which model to use and how to sign tokens:

```dart title="lib/providers/auth_provider.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:blog/config/env.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Auth provider
/// --------------------------
/// Sets up JWT login with the User model.
/// Tokens are signed with APP_KEY and last 7 days.
class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(
      AuthConfig(
        defaultGuard: 'api',
        guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
          'api': AuthGuard(
            driver: JwtAuthDriver(
              secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
              expiresIn: const Duration(days: 7),
            ),
            provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
          ),
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}
```

Dox finds the provider by itself. Run `dart run build_runner build` and it is in `lib/generated/container.g.dart`.
You do not add it to a list.

## 5. Write the auth controller

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class AuthController {
  /// POST /api/auth/register
  Future<DoxResponse> register(RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    String? token = Auth().login(user);
    return response(<String, dynamic>{
      'token': token,
      'user': user,
    }).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/login
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> login(LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth();
    String? token = await auth.attempt(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (token == null) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': auth.user<User>()};
  }

  /// GET /api/auth/user
  User? user(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }
}
```

- `Hash.makeAsync()` makes a bcrypt hash. It runs in another isolate, so other requests do not wait. Never save a plain password.
- `Auth().attempt()` finds the user by email and checks the password. It gives a token, or `null`.
- `Auth().login(user)` gives a token without a password check. Register uses it, because the user was just made.

## 6. Protect the write routes

Replace `Route.resource` with single routes. The routes inside `Route.middleware` need a valid token:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (ApiController c) => c.pong);

    // Anyone can read posts.
    Route.get('/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
    Route.get('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.show);

    // Register and log in.
    Route.post('/auth/register', (AuthController c) => c.register);
    Route.post('/auth/login', (AuthController c) => c.login);

    // Only a logged in user can write posts.
    Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () {
      Route.get('/auth/user', (AuthController c) => c.user);
      Route.post('/posts', (PostController c) => c.store);
      Route.put('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.update);
    });
  }
}
```

`AuthMiddleware` reads the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header and loads the user.
When the token is missing or wrong, it answers `401 Authentication failed`.
On a public route, `AuthMiddleware(optional: true)` loads the user when there is a good token, and lets guests through.

## 7. Run the generator

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

`dox s` runs it for you. There is no new migration in this step, because the `users` table already exists.

## Check it

Register:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/register \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...

{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...","user":{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z"}}
```

The same email again gives `422`:

```json
{"email":"The email has already been taken"}
```

A wrong password gives `401`:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ann@example.com","password":"wrong"}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
...

{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}
```

Log in and keep the token in a shell variable:

```bash
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  | sed -E 's/.*"token":"([^"]+)".*/\1/')
echo $TOKEN
```

A post without a token is refused:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Third post","body":"Written with a token."}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
...

{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}
```

With the token it works:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Third post","body":"Written with a token."}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
...

{"id":3,"title":"Third post","body":"Written with a token.","created_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:08.094211Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:08.094211Z"}
```

Who am I:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/auth/user -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

```json
{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z"}
```

No `password` in the answer, because it is in `hidden`.

# Step 6: Test

# Step 6: Test

This step writes one HTTP test for the list route and runs it.

## 1. Write the test

The template has `test/http_test.dart`. Replace it with this:

```dart title="test/http_test.dart"
import 'package:blog/config/app.dart';
import 'package:blog/config/database.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/posts gives a list', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/posts');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectJson(isA<List<dynamic>>());
  });
}
```

- `DoxTestClient.start` runs the app inside the test, on a free port. It does not clash with `dox s`.
- It runs the migrations first, so the test also works on an empty database.
- `package:test` is already in `dev_dependencies` of the template.

## Check it

```bash
dart test test/http_test.dart
```

```text
00:01 +1: All tests passed!
```

!!! tip "Use another database for tests"
    The test uses the `.env` file, so it reads and writes `db/dox.sqlite`.
    To keep test data out of it, make a `.env.testing` file with `DB_NAME=test.sqlite`.
    `dart test` reads it on top of `.env`.

# Step 7: Build and deploy

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/07-build-and-deploy/

# Step 7: Build and deploy

This step compiles the app to one native binary, runs it, and shows the `Dockerfile` of the project.

!!! warning "Never run production with `dox s` or `dart run`"
    They use the JIT compiler. It needs about 25 times more memory and starts slower.
    Build a native (AOT) binary for production.

## 1. Build the binary

```bash
dox build
```

```text
Built with build_runner/aot in 1s; wrote 0 outputs.
Running build hooks...Running link hooks...
Generated: /.../blog/build/bundle/bin/server
[Dox] Built build/bundle. Run it with: cd build/bundle && ./bin/server
```

`dox build` runs the code generator, then `dart build cli`. The result is in `build/bundle`:

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `bin/server` | the binary, about 10 MB. It needs no Dart SDK. |
| `bin/queue` | the [queue worker](../digging-deeper/queue.md). Run it as its own process. |
| `bin/schedule` | the [scheduler](../digging-deeper/scheduler.md). Run it as its own process. |
| `lib/` | native libraries from build hooks, like `libsqlite3`. Keep it next to `bin/`. |
| `db/` | your migrations. Your local SQLite file is not copied. |
| `.env.example` | a copy of the example env file. |

## 2. Run the binary

The binary reads `.env` from the folder you start it in. Copy yours there.
The `db` folder for the SQLite file is already in `build/bundle`.

```bash
cd build/bundle
cp ../../.env .env
./bin/server
```

```text
Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_25_000000000_create_queue_tables
Migrated: 2026_10_25_000000000_create_queue_tables
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
... "message":"Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 8 isolate (native)" ...
```

The migrations run again, because `db/dox.sqlite` is a new file in `build/bundle`.
The migration list is compiled into the binary, so no source code is needed.
On a server you can skip `.env` and set real environment variables. They win over `.env`.

## Check it

In a second terminal:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/ping
curl http://localhost:3000/api/posts
```

```text
pong
[]
```

The list is empty, because this is a new database file. Stop the server with `Ctrl+C`.

## 3. Docker

The project has a `Dockerfile`. It builds the same bundle and copies it to an empty (`scratch`) image:

```dockerfile title="Dockerfile"
FROM dart:stable AS build

# Resolve dependencies first, so this layer is cached.
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get

COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline

# The dox CLI. `dox build` runs build_runner, then AOT-compiles
# bin/server.dart, bin/queue.dart and bin/schedule.dart with
# `dart build cli`. It puts all of them in build/bundle/bin, the native
# libraries in build/bundle/lib and the migrations in build/bundle/db.
# The queue worker and the scheduler run as their own processes:
# `/app/bin/queue work` and `/app/bin/schedule work`.
ARG DOX_VERSION=^3.2.0
RUN dart pub global activate dox "$DOX_VERSION"
RUN /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build

# Lay out the final file tree:
# /app/bin/server, /app/bin/queue, /app/bin/schedule, /app/lib (native
# libraries), /app/db/migration, /app/storage and a writable /tmp
# (uploads bigger than 1 MB are streamed to a temp file).
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  # the native HTTP server (Rust) needs libgcc_s, which /runtime/ does not have
  && LIBGCC=$(find / -name libgcc_s.so.1 -path '*lib*' | head -n 1) \
  && mkdir -p /out$(dirname $LIBGCC) && cp $LIBGCC /out$LIBGCC

# Minimal serving image: the AOT runtime files from the dart image
# (`/runtime/`) plus our bundle. No Dart SDK, no source code.
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app

# Config comes from env variables. The image has no .env file,
# so secrets stay out of it.
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]
```

Build and run it. The image has no `.env` file, so pass the config as environment variables.
`APP_KEY` must be exactly 32 characters. The app does not start with a shorter or longer key.

```bash
docker build -t blog .
docker run -p 3000:3000 \
  -e APP_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 16) \
  -e DB_CONNECTION=sqlite \
  -e DB_NAME=storage/blog.sqlite \
  blog
```

!!! note "SQLite in Docker"
    The database file lives inside the container. It is lost when the container is removed.
    Mount a volume for it: `-v blog-data:/app/storage`.
    For a busy app, use Postgres or MySQL. See [Database](../database/index.md).

- [Deployment](../digging-deeper/deployment.md): HTTPS with a proxy, systemd, many machines.
- [Model](../database/model/index.md): relationships and events.

- [Authentication](../security/authentication.md): all options of `dox_auth`.
- [OpenAPI](../packages/openapi.md): API docs from your routes and DTOs.

# How Dox works

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/concepts/how-dox-works/

# How Dox works

This page explains what happens inside Dox when a request comes in, how isolates work and what each folder of an app is for.

## The life of a request

Dox has two parts:

- A native server, written in Rust (`dox_http_native`). It owns the sockets and parses HTTP.
- Your app, written in Dart. Routes, middleware, DTOs, controllers and the ORM all run here.

A request goes through these steps:

1. Rust accepts the connection and reads the request. It parses the HTTP request line, the headers and the body.
   A bad request gets `400`. Headers over 16 KB get `431`. A body over the size limit gets `413`. Dart never sees these requests.
2. Rust hands the requests to Dart in a batch. One message holds many requests.
3. Dart finds the route. It matches the method, the `Host` (for domain routes) and the path.
   A plain path is a map lookup. A path with `{params}` is a pattern match.
   No match gives `404`. A CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`) gets `204`.
4. Dart adds the CORS headers of the route.
5. Dart reads the body, only when the request has a `Content-Type`. A request without a body skips this step.
6. Dart runs the middleware list of the route, in this order: global middleware, router middleware, group middleware, route middleware.
   A middleware returns the request to go on. Anything else is sent as the response, and the controller does not run.
7. Dart fills the controller parameters. Path params are converted first. A value that does not fit its type (`abc` for `int id`) gets `404`.
   Then the DTO is read and checked. Bad input gets `422`. A body that is not JSON gets `400`. A content type Dox can not read gets `415`.
8. The controller runs and returns a value.
9. The `responseHandler` from `AppConfig` runs, when you set one. It can change every response.
10. Dox turns the value into the response: a `String` is text, a `Map` or model is JSON, a `File` is streamed.
11. Dart sends the answers of the batch back to Rust in one call. Rust writes the bytes to the socket.

When a step throws, Dox catches the error. An `IHttpException` (like `NotFoundHttpException`) gives its own status.
Any other error gives `500` and goes to the `report` method of the `ExceptionHandler` in `AppConfig`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant R as Rust (dox_http_native)
    participant D as Dart isolate
    participant M as Middleware
    participant K as Controller

    C->>R: TCP connection, HTTP request
    R->>R: parse request, check size limits
    R->>D: batch of requests (one message)
    D->>D: router: method, host, path
    D->>D: CORS headers, read body
    D->>M: global, router, group, route middleware
    M-->>D: request (go on) or a response
    D->>D: path params, DTO check
    D->>K: call with typed parameters
    K-->>D: return value
    D->>D: responseHandler, build the response
    D->>R: batch of answers (one call)
    R->>C: bytes
```

!!! note "No reflection"
    Dox reads the parameter types of every controller once, at start.
    It does not use `dart:mirrors`. DTOs come from a generated list (`lib/generated/dtos.g.dart`).
    This is why `dox build` can make a native (AOT) binary.

### Where things are decided

| Step | Code | What it decides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Route match | `lib/routes/*.dart`, `Route.get(...)` | which controller runs |
| Middleware | `AppConfig(globalMiddleware:)`, `Router.middleware`, `Route.middleware(...)`, the route list | go on, or answer early |
| Input | a `@Dto` class in `lib/app/dtos/<name>/` | what the controller gets, or `422` |
| Output | the return value, `response(...)`, `responseHandler` | status, headers, body |
| Errors | `IHttpException`, `AppConfig(exceptionHandler:)` | the error response, logging |

See [Routing](../the-basic/routing.md), [Middleware](../the-basic/middleware.md),
[Validation](../the-basic/validation.md) and [Response](../the-basic/response.md).

## Isolates

Dart runs code on isolates. An isolate is like a thread, but it has its own memory.
Dox starts one isolate per CPU core (`Platform.numberOfProcessors`). Every isolate runs the full app.

### One port, many isolates

Every isolate runs its own HTTP server on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections.

| System | Native server |
| --- | --- |
| Linux | one socket per isolate (`SO_REUSEPORT`) |
| macOS | the isolates share one socket |
| Windows | only one isolate serves HTTP |

Each isolate does its own socket work on its own thread. See [Native server](../digging-deeper/native-server.md#how-it-works).

### What each isolate gets

Before it starts an isolate, Dox copies three things to it:

- the `AppConfig`,
- the list of providers,
- the routes and route binders (`Route.bind`) you added before `startServer()`.

Then each isolate does this, once:

1. It runs `setup()` of every provider, in list order. This is where a database pool is opened.
2. It registers the routes of your routers.
3. It reads the parameter types of every controller.
4. It starts its HTTP server.

Nothing in this list runs per request.

Because the config and the providers are copied, they must not hold open sockets or pools.
Open these in `setup()`. See [Providers](../digging-deeper/providers.md).

### Each isolate has its own memory

- A static value or a singleton exists once per isolate. A change in one isolate is not seen in the others.
- The `memory` cache store is per isolate. Use the `redis` store to share cache data.
- To share data between isolates, use the database, Redis or files.
- `Dox().isolateId` tells you which isolate runs the code. The first one is `1`.

### When an isolate crashes

- An error in a request is caught. Dox answers `500` and keeps going.
- An async error outside a request is caught and passed to the `ExceptionHandler`. The isolate keeps running.
- When a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints `[dox] isolate N exited, restarting` and starts a new one after 1 second.
- When the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. A supervisor (Docker `restart:`, systemd `Restart=always`) must start it again.

### How many isolates

Set `totalIsolate` in `AppConfig`, or `APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE` in `.env`. In code, `Dox().totalIsolate(2)` before `startServer()` wins over the config.
Use `1` in tests. See [Isolate](../digging-deeper/isolate.md).

## Where the database pools live

The ORM is started in a provider (`ORMProvider`). Every isolate runs `setup()`, so every isolate opens a pool.
The native drivers live in Rust. There, isolates that open the same settings get the same pool.

| Driver | Per isolate | Per process |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres native (`dox_postgres_native`) | nothing | one pool of `maxConnectionCount` connections per settings, and one Rust runtime (`extra['threads']`, default `1`) |
| MySQL native (`dox_mysql_native`) | nothing | one pool of `maxConnectionCount` connections per settings, and one Rust runtime |
| SQLite | one connection | nothing shared |

So for Postgres and MySQL, the app opens at most `maxConnectionCount` connections, for any number of isolates.
The pool size is always your choice. Set it below the `max_connections` of the database.

The pool closes when the last isolate that uses it closes it.
See [Native Postgres driver](../database/postgres-native.md#options).

Postgres and MySQL have only the native drivers. When the native library does not load, the app stops with an error that says why and how to fix it. See [Database](../database/index.md).

## The layout of a Dox app

`dox create my_app` copies the [dox-sample](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-sample) template. It looks like this:

```text
my_app/
├── bin/
│   ├── server.dart          # starts the app
│   ├── migrate.dart         # runs the migrations (dox migration:*)
│   ├── seed.dart            # runs the seeders (dox db:seed)
│   ├── queue.dart           # the queue worker (dox queue:*)
│   └── schedule.dart        # the scheduler (dox schedule:*)
├── db/
│   ├── factories/           # model factories, *.factory.dart
│   ├── migration/           # migrations (.dart with a registry, or .sql)
│   └── seeders/             # seeders, *.seeder.dart
├── lib/
│   ├── app/
│   │   ├── http/
│   │   │   └── controllers/     # *.controller.dart
│   │   ├── jobs/                # queue jobs, *.job.dart
│   │   └── models/              # one folder per model, *.model.dart
│   ├── config/
│   │   ├── app.dart             # AppConfig: port, isolates, middleware
│   │   ├── cache.dart           # cache stores
│   │   ├── cors.dart
│   │   ├── database.dart        # DatabaseConfig: connections
│   │   ├── env.dart             # typed env class (@DoxEnv)
│   │   ├── logger.dart
│   │   ├── queue.dart           # QueueConfig
│   │   ├── schedule.dart        # ScheduleConfig and your tasks
│   │   └── storage.dart         # storage disks
│   ├── routes/
│   │   ├── api.dart             # ApiRouter, prefix `api`
│   │   └── web.dart             # WebRouter
│   ├── providers/               # one DoxProvider per file, runs in every isolate
│   │   ├── orm_provider.dart        # opens the database
│   │   ├── queue_provider.dart
│   │   ├── schedule_provider.dart
│   │   └── storage_provider.dart
│   └── generated/               # made by build_runner, do not edit
│       ├── container.g.dart     # @Inject classes, routers, providers
│       ├── jobs.g.dart          # the list of queue jobs
│       └── openapi.g.dart       # the OpenAPI docs
├── test/
├── .env                         # local settings, not in git. `dox create` makes it
├── .env.example
├── Dockerfile
├── docker-compose.yml
└── pubspec.yaml
```

The `dox make:*` commands add more folders when you need them:

- `dox make:dto` adds `lib/app/dtos/<name>/<name>.dto.dart`. Then `build_runner` writes `lib/generated/dtos.g.dart`, the list of DTOs.
- `dox make:middleware` adds `lib/app/http/middleware/`.
- `dox make:serializer` adds `lib/app/serializers/`.

The app makes `storage/` when it writes files (the local disk, the file cache, uploads).

| Folder | What goes there |
| --- | --- |
| `bin/` | `server.dart` calls `Dox().initialize(appConfig)`, runs the migrations, then `Dox().startServer()`. The other files are the entry points that the `dox migration:*`, `db:seed`, `queue:*` and `schedule:*` commands run. |
| `db/` | Your migrations, factories and seeders. Dart migrations are listed in `db/migration/migrations.dart`, which the CLI writes. |
| `lib/app/http/` | Everything about HTTP: controllers and middleware. |
| `lib/app/serializers/` | Serializers. They are not only for HTTP: MCP and websocket use them too. |
| `lib/app/dtos/` | One folder per DTO: typed and checked input. |
| `lib/app/jobs/` | Queue jobs. |
| `lib/app/models/` | One folder per model. `build_runner` writes the `.g.dart` file next to it. |
| `lib/config/` | One file per config object. `app.dart` puts them together in `AppConfig`. |
| `lib/routes/` | One `Router` class per file. Dox finds each router by itself. |
| `lib/providers/` | Classes that extend `DoxProvider`. Their `setup()` runs in every isolate. Dox finds each provider by itself. |
| `lib/generated/` | Generated files. Do not edit them. Run `dox build_runner:build` to make them again. |
| `storage/` | Files the app writes: uploads, the file cache, SQLite files. |

`build_runner` with `dox_builder` makes the model classes, the DTO checks, the typed env class, the OpenAPI docs and the list of queue jobs.
