# Inertia

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/inertia/

# Inertia

Inertia lets you build a single page app with React, Vue or Svelte, and keep routes and controllers in Dox.

You do not write an API. A controller gives a page name and its props. Inertia shows the page in the browser.
The first visit gets a full HTML page. After that, links and forms get only JSON, and the page changes without a reload.

The `dox_inertia` package is the server side of Inertia. Use it with the Inertia 3 client for your front-end (`@inertiajs/react`, `@inertiajs/vue3` or `@inertiajs/svelte`, version 3) and Vite.

## Install

```bash
dox add inertia
```

It adds the package and does steps 1 to 3 of [Set it up by hand](#set-it-up-by-hand) (root view, config, provider).
Then do steps 4 to 6 (Vite, the built files and the middleware) yourself. It prints a short list of them.
It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

## Set it up by hand

```bash
dart pub add dox_inertia
```

### 1. Root view

The root view is the HTML page of the first visit. Dox puts the script and style tags in place of `@vite`, and the page in place of `@inertia`. It is plain HTML, with no template engine. It can hold `{{ key }}` marks for values like the title, see [Root view data](#root-view-data).

```html title="resources/views/app.html"
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>My app</title>
    @vite
  </head>
  <body>
    @inertia
  </body>
</html>
```

`@inertia` becomes the page data and the element the app renders into:

```html
<script data-page="app" type="application/json">{"component":"Home",...}</script><div id="app"></div>
```

This is the format of the Inertia 3 client. In the JSON, `<`, `>` and `&` are written as `\u003c`, `\u003e` and `\u0026`, so a prop can not end the script tag.

### 2. Config

```dart title="lib/config/inertia.dart"
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  /// the Vite entry files
  entryPoints: <String>['resources/js/app.jsx'],

  /// load the scripts from the Vite dev server. null in production.
  devServerUrl: 'http://localhost:5173',

  /// add the React Fast Refresh code in dev mode
  reactRefresh: true,
);
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rootView` | `resources/views/app.html` | the HTML page of the first visit. One request can use another file with `Inertia.setRootView` |
| `entryPoints` | `['resources/js/app.js']` | the Vite entry files |
| `publicPath` | `public` | the folder of public files |
| `buildDirectory` | `build` | the folder in `publicPath` where `vite build` writes its files |
| `devServerUrl` | `null` | the url of the Vite dev server, see [Vite](#vite) |
| `reactRefresh` | `false` | add the React Fast Refresh code in dev mode |
| `version` | hash of the manifest | the asset version, see [Asset version](#asset-version) |
| `encryptHistory` | `false` | encrypt the browser history of every page, see [History encryption](#history-encryption) |
| `ssr` | `null` | server side rendering, see [SSR](#server-side-rendering-ssr) |

Paths are from the project root, where the app runs.

### 3. Provider

The provider sets up Inertia in every isolate. Put it in `lib/` so the generated container finds it.

```dart title="lib/providers/inertia_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

import '../config/inertia.dart';

class AppInertiaProvider extends InertiaProvider {
  AppInertiaProvider() : super(inertiaConfig);
}
```

With no provider, Dox uses the defaults of `InertiaConfig`.

### 4. Vite

```js title="vite.config.js"
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'

export default defineConfig(({ command }) => ({
  plugins: [react()],
  // public/ holds the Dox public files. The build goes into public/build,
  // so do not let Vite copy public/ into the build.
  publicDir: false,
  // the built files are served from /build/
  base: command === 'build' ? '/build/' : '/',
  server: { origin: 'http://localhost:5173' },
  build: {
    manifest: true,
    outDir: 'public/build',
    rollupOptions: { input: 'resources/js/app.jsx' },
  },
}))
```

```jsx title="resources/js/app.jsx"
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'

createInertiaApp({
  resolve: (name) => {
    const pages = import.meta.glob('./Pages/**/*.jsx', { eager: true })
    return pages[`./Pages/${name}.jsx`]
  },
  setup({ el, App, props }) {
    createRoot(el).render(<App {...props} />)
  },
})
```

### 5. Serve the built files

In production the browser loads `/build/assets/...`. Add a route for them, or let your proxy (nginx, Caddy) serve `public/build`.

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
Route.get('/build/{path*}', (String path) {
  if (path.contains('..')) throw NotFoundHttpException();
  // the file names have a hash, so the browser can keep them for a year
  return response(File('public/build/$path')).cache(const Duration(days: 365));
});
```

### 6. Middleware

Add three middleware to `globalMiddleware`, in this order:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(),
    HandleInertiaRequests(),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

- `SessionMiddleware` gives each request a session. Inertia uses it for validation errors and flash data.
- `CsrfMiddleware` stops cross site form posts. It sets the `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie. The Inertia client reads it and sends it back in the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header. You do not write any code for this.
- `HandleInertiaRequests` is your `InertiaMiddleware`, see [Shared props](#shared-props). With no props to share, use `const InertiaMiddleware()`.

You can also add them to a router, in the same order, if only some routes are Inertia pages.

## Render a page

Give the request, the page name and the props. The page name is the file in `resources/js/Pages`, without the extension.

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  Future<DoxResponse> index(DoxRequest req) {
    return inertia(req, 'Users/Index', <String, dynamic>{
      'title': 'Users',
      'users': () => User().query().all(),
    });
  }
}
```

- A normal request gets the root view as HTML.
- An Inertia request (`X-Inertia: true`) gets the page as JSON, with `X-Inertia: true` and `Vary: X-Inertia`.

A prop can be a function, like `users` above. It runs only when the prop is sent. It can give a `Future`.
Props become JSON. A model or any object with `toJson()` works. A `DateTime` becomes ISO text.
A Dart `int` above 2^53 in a prop loses precision. JavaScript reads the page JSON, in the browser and on the SSR server. Send such a number as a string.

`Inertia.render(req, 'Users/Index', {...})` does the same as `inertia(...)`.

## Shared props

Shared props go to every page, like the signed in user or the app name. Extend `InertiaMiddleware` and add it to `globalMiddleware` (see [Middleware](#6-middleware)).

```dart title="lib/app/http/middleware/handle_inertia_requests.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

class HandleInertiaRequests extends InertiaMiddleware {
  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> share(DoxRequest req) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'appName': 'My app',
      'auth': () => req.auth?.toJson(),
    };
  }
}
```

A page prop with the same name wins over a shared prop. `share` can be `async`.
The page lists the names of the shared props in `sharedProps`. The client keeps them on an instant visit.
You can also share from any middleware or controller with `Inertia.share(req, {...})`.

For a value that is the same for the whole app, use `Inertia.shareGlobal(key, value)`. Call it once in the `setup()` of your `InertiaProvider`, so it runs in every isolate:

```dart
class AppInertiaProvider extends InertiaProvider {
  AppInertiaProvider() : super(inertiaConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    Inertia.shareGlobal('appName', 'Dox');
  }
}
```

A global value is kept for all users and all requests. Use it only for a constant, or a function that does not read a request. Data of one user, like the signed in user, must go in `InertiaMiddleware.share`. A prop shared for the request wins over a global one.

## Partial reloads

The client can ask for some props only: `router.reload({ only: ['users'] })`. Dox reads the headers and sends only those props. Function props that are not sent do not run.

Four helpers change when a prop is sent:

```dart
return inertia(req, 'Users/Index', <String, dynamic>{
  /// only when a partial reload asks for it
  'stats': Inertia.optional(() => Stats.load()),

  /// on every request, also on a partial reload that does not ask for it
  'notices': Inertia.always(notices),

  /// not on the first visit: the page loads it right after
  'comments': Inertia.defer(() => Comment().query().all()),
  'likes': Inertia.defer(() => Like().query().count(), group: 'side'),

  /// deferred, and the page adds the new items to the old ones
  'feed': Inertia.defer(() => Post().query().all()).merge(),

  /// the page adds the new items to the old ones (infinite scroll)
  'posts': Inertia.merge(posts),
});
```

| Helper | First visit | Partial reload |
| --- | --- | --- |
| plain value or function | sent | sent when asked |
| `Inertia.optional` | not sent | sent when asked |
| `Inertia.always` | sent | always sent |
| `Inertia.defer` | not sent, listed in `deferredProps` | sent when asked |
| `Inertia.merge` | sent, listed in `mergeProps` | sent when asked |

Deferred props of the same `group` load in one request. The default group is `default`.
`Inertia.lazy` is the same as `Inertia.optional`.
A deferred prop with `.merge()` (or `merge: true`) is also listed in `mergeProps` when it is sent.

## Forms and validation errors

A form post needs no extra code for errors. The flow is:

1. The page posts the form: `router.post('/users', data)` or `useForm`.
2. The controller validates. The validation fails.
3. Dox flashes the errors and the old input to the session, and redirects back.
4. The page loads again. It gets the errors in the `errors` prop.

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
  await req.validateSchema(
    v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
      'name': v.string().min(2),
      'email': v.string().email(),
    }),
  );
  // ... save the user
  return redirect('/users');
}
```

```jsx
const { data, setData, post, errors } = useForm({ name: '', email: '' })
// errors.email holds the message, or is undefined
```

Every page gets `errors`. It is `{}` when there are no errors. It is sent on every request, also on a partial reload.
The old input is in `req.session.old('email')`. Password fields are not kept.

With `router.post(url, data, { errorBag: 'login' })` or `form.post(url, { errorBag: 'login' })`, the client sends the `X-Inertia-Error-Bag` header. Then the errors are under the bag name: `errors.login.email`. Use it when one page has two forms.

You do not need to pass `errors` yourself. A page prop named `errors` still wins.

## Redirects

After a form, redirect with `redirect(url)` or `back(req)` from Dox.

After `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`, the browser must follow the redirect with `GET`, not with the same method. So `InertiaMiddleware` turns a `302` into `303` for these Inertia requests. You do not need to do anything.

When a controller gives an empty `200` answer to an Inertia request (eg. it returns nothing), `InertiaMiddleware` sends the browser back to the page it came from, like `back(req)`. Only a `Referer` of the same site is used. Any other `Referer` goes to `/`. A request without `X-Inertia` gets the empty answer as it is.

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> update(DoxRequest req, int id) async {
  // ... save the user
  return redirect('/users'); // 303 for an Inertia PUT
}
```

To go to an outside site, or any page that is not an Inertia page, use `Inertia.location`. An Inertia request gets `409` with `X-Inertia-Location`, and the client loads the url with a full page load. Other requests get `302`.

```dart
return Inertia.location(req, 'https://checkout.example.com/pay/1');
```

## Flash data

Flash data is a short message for the next page, like "User saved". Use `Inertia.flash`. The next page gets it in `page.flash`, once.

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
  // ... save the user
  Inertia.flash(req, 'message', 'User saved');
  return redirect('/users');
}
```

```jsx
import { usePage } from '@inertiajs/react'

const { flash } = usePage()
// flash.message is 'User saved'
```

The client also fires a `flash` event, and calls the `onFlash` callback of the visit.
`Inertia.flash` needs `SessionMiddleware`.

## Vite

In dev mode, `@vite` loads `@vite/client` and the entry files from the Vite dev server. With `reactRefresh: true` it adds the React Fast Refresh code first.

Dox is in dev mode when:

- `devServerUrl` is set, or
- the file `public/hot` exists. Its text is the dev server url. Some Vite plugins write this file while `vite` runs. Dox ignores this file only when `APP_ENV` is `production` (in any case, like `Production`), and prints a warning. Other values, like `staging` or an empty value, still use it.

In production (no dev server), Dox reads `public/build/.vite/manifest.json`. `@vite` gives a `<link>` tag for the css of each entry and of the chunks it imports, and a `<script type="module">` tag for each entry.

Set `devServerUrl` from the env, so production does not use it:

```dart title="lib/config/inertia.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  entryPoints: <String>['resources/js/app.jsx'],
  devServerUrl: Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'development'
      ? 'http://localhost:5173'
      : null,
  reactRefresh: true,
);
```

## Asset version

Each page has a version. When you deploy new assets, the version changes. A browser with the old version that makes an Inertia `GET` request gets `409` with `X-Inertia-Location`. The client then loads the whole page again, with the new assets.

The default version is a hash of the Vite manifest. Dox reads it once per isolate, so restart the server after `vite build` (a deploy does this). To set your own, use `version` in the config, eg. the git commit.

## Root view data

Page props go to the JavaScript page. Sometimes the root view itself needs a value, like the `<title>` or a CSRF meta tag. Use `Inertia.withViewData` for that.

Write `{{ key }}` in the root view:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="csrf-token" content="{{ csrfToken }}">
    <title>{{ title }}</title>
    @vite
  </head>
  <body>
    @inertia
  </body>
</html>
```

Set the values in the controller:

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> index(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.withViewData(req, <String, Object?>{'title': 'Users'});
  return inertia(req, 'Users/Index', <String, dynamic>{
    'users': () => User().query().all(),
  });
}
```

- The values are for the root view only. They are not page props. They are never sent as JSON, so an Inertia request (a link or a form) does not get them.
- Each value is HTML escaped (`&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'`). A `null` value gives empty text.
- Put a value in text or in a quoted attribute only. It is not safe inside a `<script>` block, an unquoted attribute or a link address.
- You can call `withViewData` many times, also in a middleware. The data is merged. For the same key, the last call wins.
- A key has letters, digits and `_`. The spaces are optional: `{{title}}` works too.
- `{{ key }}` with a key that you did not set stays as it is. So set every key that the root view uses.
- `{{ csrfToken }}` is filled for you with the CSRF token of the session. It needs `SessionMiddleware`. With no session it stays as it is. Your own `csrfToken` value wins.
- Only `{{ key }}` in the root view file is replaced. The same text in a prop, or in the HTML from the SSR server, is not touched.

A title set this way is for the first page load only. On later visits the browser does not load the root view again. There, the `<Head>` component of the Inertia client changes the title. So set the title in `<Head>` too. With SSR, the `<Head>` title is also added to the first page, so use only one of the two for the title.

### Another root view for some pages

`Inertia.setRootView` uses another HTML file for one request, eg. for an admin area:

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> dashboard(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.setRootView(req, 'resources/views/admin.html');
  return inertia(req, 'Admin/Dashboard');
}
```

`RootViewMiddleware` does the same for every page of a router:

```dart
class AdminRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[
    const RootViewMiddleware('resources/views/admin.html'),
  ];

  // ...
}
```

The path is from the project root, like `rootView` in the config. Use a fixed path. Never pass a value from the request: it could show any file of the server as the page. The file works like the default root view, with `@vite`, `@inertia` and `{{ key }}`.

## History encryption

The browser keeps the props of each page in its history, so the back button is fast. After a logout, the back button can still show a page with private data. History encryption stops this.

With it, the browser encrypts the page data before it goes into the history. The key stays in the browser, in session storage. When you clear the history, the browser makes a new key, and the old pages can not be read any more. The back button then asks the server for the page again.

The browser can only encrypt on HTTPS, and on `localhost`.

Turn it on for all pages in the config:

```dart title="lib/config/inertia.dart"
InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  encryptHistory: true,
);
```

Or for one page, in the controller. `false` turns it off for one page when the config turns it on.

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> show(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.encryptHistory(req);
  // Inertia.encryptHistory(req, false);
  return inertia(req, 'Account/Show', props);
}
```

Or for all pages of a router, with `EncryptHistoryMiddleware`:

```dart
class AccountRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[const EncryptHistoryMiddleware()];

  // ...
}
```

Call `Inertia.clearHistory(req)` to clear the history, for example on logout:

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> logout(DoxRequest req) async {
  // ... sign the user out
  Inertia.clearHistory(req);
  return redirect('/login');
}
```

The next Inertia page tells the browser to clear its history, once. The mark is kept in the session, so it works with a redirect. It needs `SessionMiddleware`. With no session, it only works when the same request renders a page with `inertia(...)`.

## Server side rendering (SSR)

By default, the first visit gets an empty page, and the browser renders it. With SSR, the first visit gets the full HTML of the page. Search engines can read it, and the visitor sees the page sooner.

The page is rendered by the Inertia SSR server. It is a Node process that you build with Vite and run next to your Dox app. On a first visit, Dox sends the page to it and puts the answer in the root view. Inertia requests (links and forms) never use it.

### 1. The SSR entry file

```jsx title="resources/js/ssr.jsx"
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'
import createServer from '@inertiajs/react/server'
import ReactDOMServer from 'react-dom/server'

createServer(
  (page) =>
    createInertiaApp({
      page,
      render: ReactDOMServer.renderToString,
      resolve: (name) => {
        const pages = import.meta.glob('./Pages/**/*.jsx', { eager: true })
        return pages[`./Pages/${name}.jsx`]
      },
      setup: ({ App, props }) => <App {...props} />,
    }),
  { host: '127.0.0.1' },
)
```

Vue and Svelte have the same `createServer`, in `@inertiajs/vue3/server` and `@inertiajs/svelte/server`.

The SSR server listens on port `13714`. Set `host` to `127.0.0.1`, so only your own machine can reach it.

### 2. Hydrate in the browser

The browser must reuse the HTML from the server, and not render the page again. Change `setup` in your app file:

```jsx title="resources/js/app.jsx"
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'
import { createRoot, hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client'

createInertiaApp({
  resolve: (name) => {
    const pages = import.meta.glob('./Pages/**/*.jsx', { eager: true })
    return pages[`./Pages/${name}.jsx`]
  },
  setup({ el, App, props }) {
    if (el.hasAttribute('data-server-rendered')) {
      hydrateRoot(el, <App {...props} />)
    } else {
      createRoot(el).render(<App {...props} />)
    }
  },
})
```

The `else` part is for a page that was sent without SSR.

### 3. Build and run

Build the browser files, then the SSR file. Then start the SSR server with Node.

```bash
vite build
vite build --ssr resources/js/ssr.jsx --outDir bootstrap/ssr
node bootstrap/ssr/ssr.js
```

The file is `ssr.js` when your `package.json` has `"type": "module"`. Else it is `ssr.mjs`.
The SSR file loads your packages from `node_modules`, so keep that folder on the server.
Keep the Node process running with your process manager, like the Dox app. Build and start it again on each deploy.

### 4. Turn it on

```dart title="lib/config/inertia.dart"
InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  entryPoints: <String>['resources/js/app.jsx'],
  ssr: InertiaSsr(),
);
```

With no `ssr`, SSR is off. `InertiaSsr` has two options:

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | `http://127.0.0.1:13714/render` | the render url of the SSR server |
| `timeout` | 2 seconds | how long Dox waits for the answer. Then it stops the request. |

The `url` must be a full `http` or `https` url. A wrong url gives an error when the app starts.

To use SSR only in production, set it from the env:

```dart
ssr: Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'production' ? InertiaSsr() : null,
```

### The root view with SSR

The root view needs no change. It must have `@inertia`. Head tags also need a `</head>` tag.

- The HTML from the SSR server goes in place of `@inertia`. It holds the page data and the rendered `<div id="app">`.
- The head tags of the page (from the `<Head>` component, like `<title>`) go right before the first `</head>`. `</HEAD>` works too. A root view with no `</head>` gets no head tags.

When your pages set a title with `<Head>`, remove the `<title>` from the root view, so the page does not have two.

### When the SSR server fails

When the SSR server is down, is too slow, or gives a bad answer, the visitor gets the normal page and the browser renders it. No error is shown. Dox prints one warning to stderr for the first failure, and no more until the SSR server works again.

## Not included

- The Inertia 1 and 2 clients. They read the page from `<div id="app" data-page="...">`. Use the Inertia 3 client.
- Once props, scroll props (infinite scroll), `prependProps`, `deepMergeProps` and `matchPropsOn`.
- Partial reloads of nested props with dots, like `only: ['auth.user']`. Ask for the top level prop (`auth`).
- Starting the SSR server from Dox. You run the Node process yourself.

Inertia needs [sessions](session.md) for the errors, flash data and redirects. The client sends the CSRF token by itself, see [CSRF](../security/csrf.md#axios-and-inertia).

# Serializer

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/serializer/

# Serializer

A serializer sets the JSON shape of a response: which keys the client gets, their names and their values.

It works with any Dart type: a model, a plain class, or a map.

!!! tip
    You do not always need a serializer.
    A controller can return a model, a `Map` or a `List` as it is. See [Response](response.md#return-a-value).
    To only hide some model fields, use [`hidden`](../database/model/index.md#hide-fields).

## Create a serializer

```bash
dox make:serializer Blog
```

This makes `lib/app/serializers/blog.serializer.dart`.
The file is for a model with the same name. Change the type to use it for something else.

## How it works

Extend `Serializer<T>` and write `convert`.
`convert` gets one value of type `T` and gives back one JSON object.

```dart title="lib/app/serializers/blog.serializer.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

import 'package:my_app/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart';

class BlogSerializer extends Serializer<Blog> {
  BlogSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Blog m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'uid': m.id,
      'title_en': m.title,
    };
  }
}
```

Return the serializer from a controller. Dox sends its `toJson()`.

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart"
class BlogController {
  Future<BlogSerializer> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    List<Blog> blogs = await Blog().all();
    return BlogSerializer(blogs); // a list
  }

  Future<BlogSerializer> show(DoxRequest req, String id) async {
    Blog? blog = await Blog().find(id);
    return BlogSerializer(blog); // one model
  }
}
```

The response of `show`:

```json
{
  "uid": 1,
  "title_en": "This is title"
}
```

What you give, and what the client gets:

| You give | The client gets |
| --- | --- |
| one value of type `T` | one JSON object |
| a `List<T>` | a JSON list (`[]` when the list is empty) |
| `null` (for example, `find` found nothing) | `null` |
| any other type | `null` |

!!! warning "The list type must be `List<T>`"
    A `List<dynamic>` is not a `List<T>`, so the response is `null`.
    This happens with a list from `jsonDecode`. Call `.cast<T>()` first.
    See [JSON from another API](#json-from-another-api).

## Examples with models

### Change values

`convert` is plain Dart. You can format dates, join fields and add new keys.

```dart title="lib/app/serializers/user.serializer.dart"
class UserSerializer extends Serializer<User> {
  UserSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(User m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'id': m.id,
      'name': '${m.firstName} ${m.lastName}',
      'is_active': m.status == 'active',
      'joined_at': m.createdAt?.toIso8601String(),
    };
  }
}
```

### A serializer inside a serializer

Use one serializer for a relation inside another.
Load the relation first, for example with [`preload`](../database/model/relationship/belongs-to.md#load-it).

```dart title="lib/app/serializers/comment.serializer.dart"
class CommentSerializer extends Serializer<Comment> {
  CommentSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Comment m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'id': m.id,
      'content': m.content,
      'user': UserSerializer(m.user).toJson(), // null when there is no user
    };
  }
}
```

```dart
Future<CommentSerializer> index(DoxRequest req) async {
  List<Comment> comments = await Comment().preload('user').all();
  return CommentSerializer(comments);
}
```

### With pagination

`page.data` is a `List<User>`. Put the serializer output in place of `data`.

```dart
Future<Map<String, dynamic>> index(ListUsers query) async {
  Pagination<User> page = await User()
      .orderBy('id', 'desc')
      .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  return <String, dynamic>{
    ...page.toJson(),
    'data': UserSerializer(page.data).toJson(),
  };
}
```

See [Pagination](../guides/pagination.md) for the full example.

## Examples without models

`T` can be any type. You do not need the ORM.

### A plain Dart class

```dart title="lib/app/serializers/weather.serializer.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class Weather {
  final String city;
  final double celsius;

  Weather(this.city, this.celsius);
}

class WeatherSerializer extends Serializer<Weather> {
  WeatherSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Weather m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'city': m.city,
      'celsius': m.celsius,
      'fahrenheit': m.celsius * 9 / 5 + 32,
    };
  }
}
```

```dart
WeatherSerializer today(DoxRequest req) {
  return WeatherSerializer(<Weather>[Weather('Yangon', 30)]);
}
```

### Rows from the query builder

`QueryBuilder.table(...)` gives rows as maps, not models.
Use `Serializer<Map<String, dynamic>>` to pick and rename the keys.

```dart title="lib/app/serializers/sales_report.serializer.dart"
class SalesReportSerializer extends Serializer<Map<String, dynamic>> {
  SalesReportSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Map<String, dynamic> m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'product': m['name'],
      'sold': m['total'],
    };
  }
}
```

```dart
Future<SalesReportSerializer> report(DoxRequest req) async {
  List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('orders')
      .selectRaw('name, count(*) as total')
      .groupBy('name')
      .get();
  return SalesReportSerializer(rows);
}
```

### JSON from another API

`jsonDecode` gives a `List<dynamic>`. Cast it to the type of the serializer first.

```dart
Future<SalesReportSerializer> remote(DoxRequest req) async {
  String body = await fetchReport(); // your HTTP call
  List<dynamic> rows = jsonDecode(body);
  return SalesReportSerializer(rows.cast<Map<String, dynamic>>());
}
```

## See also

- [CLI: `dox make:serializer`](../reference/cli.md#dox-makeserializer)

# Error handling

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/errors/

# Error handling

Every error that a route throws goes to one place: the exception handler.
It does two things:

- `report(error, stackTrace)` logs the error.
- `render(error, req)` decides what the client gets.

## The default answer

You do not need to set anything. With the default handler:

| Error | Status | Body |
| --- | --- | --- |
| an `IHttpException`, like `NotFoundHttpException` | its `code` | `{"code": "not_found", "message": "Not Found"}` |
| a `ValidationException` (bad input) | `422` | the field errors, like `{"name": "The name is required"}` |
| a `ValidationException` on a request with a [session](session.md#redirect-back-with-errors) that does not want JSON, like a form post | `302` | a redirect back. The errors and the old input are in the session. |
| a URL with no route | `404` | `{"code": "not_found", "message": "GET /x not found"}` |
| any other error | `500` | `{"code": "server_error", "message": "Server Error"}` |

For a `500`, the error text is sent only when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`.
In production the client never sees it, because it can hold SQL, file paths or hosts.

`report` is called for every error, except an `IHttpException` with a `4xx` code.
A `4xx` exception is a normal answer (like `404`), so it is not logged.
A `5xx` exception, like `InternalErrorException`, is reported.
The default `report` prints the error and the stack with the logger.

See [HTTP exceptions](../reference/http-exceptions.md) for the built-in exception classes.

## An HTML error page

By default an error is sent as JSON. In `development` or `local`, a `500` is plain text with the error text. A browser that opens a bad URL sees JSON or text, not a page.
To send an HTML page to browsers, turn on `htmlErrors`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  htmlErrors: true,
  // ...
);
```

The page has the status and its title, like `404 Not Found`.
It loads no files from outside.

- Only a request that does not want JSON gets the page. A request wants JSON (`DoxRequest.expectsJson()`) when it has an `Accept` header with json, a JSON body, or `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest`. An Inertia request does not want JSON, so it gets the page.
- Only when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`, the page also shows the error text and the stack trace.
- A JSON client gets the same answer as without `htmlErrors`.
- A validation error does not change. It keeps its `422` JSON or its redirect.
- An answer from your own `ExceptionHandler.render` does not change.

To make your own page, set `errorPage`. It gets the status, the error, the stack trace and a `debug` flag.
`debug` is `true` when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`.
Escape every value you put in the page.

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  htmlErrors: true,
  errorPage: (int status, Object error, StackTrace stack, bool debug) =>
      '<h1>Sorry, error $status</h1>',
  // ...
);
```

`defaultErrorPage` is the default. You can call it from your own function, for example for the statuses you do not handle.

## Your own handler

Extend `ExceptionHandler`. Override one method or both.

```dart title="lib/app/exception_handler.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class PaymentRequiredException implements Exception {}

class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  void report(Object error, StackTrace stackTrace) {
    // send it to your error tracker
    print('ERROR $error\n$stackTrace');
  }

  @override
  dynamic render(Object error, HttpRequest req) {
    if (error is PaymentRequiredException) {
      return response(<String, String>{'message': 'Please pay'})
          .statusCode(402);
    }
    // everything else: the default answer
    return super.render(error, req);
  }
}
```

Set it in `AppConfig`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  exceptionHandler: const AppExceptionHandler(),
  // ...
);
```

## What render can return

`render` returns anything a controller can return: a `DoxResponse`, a map, a string.
Return the error itself (this is what `super.render` does) to get the default answer.

`req` is the raw `HttpRequest`. It is there even when the error came before Dox read the body.
Use it to read headers, like `req.headers.value('accept')`.

If `render` itself throws, Dox logs that error and sends the default answer.
The client always gets a response.

## Errors outside a request

Some errors do not belong to a request.
For example a future that nobody awaits, or an error in the `shutdown()` of a provider.
Dox passes them to `report` too. The server keeps running.

## The response handler

The `responseHandler` of `AppConfig` still runs after `render`.
It sees every response, also error responses.
Use `render` to change errors, and `responseHandler` to change all responses (for example, to add a header).

See [Custom errors](../guides/custom-errors.md) for a full example with your own exception classes.


---

# Controller

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/controller/

# Controller

A controller holds the code that answers a route.

It can be a class method, a static method or a plain function.

## Class based controller

Make one with the CLI:

```bash
dox make:controller Blog
```

It writes `lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart` with an empty `index` method. Fill it in:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class BlogController {
  String index(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'all blogs';
  }
}
```

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.get('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.index);
```

`@Inject()` puts the controller in the container. Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add one.
The constructor can ask for services and repositories. See [Dependency injection](dependency-injection.md).

### Static method

```dart
class AppController {
  static String ping(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'pong';
  }
}

Route.get('/ping', AppController.ping);
```

## Function based controller

```dart
String listBlog(DoxRequest req) {
  return 'all blogs';
}

Route.get('/blogs', listBlog);
```

## Resource controller

A resource controller has the 7 methods that `Route.resource` uses.

Make one with the CLI:

```bash
dox make:controller Blog -r
```

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Route: Route.resource('path', BlogController);
@Inject()
class BlogController {
  /// GET /resource
  Future<dynamic> index(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// GET /resource/create
  Future<dynamic> create(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// POST /resource
  Future<dynamic> store(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// GET /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> show(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// GET /resource/{id}/edit
  Future<dynamic> edit(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// PUT|PATCH /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> update(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// DELETE /resource/{id}
  /// delete() gives the number of rows it deleted, so 0 is a 404:
  /// `if (await Blog().where('id', id).delete() == 0) throw NotFoundHttpException();`
  Future<dynamic> destroy(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}
}
```

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.resource('blogs', BlogController);
```

You can delete methods you do not need. `Route.resource` skips them.
See [Routing: resource routes](routing.md#resource-routes).

### API resource controller

An API has no form pages. `--api` makes the resource controller without `create` and `edit`:

```bash
dox make:controller Blog --api
```

### Resource controller for a model

`--model` makes a resource controller that uses a model:

```bash
dox make:controller Blog --model=Blog
```

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart';

/// Route: Route.resource('path', BlogController);
@Inject()
class BlogController {
  /// GET /resource
  Future<dynamic> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Blog().all();
  }

  /// GET /resource/create
  Future<dynamic> create(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// POST /resource
  /// create() takes only the fillable columns of Blog.
  /// Set fillable in the Blog model first. While it is empty, this throws.
  Future<dynamic> store(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Blog().create(req.body);
  }

  /// GET /resource/{id}
  /// Dox loads blog by the {id}. No row answers 404.
  Future<dynamic> show(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    return blog;
  }

  /// GET /resource/{id}/edit
  Future<dynamic> edit(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    return blog;
  }

  /// PUT|PATCH /resource/{id}
  /// update() takes only the fillable columns of Blog.
  /// Set fillable in the Blog model first. While it is empty, this throws.
  Future<dynamic> update(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    await blog.update(req.body);
    return blog;
  }

  /// DELETE /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> destroy(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    await blog.delete();
  }
}
```

- `show`, `edit`, `update` and `destroy` take the model. [Route model binding](dependency-injection.md#route-model-binding) loads it by the `{id}`.
- `create()` and `update()` take only the columns in the model's `fillable` list. Add your columns there.
- Use `--api` and `--model` together for an API controller with a model.
- `dox make:model Blog -r` makes the model and this controller in one step.

## Parameters

A controller asks for what it needs by **type**. Dox fills each parameter.

```dart
Route.put('/teams/{teamId}/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.update);

@Inject()
class UserController {
  Future<User> update(int teamId, int id, UpdateUser body) async { ... }
}
```

| Parameter type | Dox gives |
| --- | --- |
| `DoxRequest` | the request |
| a `@Dto` class | the checked body or query. See [Validation](validation.md). |
| `String`, `int`, `double`, `num`, `bool` | the path params, in the order of the route |
| the same types with `?` | an optional path param (`{id?}`). `null` when it is not in the URL. |
| a `@DoxModel` class | the model, loaded by the route param. See [route model binding](dependency-injection.md#route-model-binding). |
| an `@Inject()` class | the instance from the [container](dependency-injection.md#handler-parameters) |

Rules:

- The order of parameters is free. Path params are matched by position: the first path-param parameter gets the first `{...}` in the route.
- `DoxRequest` is not needed. Add it only when you use it.
- At most one `@Dto` parameter.
- Only positional parameters. Named and `[optional]` parameters are not supported.
- A catch-all `{path*}` param is a `String`.
- The same rules work for static methods and plain functions.
- Dox reads the parameter types once, at start. It does not use `dart:mirrors`.

**Path param types.** Dox converts the text from the URL:

- `int`: `"42"` is `42`. `"abc"` or `"4.5"` answers `404 Not Found`.
- `double`, `num`: `"4.5"` is `4.5`.
- `bool`: `true` or `1` is `true`. `false` or `0` is `false`.
- Any other text answers `404` too.
- Path params are checked first. When one is wrong, the DTO is not checked.

**Checked at start.** The server does not start when:

- a parameter type is not in the list above (did you run `dart run build_runner build`?),
- the method has more path-param parameters than the route has `{...}` params.

## What to return

Return a `String`, a `Map`, a model, a `File` and more. See [Response](response.md).


---

# Dependency injection

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/dependency-injection/

# Dependency injection

Dox has a container.

It makes your classes and gives each constructor what it needs.
You do not register classes by hand.
Put `@Inject()` above a class, and `dox_builder` adds it to the container.
Dox does not use `dart:mirrors`.
All the wiring is generated code.

## A full example

A repository reads the database. A service holds the business logic. A controller answers the route.

```dart title="lib/app/repositories/user.repository.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserRepository {
  Future<User?> find(int id) => User().find(id);
}
```

```dart title="lib/app/services/user.service.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/repositories/user.repository.dart';

@Inject()
class UserService {
  UserService(this.users);

  final UserRepository users;

  Future<User> show(int id) async {
    User? user = await users.find(id);
    if (user == null) throw NotFoundHttpException();
    return user;
  }
}
```

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/services/user.service.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  UserController(this.service);

  final UserService service;

  Future<User> show(int id) => service.show(id);
}
```

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.show);
  }
}
```

Run the builder:

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

It writes `lib/generated/container.g.dart`. Give it to the app once:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:my_app/generated/container.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  // ...
);
```

That is all. `GET /api/users/5` makes the repository, the service and the controller, and calls `show(5)`.

## The generated file

`lib/generated/container.g.dart` has one function. Each class gets a factory that calls its constructor.

```dart title="lib/generated/container.g.dart"
// GENERATED CODE - DO NOT MODIFY BY HAND
// Made by dox_builder. Run `dart run build_runner build`.
// ignore_for_file: type=lint

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart' as i1;
import 'package:my_app/app/repositories/user.repository.dart' as i2;
import 'package:my_app/app/services/user.service.dart' as i3;
import 'package:my_app/providers/orm_provider.dart' as i4;
import 'package:my_app/routes/api.dart' as i5;
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart' as i6;

/// Puts every class of the app into the container: the
/// `@Inject()` classes, routers, providers and model binders.
/// Use it in `AppConfig(container: registerContainer)`.
void registerContainer(IocContainer c) {
  c.singleton<i1.UserController>(
    (IocContainer c) => i1.UserController(c.get<i3.UserService>()),
  );
  c.singleton<i2.UserRepository>((IocContainer c) => i2.UserRepository());
  c.singleton<i3.UserService>(
    (IocContainer c) => i3.UserService(c.get<i2.UserRepository>()),
  );
  c.provider<i4.ORMProvider>((IocContainer c) => i4.ORMProvider());
  c.router<i5.ApiRouter>((IocContainer c) => i5.ApiRouter());
  c.bindModel<i6.User>((String id) {
    int? key = int.tryParse(id);
    if (key == null) return null;
    return i6.User().find(key);
  });
}
```

Do not edit it. Run the builder again after you add a class.

## Lifetime

- `@Inject()`: one instance per isolate. It is made on first use.
- `@Inject(singleton: false)`: a new instance each time it is asked for.

Dox runs one server per isolate. Isolates do not share objects.
So each isolate runs `registerContainer` and has its own instances.
Do not keep state in a singleton that all isolates must see. Use the cache or the database for that.

## Constructor parameters

Each constructor parameter is found by its type.

- Positional and named parameters both work.
- An optional parameter whose type is not in the container keeps its default value.
- A nullable parameter whose type is not in the container gets `null`.
- Any other parameter whose type is not in the container stops the build.

## Routes to controller methods

Pass a function that picks the method. Dox finds the controller by the parameter type:

```dart
Route.get('/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
Route.post('/posts', (PostController c) => c.store);
Route.put('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.update);
Route.delete('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.destroy);
```

The controller comes from the container. Dox gets it once per isolate, at start. A request does no extra work.
`.name()`, groups and middleware lists work the same:

```dart
Route.get('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.show).name('posts.show');
Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (AuthController c) => c.me]);
```

For resource routes, pass the class:

```dart
Route.resource('posts', PostController);
```

The method still gets its parameters as usual: `DoxRequest`, a `@Dto`, path params and bound models.
See [Controller: parameters](controller.md#parameters).

## Handler parameters

A controller method (or a plain route function) can ask for any class of the container:

```dart
Route.get('/stats', (StatsService stats) => stats.today());
```

A singleton is read once, at start. A `singleton: false` class is made on each request.

## Route model binding

Every `@DoxModel` class gets a binder in `lib/generated/container.g.dart`.
When a handler has a parameter of a model type, Dox loads the model by its primary key.

```dart
Route.get('/posts/{post}', (PostController c) => c.show);

@Inject()
class PostController {
  Post show(Post post) => post;
}
```

- The route param with the name of the model is used: `{post}` for `Post`, `{blogPost}` for `BlogPost`.
- When there is no such param, the next route param in order is used, like `{id}`.
- A missing row answers `404`.
- An `int` key that is not a number answers `404`, with no database call.
- A route without a parameter of the model type does not load the model.
- A binder from `Route.bind` wins over this one. See [Routing: route model binding](routing.md#route-model-binding).

## Routers and providers

You do not need `@Inject()` on them.

- Every class that extends `Router` is found. Its routes are registered at start.
- Every class that extends `DoxProvider` is found. Its `setup()` runs at start, in every isolate.

Their constructors get parameters from the container too.

They run in the order of their file path, then the order in the file.
To pick the order, list them in `AppConfig`:

```dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  providers: <DoxProvider>[ORMProvider()], // runs first
  routers: <Router>[ApiRouter()],       // registered first
);
```

A listed class comes first. The others follow. No class runs twice.
A listed provider is also the instance that the container gives.

A provider can add global middleware with `Dox().addGlobalMiddleware(...)` in `setup()`. They run before the app's `globalMiddleware`. See [Middleware](middleware.md).

## Use the container in code

`Dox().ioc` is the container of the current isolate.

```dart
UserService users = Dox().ioc.get<UserService>();
```

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `get<T>()` | the instance of `T`. Throws when `T` is not registered. |
| `has<T>()` | `true` when `T` is registered |
| `singleton<T>(factory)` | one instance per isolate, made on first use |
| `factory<T>(factory)` | a new instance on each `get` |
| `instance<T>(value)` | `value` is the instance, eg. a config object |
| `override<T>(value)` | replace `T`, eg. with a fake in a test |
| `clearOverrides()` | remove every override |

## Tests

Replace a class with a fake before the app starts:

```dart
setUpAll(() async {
  Dox().ioc.override<UserRepository>(FakeUserRepository());
  client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
});

tearDownAll(() async {
  await client.close();
  Dox().ioc.clearOverrides();
});
```

An override stays when the app registers its classes again.
Call it before `DoxTestClient.start`. Controllers get their objects once, at start.

## Build errors

The build stops with a clear message when:

- a required parameter has a type that is not in the container,
- a parameter has an abstract type, and two or more classes in the container implement it,
- classes need each other in a circle. The message shows the chain, like `A -> B -> C -> A`,
- `@Inject()` is on an abstract class or a generic class,
- a class has no unnamed constructor.

The message shows the file and line of the problem.

A private class (like `_AdminRouter`) is not put in the container. The build shows a warning for it. Remove the `_` to add it.

## Limits

- Dox finds classes in `lib/` only.
- The container is keyed by the class. A constructor parameter of an abstract type gets the one container class that implements it:

    ```dart
    abstract class Mailer {}

    @Inject()
    class SmtpMailer implements Mailer {}

    @Inject()
    class SignupService {
      SignupService(this.mailer); // gets the SmtpMailer

      final Mailer mailer;
    }
    ```

    This works for constructor parameters only. `c.get<Mailer>()` and handler parameters still need the class itself.
- Two classes with the same name in two files both work. But use the typed route style (`Route.get<C>(...)`) for them. They can not be handler parameters, because Dox can not tell them apart by name.


---

# Middleware

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/middleware/

# Middleware

Middleware is code that runs before the controller, and if you want, after it too.

Use it for checks like login, logging or rate limits, or to change the response.

## How it works

A middleware gets the request. It then does one of these:

- **Return the request.** Dox goes on to the next middleware, then to the controller.
- **Return something else** (a `String`, a `Map`, a `response(...)`). Dox sends it as the response. The controller does not run.
- **Throw an exception**, like `NotFoundHttpException()`. Dox sends the error response. See [Response: errors](response.md#errors).

A middleware can be `async`. Dox waits for it.

## Class based middleware

Create one with the CLI. It writes `lib/app/http/middleware/logger.middleware.dart`.

```bash
dox make:middleware Logger
```

Write your code in `handle`. For example:

```dart title="lib/app/http/middleware/logger.middleware.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class LoggerMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware {
  @override
  dynamic handle(IDoxRequest req) {
    print('${req.method} ${req.uri.path}');
    return req; // go on to the next middleware
  }
}
```

Then put it on a route:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.get('/ping', <dynamic>[LoggerMiddleware(), (WebController c) => c.pong]);
```

!!! note
    `handle` takes an `IDoxRequest`, not a `DoxRequest`.

!!! warning
    Do not forget `return req`. A middleware that returns `null` ends the request with an empty `200`, and the controller does not run.
    When `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`, Dox prints a warning to stderr the first time a middleware does this.

## Function based middleware

A function that takes a `DoxRequest` also works as middleware.

```dart title="lib/app/http/middleware/api_key.middleware.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

dynamic apiKeyMiddleware(DoxRequest req) {
  String apiKey = Env.get<String>('API_KEY');
  String given = req.header('X-Api-Key') ?? '';
  if (apiKey.isEmpty || !Hash.equals(given, apiKey)) {
    return response(<String, String>{'message': 'Unauthorized'}).statusCode(401);
  }
  return req;
}
```

The key comes from the `API_KEY` env variable, not from the code.
`Hash.equals` takes the same time for every wrong key, so the time does not tell how much of the key was right. A normal `==` stops at the first wrong character.

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.get('/ping', <dynamic>[apiKeyMiddleware, (WebController c) => c.pong]);
```

## Run code after the controller

A middleware can also get a `next` function. `await next()` runs the rest of the middleware and the controller, and gives the response.
Code after that line runs after the controller. Change the response, then return it.

```dart title="lib/app/http/middleware/see_other.middleware.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// a redirect after a form post becomes 303, so the browser does a GET
class SeeOtherMiddleware implements IDoxNextMiddleware {
  @override
  Future<DoxResponse> handle(DoxRequest req, Next next) async {
    // before the controller
    DoxResponse res = await next();
    // after the controller
    if (res.status == 302 && req.httpRequest.method != 'GET') {
      res.statusCode(303);
    }
    return res;
  }
}
```

The response from `next()` is always a `DoxResponse`, so you can use all its methods:
`statusCode(...)`, `header(...)`, `cookie(...)`, `content(...)`.
Read the status with `res.status` (`null` means 200) and the headers with `res.headers`.

When the controller (or a later middleware) throws an error, `next()` does not throw.
It gives the error response from the [ExceptionHandler](errors.md), like a `404` or a `422`. So the code after `next()` always runs.

A function works too. It takes the request and `next`:

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> timerMiddleware(DoxRequest req, Next next) async {
  Stopwatch watch = Stopwatch()..start();
  DoxResponse res = await next();
  return res.header('X-Time', '${watch.elapsedMilliseconds}ms');
}
```

To stop early, return a response and do not call `next()`.

!!! note "Speed"
    A route with no `next` middleware runs exactly as before. Only routes that have one pay for the extra step.

## Run code after the answer is sent

A middleware can run code after the answer has gone to the client, in its `terminate` method.
Use it for work the client should not wait for: logs, metrics, cleanup.
Implement `IDoxTerminableMiddleware`:

```dart title="lib/app/http/middleware/metrics.middleware.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class MetricsMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware, IDoxTerminableMiddleware {
  @override
  dynamic handle(IDoxRequest req) => req; // before the controller

  @override
  void terminate(DoxRequest req, DoxResponse res) {
    // the answer is already sent
    print('${req.method} ${req.uri.path} ${res.status}');
  }
}
```

- `res.status` is the status that was sent, also for an error answer.
- `terminate` can be `async`.
- An error in `terminate` goes to `ExceptionHandler.report`. It never changes the answer.
- The `handle` part is not needed. A class can implement only `IDoxTerminableMiddleware`.

!!! note "Speed"
    Dox checks each route once for such a middleware. Other routes do not pay for it.

### From any code, with `AfterResponse`

A middleware needs to be on the route. `AfterResponse` lets any code (a controller, a service, a package) add work that runs after the answer of the current request is sent. The code does not need the request.

It is off by default. Turn it on once, in the `setup()` of a provider. `setup()` runs in every isolate.

```dart title="lib/providers/app_provider.dart"
@override
void setup() {
  AfterResponse.enable();
}
```

Then add work anywhere in the request:

```dart
AfterResponse.run(() => mailer.sendWelcome(user));
```

- The work runs after the answer is sent, one after the other, in the order it was added. The next one starts only when the one before it ends. So work that never ends blocks the rest of the work of that request.
- Outside a request, or when it is off, the work runs soon, after the code that runs now.
- An error in the work goes to `ExceptionHandler.report`. It never reaches the client and never stops the server.
- The work is not saved anywhere. When the server stops, work that did not run yet is lost. Use a [queue](../digging-deeper/queue.md) for work that must run. To run a queue job this way, see `dispatchAfterResponse()` in [Queue](../digging-deeper/queue.md#dispatch-a-job).

## Request id

`RequestId` gives each request an id. It is sent back in the `X-Request-Id` header, and you can read it as `req.requestId`.

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const RequestId(),
    LogMiddleware(enabled: true),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

- When the client (or a proxy) sends a safe `X-Request-Id` (1 to 128 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -`), Dox keeps it. Else it makes a new one of 32 hex characters.
- `RequestId(trustClient: false)` always makes a new one.
- `LogMiddleware` adds `http.request_id` to each log line. Put `RequestId` before it.
- The default `ExceptionHandler.report` prints the id with the error. In your own `report`, read `ExceptionHandler.requestId`.

## ETag and 304 Not Modified

`ETag` adds an `ETag` header to GET and HEAD answers. When the client sends the same ETag back in `If-None-Match`, Dox answers `304 Not Modified` with no body.

```dart
Route.get('/posts', <dynamic>[const ETag(), (PostController c) => c.index]);
```

- It works on `200` answers with a body in memory: a `String`, a `Map`, a `List` or a model. Files and streams are not touched.
- An answer that already has an `ETag` header or `Cache-Control: no-store` is not touched.
- The ETag is weak (`W/"..."`), made from a fast 64-bit hash of the body. It is not a secure hash.
- The controller still runs. A `304` saves bandwidth, not server time.

## Request timeout

`RequestTimeout` answers `503 Service Unavailable` when the middleware after it and the controller take too long.

```dart
Route.get('/report', (ReportController c) => c.show)
    .timeout(Duration(seconds: 30));

// the same as
Route.get('/report', <dynamic>[
  RequestTimeout(Duration(seconds: 30)),
  (ReportController c) => c.show,
]);
```

The answer is the normal error JSON:

```json
{"code": "request_timeout", "message": "The request took too long"}
```

- For every route, add `RequestTimeout(...)` to `globalMiddleware`.
- Dart can not stop a running Future. The controller keeps running in the background. Its late result is dropped, so nothing is sent twice.
- It is `503`, not `504`. `504 Gateway Timeout` is what a proxy sends when the app is slow. `503` says the app itself gave up.

## Server timing

`ServerTiming` adds a `Server-Timing` header to the answer. The browser dev tools show it in the Network tab, under Timing.

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    if (Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'development') const ServerTiming(),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

It always sends two times, in milliseconds:

- `handler`: the time in the controller.
- `total`: the time of the middleware after `ServerTiming` and the controller.

Add your own times to the current request from any code. You do not pass the request:

```dart
ServerTiming.add('db', Duration(milliseconds: 4));

String html = await ServerTiming.measure('render', () => view.render());
```

The header looks like this:

```
Server-Timing: db;dur=4.10;desc="3 calls", handler;dur=12.34, total;dur=13.02
```

- `add` with the same name again adds the times together. With more than one call, the text shows the count, like `"3 calls"`. Pass `description:` to set your own text.
- `measure` runs the function and adds the time it took, also when it throws.
- Without the middleware, or outside a request, `add` and `measure` do nothing. The cost is one small lookup.
- A name may only have letters, digits and ``!#$%&'*+-.^_`|~``. Other characters become `_`. An empty name is ignored.
- One answer keeps at most 32 names, plus `handler` and `total`.
- `handler` and `total` are kept for the built-in times. If your code adds a time named `total` or `handler`, it is sent as `app_total` or `app_handler`. It does not change the built-in times. If you also add a time named `app_total`, the two are added together.
- If the answer already has a `Server-Timing` header (set with `res.header`), the times are added after it, like `cdn;dur=1, handler;dur=12.34, total;dur=13.02`.

To add the time of every database query, listen to the queries once, for example in `setup()` of a provider. The listener runs inside the request that made the query, so `add` finds that request:

```dart title="lib/providers/query_timing_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart'; // SqlQueryBuilder and QueryEvent

void onQuery(QueryEvent event) {
  ServerTiming.add('db', event.time);
}

/// Dox finds every DoxProvider class,
/// see lib/generated/container.g.dart.
class QueryTimingProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    SqlQueryBuilder().listen(onQuery);
  }
}
```

Each `listen` call adds the listener again. If `setup()` runs a second time (for example in tests), the time of each query is counted twice. Call `SqlQueryBuilder().removeListener(onQuery)` first, or when you are done.

The header then shows the total query time and the count, like `db;dur=4.10;desc="3 calls"`. See [Listen to queries](../database/index.md#listen-to-queries).

!!! warning "Development or trusted clients only"
    The header tells every client how long your code takes. An attacker can use that, for example to guess if an email has an account. `ServerTiming` is off unless you add it. Turn it on in development, or only for clients you trust.

## Many middleware on one route

Put them in the list before the controller. They run from left to right.
You can mix class and function middleware, with or without `next`.

```dart
Route.get('/ping', <dynamic>[
  LoggerMiddleware(),
  apiKeyMiddleware,
  (WebController c) => c.pong, // the controller is always last
]);
```

## Middleware for a group of routes

```dart
Route.middleware(<dynamic>[LoggerMiddleware()], () {
  Route.get('/me', (AuthController c) => c.me);
  Route.post('/logout', (AuthController c) => c.logout);
});
```

## Middleware for a router or for all routes

For one router, set its `middleware` list:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[LoggerMiddleware()];

  @override
  void register() {
    // every route here runs LoggerMiddleware
  }
}
```

For all routes, set `globalMiddleware` in the app config:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    LogMiddleware(enabled: env.appEnv != 'production'),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

A provider can add global middleware with `Dox().addGlobalMiddleware(...)`. They run before the app's `globalMiddleware`. A second add of the same middleware is skipped.

The list is cleared at each start, before the providers run. Add package middleware from a provider's `setup()`, which runs on every start. Anything added before the app starts is cleared. Use a top-level function or a `const` instance. The providers do not run for `dox route:list`, so it does not show this middleware.

```dart
class AuditProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    Dox().addGlobalMiddleware(AuditMiddleware());
  }
}
```

The order is: package middleware from providers, then the app's global middleware, then router middleware, then group middleware, then route middleware.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Q["Request"] --> G["Global<br>globalMiddleware"]
    G --> R["Router<br>middleware getter"]
    R --> P["Group<br>Route.middleware"]
    P --> T["Route<br>list before the controller"]
    T --> C["Controller"]
    C --> S["Response"]
    G & R & P & T -.->|"returns a value or throws"| S
```

!!! tip "Built-in middleware"
    - `LogMiddleware` from `dox_core` logs one line per request through `Logger`.
        - It follows `LoggerConfig`: `enabled`, `level` and `prettyPrint`.
        - If the logger is off, `LogMiddleware(enabled: true)` does not turn logs on.
        - `enabled: false` turns only the request logs off. Leave it unset to follow the logger.
        - With `prettyPrint` it prints colored text.
        - Without it, it prints one JSON line with `status`, `message`, `network.client.ip`, `http.method`, `http.url`, `http.request_id` and `payload`.
        - The `filter` can change `status`, `message` and the other fields. It can not change `timestamp` or `logger`: `Logger` sets them. A `logger` key is ignored, also when the logger name is empty.
        - Headers are logged only with `withHeader: true`.
        - Body fields and headers whose name has a word like `password`, `secret`, `token`, `authorization`, `cookie` or `api_key` in it (upper or lower case) are logged as `[REDACTED]`. Change the list with `redact:`.
        - The new project turns it off when `APP_ENV` is `production`.
    - `AuthMiddleware` from `dox_auth` checks the JWT token. `AuthMiddleware(optional: true)` lets guests through too. `GuestMiddleware` lets only guests through, for login pages. See [Authentication](../security/authentication.md).
    - `RateLimit` from `dox_core` answers `429` when a client sends too many requests. See [Rate limiting](../security/rate-limiting.md).
    - `SecurityHeaders` from `dox_core` adds safe headers like `X-Frame-Options` to every answer. See [Security headers](../security/security-headers.md).
    - `SessionMiddleware` from `dox_core` gives each request a session. See [Session](session.md).
    - `CsrfMiddleware` from `dox_core` stops cross site request forgery. See [CSRF protection](../security/csrf.md).
    - `RequestId`, `ETag`, `RequestTimeout` and `ServerTiming` from `dox_core`. See above.
    - `ValidateSignature` from `dox_core` checks signed urls. See [Signed URLs](../security/signed-urls.md).


---

# Session

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/session/

# Session

A session keeps data for one browser between requests.

Use it for web pages: the logged in user, a cart, a "Saved" message after a form post.

An API with tokens does not need a session.

## Turn it on

Add `SessionMiddleware` to `globalMiddleware`, or to the routers or routes that need it.
Add `CsrfMiddleware` after it. See [CSRF protection](../security/csrf.md).

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*']),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

Now every request has `req.session`. Using `req.session` on a route without the middleware throws an error.

## Use the session

```dart
// store a value
req.session.put('cart', <int>[1, 2]);

// read a value, with a default
List<dynamic> cart = req.session.get('cart', <int>[]);

// is it there (and not null)?
bool hasCart = req.session.has('cart');

// read and remove
dynamic removed = req.session.pull('cart');

// remove one value, or all of them
req.session.forget('cart');
req.session.flush();

// all values, as a copy
Map<String, dynamic> all = req.session.all();
```

Values must be JSON types: `Map`, `List`, `String`, `num`, `bool` or `null`.

## Flash data

Flash data lives for this request and the next one. Use it for a message after a redirect.

```dart
Route.post('/posts', (DoxRequest req) async {
  // ... save the post
  req.session.flash('message', 'The post is saved');
  return redirect('/posts');
});

Route.get('/posts', (DoxRequest req) {
  String? message = req.session.get('message'); // 'The post is saved'
  // ...
});
```

"The next request" means the next request that uses the session. A request that never reads the session (like an image) does not remove it.

To keep flash data for one more request, call `req.session.reflash()`, or `req.session.keep(['message'])` for some keys only.

## Redirect back with errors

`back(req)` redirects to the page the request came from (the `Referer` header), or to `/` when there is none. A `Referer` of another host is not used, so it also goes to `/`.
`redirect('/path')` redirects to any path.

When a form post fails validation, Dox does this for you on a route with a session:

1. It flashes the errors as `errors`, like `{'email': 'The email is not a valid email'}`.
2. It flashes the old input. Password fields (`password`, `password_confirmation`, `current_password`) and files are never kept.
3. It redirects back with `302`.

The next page reads them:

```dart
Route.get('/register', (DoxRequest req) {
  Map<String, dynamic> errors = req.session.errors; // empty when there are none
  String? email = req.session.old('email');
  // ...
});
```

A request that wants JSON still gets the normal `422` JSON answer. A request wants JSON when it has an `Accept` header with `json`, a JSON body, or `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest`.
An Inertia request (it has the `X-Inertia` header) is redirected like a form post.

You can do the same by hand:

```dart
req.session.flashErrors(<String, String>{'email': 'The email is taken'}, input: req.all());
return back(req);
```

## After login and logout

```dart
// after login: a new session id and a new CSRF token, the data stays
req.session.regenerate();

// on logout: remove all data and get a new session id
req.session.invalidate();
```

Always call `regenerate()` after login. Then an id that someone saw before the login is of no use.

`regenerate(keepToken: true)` gives a new id but keeps the CSRF token, so forms open in other tabs keep working.
Do not use it at login. A token from before the login would stay valid after the login.

With the default `cookie` session driver, all session data sits in the cookie. So an old copy of the cookie still works after logout. If logout must really end old cookies, use the `cache` session driver, like `SessionConfig(driver: 'cache', store: 'redis')`.

`dox_auth` does this for you. See [Session login](../security/authentication.md#session-login-for-web-pages).

## Config

Set `session` in the app config. All options have a default.

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  session: const SessionConfig(
    driver: 'cache',
    store: 'redis',
    lifetime: Duration(hours: 2),
  ),
  // ...
);
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `driver` | `cookie` | `cookie` or `cache`. See below. |
| `store` | `null` | The cache store for the `cache` driver, like `redis`, `memory` or `file`. `null` uses the default store of `AppConfig.cache`. |
| `cookie` | `dox_session` | The name of the session cookie. |
| `lifetime` | 2 hours | The session ends after this long with no use. The `cookie` driver keeps the save time in the encrypted cookie and checks it, so a copied old cookie stops working too. |
| `path` | `/` | `Path` of the cookie. |
| `domain` | `null` | `Domain` of the cookie. `null` means only the host that set it. |
| `httpOnly` | `true` | Page scripts can not read the cookie. |
| `secure` | `null` | `null` sets `Secure` when the request came over https. |
| `sameSite` | `SameSite.lax` | `SameSite` of the cookie (from `dart:io`). |

You can also give a config to one middleware: `SessionMiddleware(SessionConfig(...))`.

### The cookie driver

All session data is in the cookie, encrypted with AES-GCM and your `APP_KEY`. The browser can not read or change it.
There is nothing to store on the server.

A cookie can hold about 4 KB. A session that is too big gives an error. Keep the data small (an id, not a whole object), or use the `cache` driver.

### The cache driver

The cookie only has a random session id (encrypted too). The data lives in a cache store.
Use `redis` when you run more than one isolate or more than one server: then all of them see the same sessions.
A `memory` store is good for tests. It is not shared between isolates.
With no Redis, a [database store](../packages/cache.md#database-store) shares the sessions too: `SessionConfig(driver: 'cache', store: 'database')`.

## When the session is read and saved

- **The cookie driver reads the session on first use.** A request that never uses `req.session` does not decrypt anything.
- **The cache driver reads the store before the controller**, but only when the request has a session cookie. A new visitor costs nothing.
- **The session is saved only when it changed.** Only then is the cookie sent. A session that is used but not changed is saved again after half of its `lifetime`, so it does not end while the user is active.

## Read the session from a package

Other packages (like an Inertia adapter) can read the same data:

```dart
if (req.hasSession) {
  Map<String, dynamic> errors = req.session.errors;
  dynamic message = req.session.get('message');
}
```

## Load a session with no request

Code that has no request, like a Socket.IO login, can load the session from the cookie value:

```dart
Session session = await SessionMiddleware().fromCookie(value);
dynamic userId = session.get('auth_web');
```

- Give the value as the browser sent it (still encrypted). Do not decrypt it first.
- The checks are the same as for a request. A changed cookie, a cookie of another name, a cookie made with another `APP_KEY`, an expired session or an unknown id gives an empty session.
- Changes to this session are not saved.
- With the `cookie` driver, an old copy of the cookie still works after logout, until the session `lifetime` ends. If a logout must stop old cookies, use the `cache` driver.
- `SessionMiddleware(config)` uses another `SessionConfig`, like on a route.

## Tests

`client.withSession()` gives a test client that keeps cookies like a browser. It also sends the `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie back in `X-XSRF-TOKEN`, so `CsrfMiddleware` lets its posts in:

```dart
DoxTestClient browser = client.withSession();
await browser.get('/cart/add?id=1');
(await browser.get('/cart')).expectJson(isNotEmpty);
```

See [Testing: keep a session](../digging-deeper/testing.md#keep-a-session-cookies-and-csrf).


---

# Validation

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/validation/

# Validation

This page shows how to check request input with typed DTO classes.

Write a class with `@Dto()`. Ask for it in your controller.
Dox reads the request, checks it, and gives you a typed object.
When the input is wrong, Dox answers `422` with the errors. Your controller does not run.

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/create_user/create_user.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'create_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class CreateUser {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 50)
  final String name;

  @Email()
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  @Min(18)
  final int? age; // nullable, so optional

  const CreateUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
    this.age,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<CreateUser> schema = $CreateUserDto;
}
```

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart"
class UserController {
  Future<User> store(CreateUser body) async {
    // body is already checked
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();
    return user;
  }
}
```

## Setup

You do this once per app.

1. Make a DTO with `dox make:dto CreateUser`. It writes `lib/app/dtos/create_user/create_user.dto.dart`.
2. Run the generator: `dox build_runner:build` (or `dox build_runner:watch`).
   It writes a `.dto.g.dart` file next to each DTO, and one list of all DTOs in `lib/generated/dtos.g.dart`.
3. Give that list to the app:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos, // from lib/generated/dtos.g.dart
  // ...
);
```

Dox uses no reflection, so it needs this list to find your DTOs. Without it, the server stops at start with a clear error.

## Use a DTO

Add a parameter with the DTO type. Dox checks the request before your method runs.

```dart
Future<User> store(CreateUser body) async { ... }

// with the request and a path param
Future<User> update(DoxRequest req, int id, UpdateUser body) async { ... }
```

Or check inside the method. `req.validate<T>()` returns the object, or throws the `422` error.

```dart
CreateUser data = await req.validate<CreateUser>();
```

See [Controller: parameters](controller.md#parameters) for the full rules.

## Required and optional

The Dart type decides. You do not write `required` or `nullable`.

| Field | Key missing | Value `null` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `final String name;` | error `required` | error `required` |
| `final int? age;` | `null` | `null` |
| `final Role role;` with `this.role = Role.user` | `Role.user` | error `required` |

- Rules on an optional field run only when it has a value.
- A default value is used only when the key is missing. The rules do not check it.
- **An empty string counts as missing.** So a required `String` rejects `""`. Add `@AllowEmpty()` to keep `""`.
- **Spaces are kept.** So `"   "` passes `required`, unless the field has `@Trim()`. To trim every text field of a DTO, use `@Dto(trim: true)`. Then `"   "` counts as missing. It works like `@Trim()` on each `String` field and on the text items of its lists and maps. A nested DTO uses its own `@Dto(trim:)`.
- To read `""` as `null` instead, use `@Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true)`. With `@Dto(trim: true)` too, blank text like `"  "` is `null` as well. Then `{"bio": ""}` clears a `Maybe<String?>` field. A required field still gets `required`. A field that is not nullable but has a default gets `required` too, because `null` is not a missing key.
- `@OrDefault()` turns a bad value into the default, with no error.
    - It works on any field, in a body or a query.
    - Example: `@OrDefault() @NotIn(<int>[0]) final int page;` with `this.page = 1` reads `page=abc` and `page=0` as `1`.
    - The field needs a default, a nullable type or a `Maybe` type. A `Maybe` field gets `Maybe.missing()`.
    - Errors from async rules (`@Unique`, `@Exists`, your `AsyncRule`) and from `validate()` are not dropped. They run later, on the built object, and still give `422`.
