# Notifications

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/notifications/

# Notifications

Notifications are in the `dox_mailer` package.

Set up [mail](mail.md) first.

A notification tells a user about something, like "your invoice is paid". It can go out on more than one channel: email, a database table, SMS. Each notification is a class. `via()` picks the channels.

```dart
class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  InvoicePaid(this.invoiceId);

  final int invoiceId;

  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Mailable toMail(Object notifiable) {
    return MailMessage(subject: 'Invoice paid')
      ..line('We got your payment.')
      ..action('View invoice', 'https://example.com/invoices/$invoiceId');
  }
}
```

`toMail()` can return any mailable, so a `WelcomeMail` with a template works too.

## Who gets it

Add the `Notifiable` mixin to the class that gets notifications, usually the user model. `routeNotificationFor('mail')` gives the email address:

```dart
class User extends Model<User> with Notifiable {
  @override
  Object? routeNotificationFor(String channel) {
    return channel == 'mail' ? Address(email!, name) : null;
  }
}
```

The route can be an `Address`, an email text like `Ann <ann@example.com>`, or a list of these.

Then send:

```dart
await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));

// many users
await Notification.send(users, InvoicePaid(1));

// an address with no user
await Notification.send(<Object>[Address('ann@example.com')], InvoicePaid(1));
```

When the mailable has its own `to` address, that address is used and the route is not.

When a channel throws, the other channels and the other notifiables still get the notification. At the end, `Notification.send()` throws a `NotificationException`. Its `errors` list says which notifiable and channel failed, and why. When `via()` throws, the channel is null. The error text has one line per failure: the place and the type of the notifiable, the channel, and the error type. It has no email addresses and no error text, so it is safe for logs. For the details, read `errors`.

With one notifiable and one error, like `user.notify()`, the error is thrown as it is. So `on MailException catch (e)` still works there.

## Queue it

Override `shouldQueue`. The mail channel then puts the email on the job queue, like `Mail.queue()`. This needs [a queue](queue.md).

```dart
@override
bool get shouldQueue => true;
```

The email is rendered at once. The worker sends the finished email.

These getters set the queue options. They work like the options of `Mail.queue()`:

| Getter | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `queue` | null (`default`) | the queue name |
| `delay` | null | the worker sends the email after this wait |
| `encrypt` | `false` | save the job data encrypted with the app key |

When `shouldQueue` is false, the email is sent at once and these options do nothing. `shouldQueue` and these options only change the mail channel. Your own channels still run at once. To queue them, dispatch a job in the channel.

## Your own channel

Write a class that implements `NotificationChannel`. `toArray()` of the notification gives its data. For example, a channel that saves notifications in a table:

```dart
import 'dart:convert';

class DatabaseChannel implements NotificationChannel {
  @override
  Future<void> send(Object notifiable, Notification notification) async {
    // only a user has a row. An Address or an email text has none.
    if (notifiable is! User) return;
    AppNotification row = AppNotification()
      ..userId = notifiable.id
      ..data = jsonEncode(notification.toArray(notifiable));
    await row.save();
  }
}
```

```dart
class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel(), DatabaseChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> toArray(Object notifiable) {
    return <String, Object?>{'type': 'invoice_paid', 'invoice_id': invoiceId};
  }

  // ...
}
```

dox_mailer has no database channel of its own, so it does not need the ORM.

## Test it

`Mail.fake()` catches the emails of the mail channel too:

```dart
ArrayTransport mail = Mail.fake();
await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));
expect(mail.messages.single.subject, 'Invoice paid');
```

With `shouldQueue`, the email goes to `mail.queued`, not to `mail.messages`. It does not reach the job queue. Check it with `mail.assertQueued()`. See [Mail](mail.md#testing).


---

# Broadcasting

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/broadcasting/

# Broadcasting

Broadcasting sends server events to browsers and apps over Socket.IO, on public, private and presence channels.

A client subscribes to a channel. Your code sends an event to the channel. Every client in it gets the event.
Use it for live pages, like order status, a chat or a list of who is online.

It is part of the `dox_socketio` package. It is off by default.

## Turn it on

Do the [Socket.IO setup](../packages/socketio.md#in-a-dox-app) first. Then turn on broadcasting in the config:

```dart title="lib/config/socketio.dart"
SocketIoConfig socketIoConfig = SocketIoConfig(
  broadcasting: true,
  namespaces: <NamespaceHandler>[ChatNamespace()],
);
```

Channel rules are kept per isolate. So add them where every isolate runs them. A provider is a good place:

```dart title="lib/providers/broadcast_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class BroadcastProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Broadcast.channel('orders.{id}', (Object? user, String id) {
      return (user as User).id.toString() == id;
    });
  }
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build`, so the generated container finds the provider. Without it, no rule is added, and every private subscribe gets `Forbidden`.

A client that is not logged in as a socket gets a token from the auth route. Add the route with your own auth middleware:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
@override
void register() {
  Broadcast.routes(middleware: <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()]); // POST /api/broadcasting/auth
}
```

The prefix of the router is added to the path. This router has the prefix `api`, so the path is `/api/broadcasting/auth`.

The route runs the channel rule with `req.auth` and answers `{"auth": "<token>"}`, or `403`.
Pass `path:` to use another path.
The token is signed with a key made from `APP_KEY`. It works for one socket, one channel and one minute.

## Channels

| Channel | Name | Who can subscribe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Channel('news')` | `news` | any client |
| `PrivateChannel('orders.5')` | `private-orders.5` | a client that passes the rule |
| `PresenceChannel('chat.lobby')` | `presence-chat.lobby` | a client that passes the rule. Members see each other |

`Broadcast.channel(pattern, rule)` adds a rule for private and presence channels.
The pattern has no `private-` or `presence-` prefix.
A `{name}` part matches any text with no dot.
The rule gets the user, then one string for each `{name}` part. It can be async.

- A private rule gives `true` to allow. Anything else refuses.
- A presence rule gives a map with the member info, with an `id`. Anything else refuses.
- A rule that throws refuses, and the error goes to stderr.

```dart
Broadcast.channel('chat.{room}', (Object? user, String room) {
  User u = user as User;
  return <String, Object?>{'id': u.id, 'name': u.name};
});
```

One rule serves both kinds. `orders.{id}` checks `private-orders.1` and `presence-orders.1`.
When more than one pattern matches, the first one added wins.

## Send an event

An event is a class with the `ShouldBroadcast` mixin:

```dart
class OrderShipped with ShouldBroadcast {
  OrderShipped(this.order);
  final Order order;

  @override
  List<Channel> broadcastOn() => <Channel>[PrivateChannel('orders.${order.id}')];

  @override
  String broadcastAs() => 'order.shipped'; // default: the class name

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> broadcastWith() => <String, Object?>{'id': order.id};
}
```

- `broadcastOn` gives the channels. It is required.
- `broadcastAs` gives the event name. The default is the class name.
- `broadcastWith` gives the payload. It must be JSON. The default is an empty map.

Send it:

```dart
await broadcast(OrderShipped(order));
await Broadcast.event(OrderShipped(order)); // the same
```

`toOthers` skips one socket, for example the one that made the change.
The client sends its socket id in the `X-Socket-ID` header. `Broadcast.socketId(req)` reads it:

```dart
await Broadcast.event(OrderShipped(order), toOthers: Broadcast.socketId(req));
```

Without a Socket.IO server in the process, and with no [emitter](#send-from-a-process-with-no-socketio-server), `Broadcast.event` throws a `StateError`.

## The client

Use `socket.io-client`. A public channel needs no token.
A subscription belongs to one socket. After a reconnect, the client has a new socket and is in no channel.
So subscribe inside the `connect` handler. It runs again after each reconnect.

```js
import { io } from 'socket.io-client';

const socket = io('https://app.example.com', { transports: ['websocket'] });

socket.on('order.shipped', (channel, payload) => console.log(channel, payload));
socket.on('connect', () => {
  socket.emit('subscribe', { channel: 'news' }, (ack) => console.log(ack));
});
```

For a private or presence channel, get a token first, then send it in `subscribe`.
A token works for one socket id only. So ask for a new token in the `connect` handler, after each reconnect too:

```js
socket.on('connect', async () => {
  const res = await fetch('/api/broadcasting/auth', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', authorization: `Bearer ${apiToken}` },
    body: JSON.stringify({ socket_id: socket.id, channel_name: 'private-orders.5' }),
  });
  const { auth } = await res.json();
  socket.emit('subscribe', { channel: 'private-orders.5', auth }, (ack) => console.log(ack));
});
```

A socket that is already logged in with [`SocketAuth`](../packages/socketio.md#log-in-a-socket) needs no token. The server runs the rule with `socket.user`.

- The ack of `subscribe` and `unsubscribe` is `{ok: true}` or `{ok: false, error}`.
- Events arrive as `(channel, payload)`, under the name from `broadcastAs`.
- `socket.emit('unsubscribe', { channel }, ack)` leaves the channel.

| `error` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `channel is missing` | no channel name |
| `channel name is too long` | over `Broadcast.maxChannelLength` |
| `too many channels` | over `Broadcast.maxChannelsPerSocket` |
| `already subscribing` | the same channel is still being checked |
| `Forbidden` | the rule refused, or the token is missing, wrong or old |
| `unsubscribed` | an `unsubscribe` came while it was subscribing |
| `presence is not available` | another server did not answer in time |

Send the token as a string in `auth`, like above. An object of headers is refused with `Forbidden`.

## Presence

A presence channel tells its members who else is in it. The client gets three events:

| Event | Arguments | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `presence:subscribed` | `(channel, members)` | to the new socket, with all members |
| `presence:joining` | `(channel, member)` | to the others, when a member joins |
| `presence:leaving` | `(channel, member)` | to the others, when a member leaves |

A member is `{user_id, user_info}`. `user_info` is the map from the rule.

```js
socket.on('presence:subscribed', (channel, members) => console.log(members));
socket.on('presence:joining', (channel, member) => console.log(member.user_info.name));
socket.on('presence:leaving', (channel, member) => console.log(member.user_id));
```

A user with two sockets is one member. `presence:joining` is sent for the first socket, and `presence:leaving` for the last one.
The member list covers all isolates and servers that share the adapter.

## Queued broadcasting

A queued broadcast goes through your [queue](queue.md). The request does not wait for it.

`dox_socketio` does not depend on `dox_queue`. You connect them with a hook and a small job. Follow these steps.

### 1. Mark the event

Use `ShouldBroadcastQueued` in place of `ShouldBroadcast`:

```dart
class OrderShipped with ShouldBroadcastQueued {
  OrderShipped(this.order);
  final Order order;

  @override
  List<Channel> broadcastOn() => <Channel>[PrivateChannel('orders.${order.id}')];

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> broadcastWith() => <String, Object?>{'id': order.id};
}

await broadcast(OrderShipped(order)); // goes to the queue
```

### 2. Write the job

The worker runs this job. It sends the saved broadcast to the clients:

```dart title="lib/app/jobs/broadcast.job.dart"
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';

/// Sends one queued broadcast to the clients.
@Job()
class BroadcastJob extends DoxJob {
  BroadcastJob({required this.payload});

  final Map<String, dynamic> payload;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    await Broadcast.deliver(BroadcastPayload.fromJson(payload));
  }
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build`. It adds the job to `lib/generated/jobs.g.dart`. The queue needs this file to save and load the job. See [how the queue works](queue.md#how-it-works).
Make sure `jobs: jobRegistry` is set in your [queue config](queue.md#1-config).

### 3. Set the hook

The hook gets the broadcast and puts it on the queue. Add it to the `setup()` of the `BroadcastProvider` from [Turn it on](#turn-it-on), next to the channel rules. Keep the rules:

```dart title="lib/providers/broadcast_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

import '../app/jobs/broadcast.job.dart';

class BroadcastProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Broadcast.channel('orders.{id}', (Object? user, String id) {
      return (user as User).id.toString() == id;
    });

    // puts ShouldBroadcastQueued events on the queue
    Broadcast.useQueue(queueBroadcast);
  }

  static Future<void> queueBroadcast(BroadcastPayload payload) async {
    await Queue.dispatch(BroadcastJob(payload: payload.toJson()));
  }
}
```

The payload is JSON: `{channels, event, data, except}`. `except` is the `toOthers` socket id.

### 4. Use the Redis adapter

The worker is its own process. It starts your providers, so it gets its own Socket.IO server. That server has no clients.
So the worker must reach the clients of the web server through Redis.

Set the [Redis adapter](../packages/socketio.md#many-servers-redis-adapter) in `SocketIoConfig`. The web server and the worker use the same config, so both use the same Redis.
A `Broadcast.emitter` does not help here. The worker has its own Socket.IO server, and `Broadcast.deliver` sends through that server first.

### 5. Run the worker

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart
```

Deploy the worker together with the web app. See [run the worker](queue.md#run-the-worker).

### Rules

- With no hook set (`Broadcast.useQueue` not called), a `ShouldBroadcastQueued` event is sent at once, like a normal one. So tests and small apps work without a queue.
- Normal `ShouldBroadcast` events never use the hook.
- `Broadcast.deliver` throws a `StateError` when the worker has no way to send. This is when broadcasting is off and there is no `Broadcast.emitter`.
- `deliver` prints a warning once when it sends through an in-memory adapter with no clients. The clients of the web server do not get that broadcast.
- In tests, `Broadcast.fake()` keeps queued events too. Check them with `fake.assertQueued<OrderShipped>()`. `fake.delivered` holds the payloads that `deliver` got.

## Send from a process with no Socket.IO server

A queue worker or a command has no Socket.IO server. Set an emitter, so `Broadcast.event` can send through Redis:

```dart
Redis redis = Redis(RedisOptions(host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379));
Broadcast.emitter = SocketIoEmitter(redis);

await Broadcast.event(OrderShipped(order));
```

The servers must use the [Redis adapter](../packages/socketio.md#many-servers-redis-adapter).
When the emitter is for another namespace than `/`, use `SocketIoEmitter(redis).of('/chat')`.
With no server and no emitter, `Broadcast.event` throws a `StateError`.

To send from a [queue](queue.md) job, use [queued broadcasting](#queued-broadcasting).

## Whisper

A whisper lets a client send an event to the other members of a private or presence channel. A typical use is "is typing".
The server only passes it on.

It is off by default. A whisper lets clients message each other with no code of yours in between. So you choose to allow it:

```dart
SocketIoConfig(broadcasting: true, whisper: true);
```

The client sends `client event` with `{channel, event, data}`. The event name must start with `client-`.
The other sockets in the channel get the event with `(channel, data)`:

```js
socket.emit('client event', {
  channel: 'presence-chat.lobby',
  event: 'client-typing',
  data: { name: 'Alice' },
}, (ack) => console.log(ack)); // the ack is optional

socket.on('client-typing', (channel, data) => console.log(channel, data));
```

- Only a socket that subscribed to the channel can whisper.
- Only private and presence channels allow it. A public channel does not.
- The sender does not get its own whisper. Its other sockets do.
- It works across isolates and servers with the Redis adapter.
- A whisper is dropped when its data is bigger than `Broadcast.maxWhisperSize`. The default is 10 KB of JSON.
- When a whisper is refused, the ack is `{ok: false, error}`. The error is, for example, `not subscribed` or `data is too big`.
- With whisper off, a `client event` is ignored, with no ack.
- The `client-` prefix keeps a whisper apart from server events. Do not give a server event (`broadcastAs`) a name that starts with `client-`.
- The event names and the whisper format follow Laravel Echo. So `channel.whisper('typing', data)` and `listenForWhisper('typing', ...)` use the same names.
- Laravel Echo sends `auth` as an object of headers. This server refuses that. So Echo can not join a private or presence channel on its own. Log the socket in with [`SocketAuth`](../packages/socketio.md#log-in-a-socket), or send your own `subscribe` with the token, as shown in [The client](#the-client). Then whispers work.

## Limits and settings

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Broadcast.maxChannelLength` | `200` | the longest channel name a client may subscribe to |
| `Broadcast.maxChannelsPerSocket` | `100` | the most channels for one socket |
| `Broadcast.tokenLifetime` | 1 minute | how long a token from the auth route works |
| `Broadcast.presenceTimeout` | 2 seconds | how long a presence join or leave waits for other servers |
| `Broadcast.maxWhisperSize` | 10 KB | the biggest `data` of a [whisper](#whisper), in bytes of JSON |

- It needs `APP_KEY`, to sign the tokens.
- Turn broadcasting on for one namespace only. With two namespaces, both accept `subscribe`, but `Broadcast.event` sends only through the last one.
- A presence `subscribe` is refused when a server does not answer in time. A leave still sends `presence:leaving`.
- Presence joins and leaves of one channel run one after another in each isolate. During a Redis outage, each one waits up to `presenceTimeout`, so keep it short.
- When two sockets of one user join or leave at the same moment on two isolates or servers, `presence:joining` or `presence:leaving` can be missed or sent twice.
- A client cannot send events to the other clients of a channel, unless you turn on [whispers](#whisper).

## Testing

`Broadcast.fake()` keeps the events and sends nothing:

```dart
test('shipping an order broadcasts', () async {
  BroadcastFake fake = Broadcast.fake();

  await shipOrder(order);

  fake.assertBroadcasted<OrderShipped>();
  fake.assertBroadcastedOn<OrderShipped>('private-orders.${order.id}');
  fake.assertBroadcastedTimes<OrderShipped>(1);
});
```

| Method | Passes when |
| --- | --- |
| `assertBroadcasted<T>([test])` | an event of type `T` was sent. With `test`, one of them passes it |
| `assertBroadcastedOn<T>(name)` | `T` was sent on the channel `name`, with its `private-` or `presence-` prefix |
| `assertBroadcastedTimes<T>(n)` | `T` was sent exactly `n` times |
| `assertNotBroadcasted<T>()` | no `T` was sent |
| `assertNothingBroadcasted()` | no event was sent |

A failed assert throws an `AssertionError`.
`fake.eventsOf<T>()` gives the events, and `fake.clear()` forgets them.
`Broadcast.restore()` turns the fake off.
`Broadcast.reset()` forgets the rules, the emitter and the fake. Call it in `tearDown`.

# Scheduler

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/scheduler/

# Scheduler

`dox_scheduler` runs your tasks on a schedule, like cron.

You write the schedule in Dart, in one file.
Each task is a plain function.
A task runs once per tick, even when many isolates or servers run the schedule.

## Install

```bash
dox add scheduler
```

It adds the package and writes the three files below. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.
A new app already has it.

### Set it up by hand

```bash
dart pub add dox_scheduler
```

## Set up in a Dox app

A new app from `dox create` already has these files. In another app, add them:

- `lib/config/schedule.dart`: the tasks and the `ScheduleConfig`. See [Define tasks](#define-tasks).
- `bin/schedule.dart`: the program that runs the schedule. See [Run the schedule](#run-the-schedule).
- `lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart` (optional): runs the schedule inside the server. See [Run inside the server](#run-inside-the-server).

Then start it next to your server:

```bash
dart run bin/schedule.dart work
```

## Without Dox

`dox_scheduler` also works in a plain Dart app. Leave out `app`:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old files, ...
}

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule).run(args);
}
```

- With no `app`, no providers start, and the locks use a memory store.
- For many servers, pass a shared lock store: `SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule, store: myRedisStore)`.
  It is a `CacheStore` from `dox_cache`.
- The commands are the same. See [Run the schedule](#run-the-schedule).

## Define tasks

Put the tasks in `lib/config/schedule.dart`.

```dart
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig();

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
  s.call('report', sendReport).hourly();
  s.call('ping', ping).cron('*/5 * * * *').timezone('Asia/Yangon');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old rows, files, ...
}
```

`s.call(name, function)` adds a task.
The name must be unique. It shows in the logs and in the lock keys.
A task with no frequency runs every minute.

### Queue jobs

The scheduler does not know about queues. Wrap the job in a function:

```dart
s.call('report', () => SendReport().dispatch()).hourly();
```

The task only puts the job on the queue. A queue worker runs it.

To send the job to a queue connection, pass `connection:` to `dispatch()`:

```dart
void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('send-report', () => SendReport().dispatch()).dailyAt('08:00');
  s.call('prune', () => PruneFiles().dispatch(connection: 'redis')).hourly();
}
```

The task name must be unique in the schedule.
`connection:` of `dispatch()` is a [queue connection](queue.md#queue-connections). Without it, the main connection is used.

### Processes and dox commands

```dart
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['-f', 'backup.sql', 'mydb']).daily();
s.command('queue:prune', args: <String>['--hours=48']).hourly();
```

`exec(executable, args: [...])` runs a process. No shell is used, so `|`, `>` and `*` are plain text.
Use `s.exec('sh', args: <String>['-c', '...'])` when you need a shell.
A non-zero exit code fails the task.
Its stdin is closed, so a program that waits for input ends at once.
With `timeout()`, the process gets SIGTERM when the time is up, and SIGKILL 5 seconds later (`Schedule.processGrace`).
Only the process itself is killed. The children of a shell (`sh -c 'a | b'`) may live on.
A stop of `work` waits for the process to end.

`command(command, args: [...])` runs a `dox` command of your app, as the process `dox <command> <args>`.
When `dox` is not on PATH, set its full path: `Schedule.doxExecutable = '/usr/local/bin/dox';`.

The task name is the command line, like `dox queue:prune --hours=48`.
It shows in the logs, the lock keys and `list`.
So do not put a secret (like `--token=...`) in `args` without your own name: `s.command('sync', args: <String>['--token=$token'], name: 'sync')`.
A name also lets you add the same command line twice.

The output is dropped. Use the [output hooks](#output-hooks) to keep it.

## Frequencies

| Method | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `everySecond()` | every second. Also `everyTwoSeconds`, `everyFiveSeconds`, `everyTenSeconds`, `everyFifteenSeconds`, `everyTwentySeconds`, `everyThirtySeconds` |
| `everyMinute()` | every minute (the default) |
| `everyTwoMinutes()` | every 2 minutes |
| `everyThreeMinutes()` | every 3 minutes |
| `everyFourMinutes()` | every 4 minutes |
| `everyFiveMinutes()` | every 5 minutes |
| `everyTenMinutes()` | every 10 minutes |
| `everyFifteenMinutes()` | every 15 minutes |
| `everyThirtyMinutes()` | at minute 0 and 30 |
| `hourly()` | at minute 0 of every hour |
| `hourlyAt(17)` | at minute 17 of every hour |
| `everyTwoHours()` | every 2 hours at minute 0. Also `everyThreeHours`, `everyFourHours`, `everySixHours`. Pass a minute: `everyTwoHours(15)` |
| `everyOddHour()` | at 01:00, 03:00 ... 23:00. Pass a minute: `everyOddHour(30)` |
| `daily()` | every day at 00:00 |
| `dailyAt('13:00')` | every day at 13:00 |
| `twiceDaily(1, 13)` | every day at 01:00 and 13:00 |
| `twiceDailyAt(1, 13, 15)` | every day at 01:15 and 13:15 |
| `at('13:00')` | same as `dailyAt('13:00')` |
| `weekly()` | every Sunday at 00:00 |
| `weeklyOn(DateTime.monday, '08:00')` | every Monday at 08:00 |
| `monthly()` | the 1st of every month at 00:00 |
| `monthlyOn(15, '12:00')` | the 15th of every month at 12:00 |
| `twiceMonthly(1, 16, '13:00')` | the 1st and 16th of every month at 13:00 |
| `lastDayOfMonth('15:00')` | the last day of every month at 15:00 |
| `quarterly()` | January, April, July and October 1st at 00:00 |
| `quarterlyOn(4, '14:00')` | January, April, July and October 4th at 14:00 |
| `yearly()` | January 1st at 00:00 |
| `yearlyOn(6, 1, '17:00')` | June 1st at 17:00. A day the month never has, like `yearlyOn(2, 30)`, throws |
| `cron('*/5 9-17 * * 1-5')` | any 5 field cron expression |

A task that runs every few seconds repeats inside each due minute.
A frequency, the days, the filters and `timezone()` still decide if the minute is due: `s.call('poll', poll).everyFiveSeconds().between('09:00', '17:00')`.
Call the seconds method first, then the other frequency.
`everyFiveSeconds()` also sets the task to every minute. If you call it last, it undoes the frequency before it.
`.everyFiveSeconds().hourly()` repeats in minute 0 of each hour. `.hourly().everyFiveSeconds()` repeats in every minute.
`when()` and `skip()` are checked before each repeat.
A run that takes longer than its step skips the steps it missed.
With such a task, `run` from cron stays until the end of the minute.

You can limit the days. The order does not matter between the day methods (like `weekdays()` or `mondays()`) and a time method like `dailyAt()`.
The day methods, `weekly()`, `weeklyOn()` and `cron()` all write the day of the week. The last call wins: `.mondays().weekly()` runs on Sundays.
`weekly()` and `weeklyOn()` also set the time, to 00:00 unless you pass one. So call `dailyAt()` after them, or pass the time to `weeklyOn()`: `.dailyAt('09:00').weekly()` runs at 00:00, but `.weekly().dailyAt('09:00')` runs at 09:00.

| Method | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `weekdays()` | Monday to Friday |
| `weekends()` | Saturday and Sunday |
| `mondays()` ... `sundays()` | only on that day of the week |
| `days(<int>[DateTime.monday, DateTime.friday])` | only on these days |

```dart
s.call('standup', remind).weekdays().dailyAt('09:00');
```

A day of the month and a day of the week join with OR, like cron.
`monthlyOn(15).fridays()` runs on the 15th and on every Friday.
`lastDayOfMonth()` is different: it runs only on the last day of the month.
`lastDayOfMonth().fridays()` runs on every last day of the month, on any day of the week. The `fridays()` part has no effect.

### Cron expressions

`cron()` takes the standard 5 fields: `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`.

| Field | Values |
| --- | --- |
| minute | 0-59 |
| hour | 0-23 |
| day of month | 1-31 |
| month | 1-12 or `JAN`-`DEC` |
| day of week | 0-7 or `SUN`-`SAT` (0 and 7 are Sunday) |

Each field takes `*`, a number `5`, a range `1-5`, a list `1,15`, and a step `*/15` or `0-30/10`.

When both day fields are set, a day matches when **either** field matches.
This is the standard cron rule. `0 0 1 * MON` runs on the 1st of the month and on every Monday.
When one day field starts with `*`, both must match.

## Time zones

The schedule uses UTC by default.
Use `timezone()` to read the time in another zone:

```dart
s.call('report', sendReport).dailyAt('08:00').timezone('Asia/Yangon');
```

The name is an IANA name, like `Europe/London` or `America/New_York`.
The zone data comes from the `timezone` package.

To use one zone for every task, set it in the config.
A task's own `timezone()` still wins.

```dart
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(timezone: 'Asia/Yangon');
```

An unknown name throws an `ArgumentError` when the schedule starts.

With summer time (DST):

- A time that does not exist that day (it is skipped when the clock goes forward) does not run that day.
- A time that happens twice (when the clock goes back) runs once.
- `hourly()` and other "every" frequencies keep running every real hour.

## Filters

```dart
s.call('sync', sync).everyFiveMinutes().between('09:00', '17:00');
s.call('night', night).hourly().between('22:00', '06:00'); // crosses midnight
s.call('quiet', quiet).hourly().unlessBetween('23:00', '04:00');
s.call('emails', sendEmails).daily().environments(<String>['production']);
s.call('promo', promo).daily().when(isPromoOn);
s.call('backup', backup).daily().skip(isHoliday);
```

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `between('09:00', '17:00')` | runs only in this time of day, both ends included, in the task zone |
| `unlessBetween('23:00', '04:00')` | does not run in this time of day, both ends included, in the task zone |
| `environments(<String>['production'])` | runs only when `APP_ENV` is one of these names. Case and spaces around the names do not matter. When `APP_ENV` is not set or empty, the task does not run. It is read at run time. An empty list or a blank name throws |
| `when(function)` | runs only when the function gives `true` |
| `skip(function)` | does not run when the function gives `true` |

`when` and `skip` take a function that gives a `bool` or a `Future<bool>`.

## Options

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `withoutOverlapping()` | does not start while the last run still runs |
| `onOneServer()` | runs once per tick across isolates and servers. **On by default** |
| `onEveryServer()` | runs on every process that runs the schedule |
| `runInBackground()` | the next task of the same minute does not wait for this one |
| `timeout(Duration(minutes: 5))` | counts the run as failed when it takes longer. It kills the process of an `exec()` or `command()` task |

### withoutOverlapping

A lock is held while the task runs.
When the next minute comes and the lock is still held, the task is skipped.
The lock expires after 24 hours, in case the process dies.
Pass another expiry like this: `withoutOverlapping(Duration(hours: 1))`.

When the process crashes, the lock stays in the store.
The task is then skipped until the lock expires.
To run it again at once, remove the lock with [`clear-cache`](#clear-cache):

```bash
dox schedule:clear-cache
```

### Once per tick

Before a task runs, the scheduler takes a lock named after the task and the minute.
The first process to take it runs the task. The others skip it.
The lock is not released, so a late server can not run the same minute again. It expires after 10 minutes.

The locks use a [cache](cache.md) store.

!!! warning "Many servers need Redis"
    A `memory` store lives inside one process. A `file` store lives on one machine.
    It works for one `work` process, or for many isolates of one server.
    When many servers run the schedule, set a Redis store:
    `ScheduleConfig(store: 'redis')`.

When the store has no locks (`null`), the scheduler uses a memory store.

At start, the scheduler prints one warning to stderr when a task uses `onOneServer()` and the lock store is `memory` or `file` (or `null`).
These stores are not shared between servers, so the lock works only inside one server.
The warning does not print when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`, because a dev machine is one server.
With one server you can ignore it.

### Timeout

Dart can not stop a running function.
After the timeout, the run counts as failed and the hooks run, but the work may go on.
The process of an `exec()` or `command()` task is killed at the timeout.

## Hooks

```dart
s
    .call('report', sendReport)
    .daily()
    .before(logStart)
    .onSuccess(logDone)
    .onFailure(alertTeam)
    .after(cleanUp);

Future<void> alertTeam(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
  await notifyTeam('report failed: $error');
}
```

| Hook | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `before` | before the task. When it throws, the task does not run and counts as failed |
| `onSuccess` | after the task worked |
| `onFailure` | after the task threw or timed out. It gets the error and the stack trace |
| `after` | after the task, always |

An error in a task is logged and the next task still runs.

### Output hooks

These work on `exec()` and `command()` tasks. On a function task they do nothing.

| Hook | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `sendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log')` | writes the output (stdout and stderr) to the file. It replaces the file each run |
| `appendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log')` | adds the output to the end of the file |
| `onOutput((String output) {...})` | gets the output after the process ends |

- The file gets the output as it comes. `onOutput` holds the whole output in memory, so do not use it for a very large output.
- Two runs at the same time write to the same file. Use `withoutOverlapping()` or `appendOutputTo()`.
- A file that can not be written fails the task. `onOutput` still gets the output first.
- A throwing `onOutput` hook fails the task.
- When more than one thing fails, the task fails with the first of: a non-zero exit code, an `onOutput` error, a file error.
- After a timeout, the file and `onOutput` finish a bit later, after the failure hooks ran. An error there is lost.

### Ping hooks

```dart
s
    .call('backup', backup)
    .daily()
    .pingBefore('https://health.example.com/backup/start')
    .pingOnSuccess('https://health.example.com/backup')
    .pingOnFailure('https://health.example.com/backup/fail');
```

| Hook | Sends a GET request |
| --- | --- |
| `pingBefore(url)` | before the task |
| `thenPing(url)` | after the task, always |
| `pingOnSuccess(url)` | after the task worked |
| `pingOnFailure(url)` | after the task failed |

Each one also has an `If` form that takes a bool first, like `pingOnFailureIf(isProduction, url)`.

- A ping fails after 10 seconds (`ScheduledTask.pingTimeout`), or on a status of 400 or more.
- A failed ping is logged. It never fails the task.
- A url that is not `http` or `https` throws an `ArgumentError` when the schedule is made.
- In tests, replace the request: `ScheduledTask.sendPing = (Uri url) async {...};`.

## Run the schedule

`bin/schedule.dart` runs the schedule:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(
    schedule: schedule,
    app: appConfig,
    config: scheduleConfig,
  ).run(args);
}
```

With `app`, the runner starts your app providers first (like the database).
It stops them at the end.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `dart run bin/schedule.dart work` | runs due tasks at every minute until you stop it. The default |
| `dart run bin/schedule.dart run` | runs the tasks due this minute once, then exits |
| `dart run bin/schedule.dart list` | shows each task, its schedule and its next run time |
| `dart run bin/schedule.dart test cleanup` | runs one task now |
| `dart run bin/schedule.dart clear-cache` | removes the `withoutOverlapping()` locks, after a crash |

The `dox` CLI runs the same file: `dox schedule:work`, `dox schedule:run`, `dox schedule:list`, `dox schedule:test <name>` and `dox schedule:clear-cache`.

### work

`work` is a long running process. Run it next to your server, with the same deploy tool (systemd, Docker, Kubernetes).

It wakes at each full minute and runs the due tasks.
With a task that runs every few seconds, it also wakes inside the minute.
On Ctrl+C or SIGTERM it starts no new task and waits for the running ones.
A second signal stops it at once.

### run

`run` is for a system cron. Add one line to the crontab:

```bash
* * * * * cd /path/to/app/build/bundle && ./bin/schedule run
```

It runs the tasks of this minute, waits for them, and exits.
The exit code is 1 when a task failed.

`./bin/schedule` is the binary that `dox build` makes in `build/bundle`. It starts fast and needs no Dart SDK.
Do not use `dart compile exe`. It can not build apps with native libraries, like SQLite.

### list

```
Task     Schedule                   Next run
cleanup  0 2 * * *                  2026-10-26 02:00 UTC
report   0 * * * *                  2026-10-25 14:00 UTC
ping     */5 * * * * Asia/Yangon    2026-10-25 20:35 Asia/Yangon
```

The next run time checks the frequency, `between()` and `unlessBetween()`. It does not check `when()`, `skip()` and `environments()`.

`lastDayOfMonth()` shows `28-31` in the day field, but it runs only on the last day of the month.
The next run time is right.

### test

`test <name>` runs one task now, with its hooks.
It does not check the schedule, the filters or the locks.

### clear-cache

`clear-cache` removes the `withoutOverlapping()` lock of each task in the schedule.
Use it after a crash, when a task is skipped because its lock is still there.

```
$ dox schedule:clear-cache
Removed the overlap lock of report.
```

When there is no lock, it prints this:

```
No overlap locks found. Nothing to clear.
```

The exit code is 0 in both cases.

It removes only the lock key of each task, by its exact name.
Other keys in the cache store stay.
It does not remove the once-per-tick locks of `onOneServer()`. Each one is for one minute only, and it expires after 10 minutes.

!!! warning "Only when the task is not running"
    Do not run it while a task really runs on another process or server.
    That task could then start a second time.

A `memory` store lives inside one process, so its locks end with the process.
`clear-cache` is for `file` and Redis stores.

## Run inside the server

You can run the schedule inside your Dox server instead of a `work` process.
Add a provider that extends `SchedulerProvider`:

```dart
// lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';

class ScheduleProvider extends SchedulerProvider {
  ScheduleProvider() : super(schedule: schedule, config: scheduleConfig);
}
```

Then turn it on in `lib/config/schedule.dart`:

```dart
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true);
```

Run `dart run build_runner build`. The generated container finds the provider.

How it works:

- Only the first isolate runs the tasks. The other isolates only serve requests.
- With many servers, each server runs the loop. The once-per-tick lock makes each task run once. Use a Redis store for this.
- When the server stops, it waits for the running tasks.

Trade-offs:

- Tasks use the CPU of the server, so they can slow down requests on the first isolate.
- A long task makes the server stop slower.
- With a separate `work` process, you can deploy, scale and restart the scheduler on its own.

Use `work` for heavy tasks. Use the in-process provider for small apps.

## Testing

`Scheduler` runs the tasks. Give it a fake clock to test a schedule with no waiting:

```dart
import 'package:dox_cache/dox_cache.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

class FakeClock extends ScheduleClock {
  FakeClock(this.time);

  DateTime time;

  @override
  DateTime now() {
    return time;
  }
}

test('cleanup runs at 02:00', () async {
  Schedule s = Schedule(timezone: scheduleConfig.timezone);
  schedule(s);
  Scheduler scheduler = Scheduler(
    tasks: s.tasks,
    store: CacheStore(MemoryDriver()),
    clock: FakeClock(DateTime.utc(2026, 10, 25, 2)),
  );
  Map<String, TaskOutcome> outcomes = await scheduler.runDue();
  expect(outcomes['cleanup'], TaskOutcome.ran);
});
```

`ScheduledTask.isDue(time)` and `ScheduledTask.nextRun(time)` check a schedule with no run at all.


---

# File Storage

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/file-storage/

# File Storage

`Storage()` saves and reads files on a disk: the local folder, AWS S3 (and R2, MinIO, Spaces), or memory.

It is in the [`dox_storage`](../packages/storage.md) package. A new project already has it.

```dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

Route.post('/avatar', (DoxRequest req) async {
  RequestFile file = req.input('avatar');
  String path = await Storage().putFile('avatars', file);
  return <String, String>{'path': path}; // /avatars/<uuid>.png
});
```

## Install

```bash
dox add storage
```

It writes `lib/config/storage.dart`, the provider, the `storage` folder and the `STORAGE_DISK=local` key. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.
Add `--disk=s3` to also add an `s3` disk and the `AWS_*` keys. `STORAGE_DISK` stays `local`, so the app starts before you fill in the keys. Fill them in, then set `STORAGE_DISK=s3`.
To set it up by hand, follow [Config](#config).

## Config

A new project already has `lib/config/storage.dart`, with one `local` disk in the `storage` folder.
`STORAGE_DISK` in `.env` picks the default disk.
To add disks, edit the file. This example adds a `url` to the local disk, an `s3` disk and a `memory` disk:

```dart title="lib/config/storage.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': 'https://app.test/files', // for signedUrl(); url() gives /storage/<path> without it
    },

    /// only when AWS_BUCKET is set
    if (env.awsBucket != null)
      's3': <String, dynamic>{
        'driver': 's3',
        'bucket': env.awsBucket,
        'region': env.awsDefaultRegion,
        'key': env.awsAccessKeyId,
        'secret': env.awsSecretAccessKey,
        'endpoint': env.awsEndpoint, // R2, MinIO, Spaces
      },
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
  },
);
```

A local disk writes a file in place by default. To write to a temp file and rename it when the write is done, add `'atomic_writes': true` to the disk. A failed or stopped upload then never leaves a partial file, and the old file stays. It is off by default.
The rename makes a new file. So the folder must be writable, the file gets the default mode and the owner of the app, a hard link keeps the old content, and a symlink is replaced.

```dart
'local': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'storage', 'atomic_writes': true},
```

A local disk has no per-file access rules by default. `setVisibility()` does nothing there, and `getVisibility()` gives the disk `visibility`.
To make visibility the file mode, add `'permissions': true`. It is off by default.
Then `setVisibility()` runs `chmod` and `getVisibility()` reads the mode of the file.
The modes are: public file `0644`, private file `0600`, public folder `0755`, private folder `0700`.
To change them, give a map with a `file` and a `dir` key. Each has a `public` and a `private` mode. A mode that is not there keeps its default. A key that is not one of these is ignored.
Each mode must be an int from 0 to 0x1ff (0777). A string like `'0644'`, a negative number or a bigger number throws `ArgumentError` when the disk is made.
Dart has no octal numbers, so write the modes in hex. `0x1a0` is `0640`, `0x1e8` is `0750`:

```dart
'local': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'storage', 'permissions': true},
'private': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 'local',
  'root': 'storage-private',
  'visibility': 'private',
  'permissions': <String, dynamic>{
    'file': <String, int>{'public': 0x1a4, 'private': 0x1a0},
    'dir': <String, int>{'public': 0x1ed, 'private': 0x1e8},
  },
},
```

How it works:

- The mode is set before the content is written. A private file is never readable by others, not even for a moment.
- A new file gets the visibility of the write, or the disk `visibility`.
- An overwrite, `append()` and `prepend()` keep the mode the file has, unless the call gives a visibility.
- A `copy()` gets the visibility of the call, or else the mode of the source. It is written to a temp file first and then renamed. Listings hide that temp file. A copy onto a symlink replaces the link.
- A `move()` keeps the mode, unless the call gives a visibility.
- Folders that a write creates get the folder mode. Folders that were there before, and the disk root, keep their mode.
- `getVisibility()` reads the real mode. The private mode is private. Any other mode is public.
- `getVisibility()` and `setVisibility()` of a symlink throw `UnsupportedOperationException`.
- When the `chmod` fails, a file that the write created is removed.
- Windows has no `chmod`. There `permissions` does nothing.

The `s3` disk reads five keys that a new project does not have yet. Add them to
`lib/config/env.dart` and run `dart run build_runner build`. They are nullable,
and the `s3` disk is only added when `AWS_BUCKET` is set. So the app starts without them:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
  String? get awsBucket;

  String get awsDefaultRegion => 'us-east-1';

  String? get awsAccessKeyId;

  String? get awsSecretAccessKey;

  /// R2, MinIO or Spaces. Null for AWS.
  String? get awsEndpoint;
```

The provider of a new project sets these disks in every isolate. It is in `lib/providers/`, so the generated container finds it:

```dart title="lib/providers/storage_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/storage.dart';

class AppStorageProvider extends StorageProvider {
  AppStorageProvider() : super(storageConfig);
}
```

| Driver | Options |
| --- | --- |
| `local` | `root` (default `storage`), `url`, `app_key` (default: your APP_KEY), `visibility`, `atomic_writes`, `permissions` |
| `s3` | `bucket`, `region`, `key`, `secret`, `token`, `endpoint`, `path_style` (MinIO), `url` (CDN), `visibility`, `acl`, `batch_delete` |
| `memory` | none. For tests |

The `s3` disk needs `bucket`, `key` and `secret`. When one is missing, the app stops at start with an `ArgumentError` that names the setting.

## Functions

```dart
// save with a new uuid file name, returns '/images/<uuid>.png'
String path = await Storage().putFile('images', file);  // a RequestFile
Uint8List bytes = Uint8List.fromList(<int>[1, 2, 3]);
String path2 = await Storage().putFile('images', bytes, extension: 'png');
String path3 = await Storage().put('images', bytes, extension: 'png'); // like putFile
String path4 = await Storage().putFileAs('avatars', file, 'user-1.png'); // your own name

// save to this exact path. String, List<int> or Stream<List<int>>
await Storage().put('notes/a.txt', 'hello', exact: true);

Uint8List? found = await Storage().get(path);  // null when missing
bool exists = await Storage().exists(path);           // files only
bool gone = await Storage().missing(path);            // not exists()
bool folder = await Storage().directoryExists('images');
await Storage().delete(path);

await Storage().copy('notes/a.txt', 'backup/a.txt');
await Storage().move('backup/a.txt', 'old/a.txt');

List<String> files = await Storage().files('images');         // direct files only
List<String> all = await Storage().allFiles('images');        // in sub-folders too
List<String> folders = await Storage().directories('images'); // direct sub-folders
await Storage().deleteDirectory('old');                       // the folder and its files

await Storage().setVisibility(path, Visibility.private);
Visibility visibility = await Storage().getVisibility(path);

int size = await Storage().size(path);                 // throws when missing
DateTime changed = await Storage().lastModified(path); // throws when missing

await Storage().append('logs/app.log', 'new line');    // a missing file is made
await Storage().prepend('logs/app.log', 'first line');
await Storage().makeDirectory('reports');              // local disk only

String url = await Storage().url(path);         // /storage/<path> when the disk has no `url`
String signed = await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10));
String same = await Storage().temporaryUrl(path); // the same as signedUrl()

// another disk
await Storage().disk('s3').put('reports/2026.pdf', bytes, exact: true);
```

`put()` and `putFile()` make a new uuid name in the folder and return the path. For bytes, they find the extension from the bytes, or you pass `extension:`.
`put()` with `exact: true` writes to the exact path, and replaces an old file there. It takes a `String`, a `List<int>` or a `Stream<List<int>>`, and returns the path.
`putFileAs()` uses your name, and replaces an old file with the same name.

`files()`, `allFiles()` and `directories()` give paths that start with `/`, like `putFile()`.
On S3 and memory disks, a folder is there when a file is under it.

`deleteDirectory()` deletes a folder and every file in it. A missing folder is not an error.
It refuses the root (`''` or `/`) with `InvalidKeyException`, so a wrong path can not empty the disk.
To empty a whole disk on purpose, use `Storage().use().deleteAll()`.

`copy()` and `move()` replace an old file at the new path. On S3 the copy runs inside S3, so the bytes do not pass through your app.
`copy()`, `move()`, `getVisibility()` and `setVisibility()` of a missing file answer `404`. On a local disk, a `copy()` or `move()` of a missing file makes no folders.

On S3, `setVisibility()` sets the ACL when `acl` is on (the default). With `'acl': false` (R2 and similar), `setVisibility()` does nothing, and `getVisibility()` gives the disk `visibility`, also for a missing file.
On a local disk, `setVisibility()` needs the `permissions` option, see [Config](#config).

On a local disk with no `url` option, `url()` gives `/storage/<path>` (no host). Dox serves it only when you add `Storage.route('storage', signed: false)`. `signedUrl()` still needs `url`.

`get()` gives `null` for a missing file, but `size()` and `lastModified()` throw `FileNotFoundException`.

`append()` and `prepend()` add a new line between the old and the new text, but only when the file is not empty. Change it with `separator`.
They keep the visibility and content type of the file.
They read the file and write it back, so two writers at the same time can lose a write.

`makeDirectory()` makes a folder only on a local disk. On any other disk it does nothing.

`exists()` finds files only. `directoryExists()` finds folders. On a local disk it checks the real folder. On S3 and memory disks, a folder exists when a file is under it.

`directoryExists('')` is always true on every disk: the empty path is the root.

`putFile` with a `RequestFile`, on the local disk, moves the upload temp file (with `permissions` on, it streams it). It does not read it into memory.

An uploaded file can store itself. `store` gives it a new uuid name, like `putFile`. `storeAs` uses your name, like `putFileAs`, and replaces an old file with the same name. Both take `disk:`:

```dart
RequestFile file = req.input('image');
String path = await file.store('images');
String onS3 = await file.store('images', disk: 's3');
String avatar = await file.storeAs('avatars', 'user-1.png');
```

`storeAs` and `putFileAs` use the name as it is. Do not use the file name from the client. Make your own name, like `user-1.png`.

`putFile` and `file.store()` take the extension of an upload from the file name. When the bytes are a known format (png, jpg, pdf, zip, ...) that does not match the name, the extension of the bytes is used. So a png sent as `a.html` is saved as `.png` and is never served as a web page.

### `stream` and `download`

```dart
Route.get('/photo', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().stream(req.input('path'));    // shown in the browser
});

Route.get('/report', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().disk('s3').download('reports/2024.pdf'); // saved as a file
});
```

Both read the file as a stream, from any disk, with `Content-Length`.
A big file is never loaded into memory. A missing file answers `404`.

`download()` saves the file with the last part of the path as its name. Pass `name:` to pick the name:

```dart
Route.get('/invoice', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().download('invoices/42.pdf', name: 'Invoice 42.pdf');
});
```

Any name is safe in the header. Quotes are escaped, a new line becomes `_`, and a name like `résumé.pdf` is also sent as `filename*=UTF-8''r%C3%A9sum%C3%A9.pdf`.

To add headers, put the download in a `response()`:

```dart
Route.get('/invoice', (DoxRequest req) async {
  DownloadableFile file = await Storage().download('invoices/42.pdf');
  return response(file).header('Cache-Control', 'no-store');
});
```

### Full disk API

`Storage().use('s3')` returns the `dox_storage` `Disk`: `listAll` with pages, `getMetaData`,
`putStream`, `deleteAll`, write options and more. See [dox_storage](../packages/storage.md).

## Serve local signed URLs

```dart
// lib/routes/web.dart
Storage.route('files');                    // GET /files/{key*}, signed URLs only
Storage.route('public', signed: false);    // any file of the disk
Storage.route('docs', disk: 'memory', signed: false); // another disk than the default
Storage.route('uploads', download: true);  // every file is a download
```

An html, svg, xml or javascript file is always sent as a download in a sandbox, so its script does not run on your site.
Every file has `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.

```dart
String url = await Storage().signedUrl('invoices/1.pdf'); // https://app.test/files/invoices/1.pdf?expires=...&signature=...
```

A missing, wrong or expired signature answers `403`.
Signed URLs work only on a `local` disk. For another disk, use `signed: false`.
A signed URL works only on the route of its own disk.
An old signed URL, made before the disk name was part of the signature, still works on any local disk with the same app key. This ends when it expires.
Set the disk `url` option to the full URL of the route (`https://app.test/files`).

## Tests

To swap a disk with a memory disk in tests, see [Testing](testing.md#test-file-storage).

## Your own driver

Implement `DriverContract` from `package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart`. Register it in a [provider](providers.md), so every isolate has it:

```dart
Storage.manager.register('dropbox', DropboxDriver());
await Storage().disk('dropbox').put('notes/a.txt', 'hello', exact: true);
```

# Environment Variables

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/env/

# Environment Variables

Declare your env keys once, in a typed class.

Then `env.appPort` is an `int`, your IDE suggests every key, and a missing key stops the app at startup.

## The typed env class

A new project already has `lib/config/env.dart`. Its keys are listed in the [Env reference](../reference/env.md#read-by-a-new-project). This example shows the kinds of getters you can write:

```dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

enum LogLevel { debug, info, error }

@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName;                       // APP_NAME, required
  String get appKey;                        // APP_KEY, required
  int get dbPort => 5432;                   // DB_PORT, default 5432
  bool get appDebug => false;               // APP_DEBUG, default false
  LogLevel get logLevel => LogLevel.info;   // LOG_LEVEL=debug
  Duration get cacheTtl => const Duration(minutes: 5); // CACHE_TTL=5m
  List<String> get corsOrigins => <String>[];          // CORS_ORIGINS=a.com,b.com

  @EnvKey('AWS_BUCKET')
  String? get s3Bucket;                     // optional, null when not set
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after each change to the class. It writes `env.g.dart`. Then use `env` anywhere:

```dart
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(port: env.dbPort /* int */, ...),
  },
);
```

### The rules

- **Key**: the getter name in UPPER_SNAKE case. `appName` reads `APP_NAME`, `s3Bucket` reads `S3_BUCKET`. A run of capitals is one word: `dbURL` reads `DB_URL`. Use `@EnvKey('X')` for another name.
- **Default**: the getter body. It can be any expression, like `Platform.numberOfProcessors`. It runs only when the key is missing. A default can read another env getter and sees its loaded value: `String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:$appPort';` uses the real `APP_PORT`.
- **Every getter is a key**: an env getter is always one env key and nothing more. Also a getter whose body uses other getters: `appUrl` above reads `APP_URL`, and when `APP_URL` is set, it wins over the body.
- **No computed values**: a value like "is development" is not an env key, so it does not go in the env class. Use `appConfig.isDevelopment` from the app config. It is `true` when `APP_ENV` is `development`.
- **Use the getter, not `env`**: in a default, write `appEnv`, never `env.appEnv`. The global `env` is not ready while it loads. The app stops at startup with a `StateError`: "A default of AppEnv reads the global `env`. Use the getter directly".
- **Only this class**: the builder reads the getters of the `@DoxEnv()` class itself. Getters from a superclass or a mixin are not read from the env. A field (`final String x = ...;`) is a build error: use a getter.
- **Optional**: a nullable getter with no body (`String? get s3Bucket;`). It is `null` when the key is missing.
- **Required**: any other getter with no body. A missing key stops the app.
- **Empty**: an empty value (or the text `null`) counts as missing.

### Types

| Type | Value in `.env` |
|------|-----------------|
| `String` | any text |
| `int`, `double`, `num` | `3000`, `0.5` |
| `bool` | `true`/`false`, `1`/`0`, `yes`/`no`, `on`/`off` (any case) |
| `Uri` | `https://dox.dev` |
| `Duration` | a number and a unit: `500ms`, `30s`, `5m`, `2h`, `1d`. A plain number is seconds: `300` is 5 minutes. |
| an enum | the name of a value, any case: `debug` |
| `List<String>` | comma separated: `a, b, c`. Empty items are dropped. |

Any other type is a build error.

### Fail fast

`AppEnv.load()` reads every key one time. Then it checks them all, and throws one `EnvException` that lists every missing or bad key:

```
EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing
  - DB_PORT must be an int
```

The error names the key, never the value. A value may be a secret, and this text goes to the log and to CI output.

This happens once, when the app starts. After that, `env.dbPort` is a plain field read.

## Where values come from

Dox reads values from these places:

1. Real environment variables (set in the shell, Docker or systemd).
2. In tests only: the `.env.testing` file. See [Testing: a test database](testing.md#use-a-test-database-with-envtesting).
3. The `.env` file in the folder where you start the app. It is optional.

!!! info "The environment wins"
    A real environment variable wins over the `.env` file.
    So you can keep `.env` for development and use real variables in production.

### The `.env` file

```ini title=".env"
APP_NAME=dox
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>
DB_PORT=5432
```

- One `KEY=value` per line.
- Quotes around a value are removed. So `APP_NAME="My app"` gives `My app`. Use `"`, `'` or `` ` ``.
- A `=` inside the value is kept: `TOKEN=a=b` gives `a=b`.
- A line that starts with `#` is a comment.
- A `#` after a space starts a comment: `APP_PORT=3000 # dev` gives `3000`.
- A `#` with no space before it is kept: `DB_PASSWORD=abc#123` gives `abc#123`, and `COLOR=#fff` gives `#fff`.
- A `#` inside quotes is kept: `DB_PASSWORD="abc # 123"` gives `abc # 123`.
- `export KEY=value` is read like `KEY=value`.
- `KEY=` (empty, or only spaces) gives the default value, like a key that is not there.
- One line is one value. A quoted value can not go over more lines, so a multi-line PEM key does not work. Turn on `envExpand` (below) and write it on one line with `\n`: `JWT_KEY="-----BEGIN KEY-----\nabc\n-----END KEY-----"`. Or keep the key in a file and put the file path in the env.

### Use one value in another

`CoreFlags.envExpand` is off by default. Turn it on to use `${OTHER}` in a value:

```ini title=".env"
HOST=localhost
PORT=3000
APP_URL=http://${HOST}:${PORT}
GREETING="Hello\nWorld"
```

- `${OTHER}` works in an unquoted value and in a `"..."` value. It does not work in `'...'`.
- Dox looks for a real environment variable first, then for a key above this line. In tests, `.env.testing` also sees the keys of `.env`.
- A name that Dox does not find stays as it is: `${OTHER}`.
- In a `"..."` value, `\n`, `\t`, `\"`, `\\` and `\$` become a new line, a tab, `"`, `\` and `$`. Use `\$` to write a `$` that is not a variable.

The `.env` file is read before `AppConfig` exists. So you must set the flag in two places:

1. `Env.flags = flags;` at the top of `main()`, before any env value is read.
2. The same flags in `AppConfig(flags: flags)`.

Set `Env.flags` at the very top of `main()`, before any env read. The first env read (like `Env.get()` or `env.appName`) loads `.env` with the flags of that moment, and the file is not read again. If the flags were not set yet, `Dox().initialize` prints a warning.

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

const CoreFlags flags = CoreFlags(envExpand: true);

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  appKey: Env.get('APP_KEY', ''),
  flags: flags,
  // ...
);
```

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';

void main() async {
  Env.flags = flags;
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
  await Dox().startServer();
}
```

`my_app` is the `name` in your `pubspec.yaml`.

A test does not run `bin/server.dart`. So set `Env.flags = flags;` at the top of the `main()` of each test file too, before the app or the client starts:

```dart title="test/http_test.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  Env.flags = flags;
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });
  // ...
}
```

Without it, `${OTHER}` stays as written in the test, and Dox prints the warning.

The server isolates follow the main isolate. You set nothing for them.
When the flag is on in `AppConfig` but `.env` was read without it, Dox prints a warning at start, once in each isolate.

## Commands

```bash
dox env:generate   # make lib/config/env.dart from .env.example
dox env:check      # load the env and print every missing or bad key
```

`dox env:generate` reads `.env.example`:

- digits become an `int` with that default: `APP_PORT=3000` gives `int get appPort => 3000;`
- `true`/`false` become a `bool` with that default
- an empty value becomes an optional `String?`
- any other value becomes a required `String`. The example value is never a default, so a secret in the example can not leak into the code.
- `#` comment lines above a key become its doc comment

It does not overwrite an existing `lib/config/env.dart`. Run `dox build_runner:build` after it.

`dox env:check` exits with code 1 when a key is missing or bad. Use it in CI or before a deploy.

## Tests

To pass your own values in a test, see [Testing](testing.md#test-the-env).

## Env.get: the low-level way

`Env.get()` reads one key by name. Use it for a key you only know at run time. For normal config, use the typed class.

```dart
Env.get<String>('APP_KEY');             // '' when missing
Env.get('APP_KEY', 'default_value');
Env.get<int>('APP_PORT', 3000);
Env.get<bool>('SOCKETIO_ENABLED', false); // true, 1, yes, on
Env.get<String?>('AWS_BUCKET');          // null when it is not set
```

A missing or empty key gives the default. With no default:

- `String` gives an empty string `''`. It is never the text `"null"`.
- `String?` and `dynamic` give `null`. With no type, like `Env.get('KEY')`, the type is `dynamic`, so you get `null`.
- `int`, `num`, `double` and `bool` throw an `ArgumentError` with the key name. A value that is not a number throws too.

`Env.get()` looks up and converts the value on every call. Do not call it on a hot path.

!!! warning "APP_KEY"
    When `APP_KEY` is missing, not 32 characters, or a public sample key, `Dox().startServer()` stops with an error.
    When `APP_ENV` is `development`, `local`, `test` or `testing`, it only logs a warning. Make a key with `dox key:generate`.

# Isolate

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/isolate/

# Isolate

This page explains how Dox runs your app on many isolates (threads), and what that means for your code.

## How it works

Dox starts many isolates. Each one runs its own [native server](native-server.md) on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections between them.

- Linux: each isolate has its own socket (`SO_REUSEPORT`).
- macOS: the isolates share one socket.
- Windows: only one isolate serves HTTP.

Each isolate has its own Rust acceptor on the port:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OS["Port 3000<br>the OS spreads the connections"] --> A1["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A2["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A3["Rust acceptor"]
    A1 --> I1["Isolate 1, main<br>own memory cache"]
    A2 --> I2["Isolate 2<br>own memory cache"]
    A3 --> I3["Isolate N<br>own memory cache"]
    I2 -. "crash: started again after 1 second" .-> I2
    I1 -. "crash: the process exits" .-> S["Supervisor restarts the process<br>Docker, systemd"]
```

With the Postgres and MySQL drivers, all isolates share one database pool in Rust. See [How Dox works](../concepts/how-dox-works.md#where-the-database-pools-live).

## How many isolates

By default Dox starts one isolate per CPU core (`Platform.numberOfProcessors`).

To change it, set `totalIsolate` in `lib/config/app.dart`. A new app reads it from `APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  totalIsolate: env.appTotalIsolate ?? Platform.numberOfProcessors,
);
```

You can also set it in code, before `startServer()`. This wins over the config:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().totalIsolate(2);
await Dox().startServer();
```

Use fewer isolates when the machine also runs the database or other heavy work.

## Each isolate has its own memory

Isolates do not share memory:

- A static value or a singleton exists once **per isolate**. When you change it in one isolate, the others do not see it.
- The `memory` cache store is per isolate. See [Cache](cache.md).
- To share data between isolates or servers, use a database, Redis or files.

`Dox().isolateId` tells you which isolate runs the code. The first isolate is `1`.

## Send a message to the other isolates

`IsolateBus` sends a message from one isolate to all the others in the same process. Use it to tell them that something changed, for example "forget this cache key". Socket.IO uses it to share broadcasts (see [Socket.IO](../packages/socketio.md#many-isolates)).

```dart
IsolateBus.instance.on('users').listen(onMessage); // in a provider's setup()
IsolateBus.instance.publish('users', <Object>['changed', 42]);
```

- A message goes to one channel. A listener on `'users'` never gets the messages of another channel.
- An isolate never gets its own message.
- `Dox().isolateCount` is the number of isolates that run, in every isolate.
- `IsolateBus.instance.size` is the number of isolates that listen, this one included.
- A message must be something a `SendPort` can send: null, bool, num, String, typed data, and lists and maps of those.
- A value that a `SendPort` can not send throws an `ArgumentError` in `publish`. Then no isolate gets the message. In the main isolate it throws only when another isolate listens on the bus. With no other isolate there, nobody gets it and nothing throws.
- It works inside one process only. For many servers, use Redis.
- There is no backpressure. `publish` never waits. A slow listener gets the messages in a queue in its memory.
- A message reaches only the isolates that listen at that moment. An isolate that calls `on()` later does not get the messages sent before.
- `size` changes a little after an isolate joins or leaves. The new number comes in a message, so it can be old for a short time.

## What each isolate does at start

Dox copies the `AppConfig`, the providers and the routes you added before `startServer()` to each new isolate. Then every isolate:

1. runs `setup()` of each provider (for example, it opens the database pool),
2. registers the routes of your routers,
3. reads the parameter types of each controller once,
4. runs `boot()` of each provider,
5. starts its HTTP server.

Because the config and providers are copied, they must not hold open sockets or database pools. Open these in `setup()`. See [Providers](providers.md).

## When an isolate crashes

- An error in a request is caught. Dox sends a `500` and keeps going.
- An async error outside a request (for example a future that nobody awaits) is caught and passed to the `report` method of the [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md). The isolate keeps running.
- If a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints `[dox] isolate N exited, restarting` to stderr. It starts a new isolate after 1 second.
- If the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. Let a supervisor start it again, like Docker `restart:` or systemd `Restart=always`. See [Deployment](deployment.md#keep-it-running).

# Providers

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/providers/

# Providers

A provider is a class that sets up one part of your app when it starts, for example the database, auth or a Redis connection.

A provider has three methods:

- `setup()` runs when the app starts. You must write it.
- `boot()` runs after `setup()` of every provider is done. It is optional. See [Boot](#boot).
- `shutdown()` runs when the app stops. It is optional.

## Why providers

Dox runs your app on many [isolates](isolate.md), and they do not share memory.
Code that you run once in `bin/server.dart` only sets up the first isolate. The others have, for example, no database connection.
A provider fixes this: each isolate runs `setup()` itself.

## Create a provider

Extend `DoxProvider` and put your code in `setup()`. `setup()` can be `async`. Dox waits for it.

A package that does not use `dox_core` imports `DoxProvider` from `package:dox_annotation/provider.dart`.

```dart title="lib/providers/orm_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}
```

To make the file, run `dox make:provider Cache`. It writes `lib/providers/cache_provider.dart` with an empty `setup()`. See [`dox make:provider`](../reference/cli.md#dox-makeprovider).

## Register it

You do not need to. Dox finds every class that extends `DoxProvider`.
Run `dart run build_runner build`. The provider is then in `lib/generated/container.g.dart`.
Each isolate makes its own instance from the container. Its constructor can ask for other classes of the container.
See [Dependency injection](../the-basic/dependency-injection.md#routers-and-providers).

Providers run in the order of their file path. To run one first, list it in `AppConfig`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  providers: <DoxProvider>[ORMProvider()], // runs before the others
);
```

A listed provider runs first. Then the others run. No provider runs twice.

You can also add a provider in code, before `startServer()`:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().addProvider(MyProvider());
await Dox().startServer();
```

## Example: auth

```dart title="lib/providers/auth_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(AuthConfig(
      defaultGuard: 'web',
      guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
        'web': AuthGuard(
          driver: JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey)),
          provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
        ),
      },
    ));
  }
}
```

The name is `AppAuthProvider`, because `dox_auth` already has a class named `AuthProvider` (it finds the user model).
See [Authentication](../security/authentication.md).

## When `setup()` runs

In each isolate, Dox runs `setup()` of each provider, one after the other: the listed ones first, then the ones of the container.
Then it registers the routes and starts the server, so routes can use what a provider set up.
See [What each isolate does at start](isolate.md#what-each-isolate-does-at-start).

`dox openapi:generate` also runs `setup()` of every provider, because it needs the routes.

## Boot

`boot()` runs in each isolate after `setup()` of every provider is done. So all other providers are ready.
Use it for work that needs them, like a background worker. The boots run one by one, in the provider order.

```dart
class ReportProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {}

  @override
  Future<void> boot() async {
    // every provider has run setup() here
  }
}
```

The web server and the queue worker (`bin/queue.dart`) run `boot()`.
The scheduler (`bin/schedule.dart`) and `dox openapi:generate` do not. They run only `setup()`.
The queue `inProcess` worker starts in `boot()`, so it does not run in the scheduler process.

## Clean up on shutdown

On `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` Dox stops the server gracefully (see [Deployment](deployment.md#graceful-shutdown)).
After the open requests are done, it runs `shutdown()` of every provider.
It runs in every isolate. Use it to close connections or flush data.
A provider that has nothing to close does not need to write `shutdown()`.

The `ORMProvider` of a new project already does this: its `shutdown()` calls `SqlQueryBuilder.close()`.
Dox closes the cache stores (eg. Redis) by itself, after the providers.

```dart title="lib/providers/redis_provider.dart"
class RedisProvider extends DoxProvider {
  late RedisConnection redis;

  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    redis = await RedisConnection.open();
  }

  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await redis.close();
  }
}
```

An error in `shutdown()` goes to the `report` method of the [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md). The other providers still run.

## Rules for a provider

- **Open connections in `setup()`, not in the constructor.** A provider listed in `AppConfig` is copied to each isolate. An open socket or database pool can not be copied, so the isolate fails to start.
- **Keep `setup()` short.** It runs once per isolate. Data you load in it is kept once per isolate, so 8 isolates keep 8 copies.
