# CORS

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/cors/

# CORS

This page shows how to let a web page on another domain call your API.

A browser blocks a request from `https://my.app` to `https://api.my.app` by default.
The API must send CORS headers to allow it.
Dox adds these headers from `CORSConfig`.

## Set up

The config is in `lib/config/cors.dart`. Pass it to `AppConfig(cors: cors)`.
A new app has this file with `enabled: false`, so it sends no CORS headers.
Set `origin` to the URL of your front end, and set `enabled: true`.

```dart title="lib/config/cors.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  enabled: true,
  origin: 'https://my.app',
  methods: <String>['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],
  headers: <String>['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],
  exposeHeaders: <String>['Content-Disposition'],
  credentials: true,
  maxAge: 600,
);
```

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  cors: cors,
  // ...
);
```

## Options

Each option sets one response header.
An option that is `null` sends no header. All options except `enabled` are `null` by default.
So with no `origin`, Dox sends no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, and the browser blocks pages on other domains.

| Option | Header | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | - | `true` adds the headers to every route. Default: `true` |
| `origin` | `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` | one origin, a `List<String>` of origins, or `'*'` for all. A text is sent as it is, so do not put many origins in one text |
| `methods` | `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` | a `List<String>` or a text like `'GET,POST'`. `'*'` allows all |
| `headers` | `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` | a `List<String>` or a text. `'*'` allows all |
| `exposeHeaders` | `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` | the response headers the page may read |
| `credentials` | `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` | `true` lets the browser send cookies |
| `maxAge` | `Access-Control-Max-Age` | how many seconds the browser keeps the preflight answer |

For `methods`, `headers` and `exposeHeaders`, a list is joined with commas.

## More than one origin

`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` accepts only one origin or `*`.
So when `origin` is a list, Dox checks the `Origin` header of the request:

- The origin is in the list: Dox sends back that one origin.
- The origin is not in the list: Dox sends no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header. The browser blocks the call.
- The list has `'*'`: Dox sends `*`.

With a list, Dox also sends `Vary: Origin`. This tells caches that the answer depends on the origin.

```dart
CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  origin: <String>['https://my.app', 'https://admin.my.app'],
);
```

!!! warning "`credentials` with `*`"
    Do not use `origin: '*'` with `credentials: true`.
    Dox then sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and the browser blocks every call that has cookies.
    When you need cookies, set `origin` to your real front-end URL, or to a list of URLs.
    A page on an allowed origin can send requests with the cookies of your users, so list only sites you trust.

## Preflight requests

Before some requests, the browser sends an `OPTIONS` request.
You do not need an `OPTIONS` route for this.
Dox answers it with `204 No Content` and the CORS headers.
It uses the CORS setting of the route that the browser asks about.

## Turn CORS on or off for some routes

`enabled` is the default for all routes.
Change it for a group of routes:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
// CORS headers only on these routes (use with enabled: false)
Route.enabledCors(() {
  Route.get('/public/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
});

// no CORS headers on these routes
Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post('/webhooks/stripe', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
});
```


---

# CSRF protection

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/csrf/

# CSRF protection

Cross site request forgery (CSRF) is an attack.

Another site makes the browser of your user send a form to your app.
The browser sends your session cookie with it, so the request looks real.

`CsrfMiddleware` stops it. Each session has a secret token. A request that changes data must send it back. Another site can not read the token, so it can not send it.

## Turn it on

It needs a session, so put it after `SessionMiddleware`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

Now every `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` request must send the token. A request with no token, or a wrong one, gets `419` with `{"code": "csrf_token_mismatch", "message": "CSRF token mismatch"}`.

`GET`, `HEAD` and `OPTIONS` requests are not checked. Do not change data in a `GET` route.

## Send the token

Dox reads the token from one of these places:

- the `_token` field of the body (not the query string: a url ends up in logs and in the `Referer` header)
- the `X-CSRF-TOKEN` header
- the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header

The token is `req.session.token`.
Do not put it in a URL. URLs are kept in logs and in the browser history.

### HTML forms

Put the token in a hidden field.
With [views](../the-basic/views.md#forms), `@csrf` writes this field for you:

```html
<form method="POST" action="/posts">
  @csrf
  ...
</form>
```

`@csrf` must be alone on its line. In the middle of a line, use `{{ csrfField() }}`. It prints the same field.

`csrfToken()` gives only the token, for example for a `<meta>` tag.

### axios and Inertia

Dox also sets an `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie with the token. It is not `HttpOnly`, so page scripts can read it.
axios reads this cookie and sends it in the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header by itself. Inertia uses axios, so it works with no code.

With `fetch`, read the cookie and send the header yourself:

```js
const token = document.cookie
  .split('; ')
  .find((c) => c.startsWith('XSRF-TOKEN='))
  ?.split('=')[1];

fetch('/posts', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'X-XSRF-TOKEN': token, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Hi' }),
});
```

## Skip some paths

Routes that other servers call (webhooks) or token based APIs can not send the token. List them in `except`:

```dart
const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']);
```

- A path that ends with `*` matches everything that starts with it: `/api/*` matches `/api/posts` and `/api/users/5`.
- Any other path must match exactly.

An excluded path is not checked and gets no `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie.
Only skip paths that do not use the session login. A webhook should check its own signature instead.

## After login

`req.session.regenerate()` also makes a new token. Dox sends the new `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie with the same response.
`regenerate(keepToken: true)` keeps the token, so forms open in other tabs keep working.
Do not use it at login. A token from before the login would stay valid after the login.


---

# Encryption

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/encryption/

# Encryption

This page shows how to encrypt and decrypt text with `Crypt` and `AESEncryptor`.

Dox uses `AESEncryptor` to encrypt cookies with your `APP_KEY`.
You can also call it yourself.

## Encrypt with the app key

`Crypt` uses the `APP_KEY` of the app. You do not pass the key.

```dart
String secret = Crypt.encryptString('card-1234');
String card = Crypt.decryptString(secret); // 'card-1234'

String data = Crypt.encrypt(<String, dynamic>{'id': 5}); // any JSON value
Map<String, dynamic> map = Crypt.decrypt(data);
```

- `decryptString` and `decrypt` also try the old keys in `AppConfig.previousKeys`.
- They throw `DecryptException` when the text was changed or made with another key.
- `Crypt.encryptString(v)` gives the same as `AESEncryptor.encode(v, appKey)`.

## Encrypt and decrypt with your own key

```dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

String secret = env.appKey;

String encoded = AESEncryptor.encode('Hello world', secret);
String decoded = AESEncryptor.decode(encoded, secret); // 'Hello world'
```

- `encode` returns base64 text.
- The same text gives a different output each time.
- `decode` throws `DecryptException` when the text was changed, or the key is wrong. It is a `400 Bad Request` error. The flag `decryptServerError` makes it a reported `500`. See [Core flags](../reference/app-config.md#core-flags).
- The AES key is not the secret itself. Dox makes a 32-byte key (AES-256) from the secret with HKDF-SHA256 (RFC 5869) and a label. The default label is `dox:encrypt`. Pick another one with `purpose:`, like `AESEncryptor.encode(text, secret, purpose: 'app:invoice')`. `decode` needs the same `purpose`.

Make a new 32-character `APP_KEY` with the CLI:

```bash
dox key:generate
```

It writes a random key of letters and digits to `APP_KEY` in `.env`.

## One key per purpose

Dox does not use `APP_KEY` as it is. It makes one key per purpose from it, with HKDF-SHA256 and a label:

| Label | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| `dox:cookie` | encrypted cookies, and the `cookie` session driver |
| `dox:jwt` | the HMAC key of `JwtAuthDriver` (with a `SecretKey`) |
| `dox:encrypt` | `AESEncryptor` when you give no `purpose` |
| `dox:signed-url` | for signed URLs |

So a value made for one purpose can not be used for another one.
`KeyDerivation.forAppKey(label)` gives the 32-byte key of a label. Each isolate makes it once.

At startup Dox checks `APP_KEY`. When it is empty, not exactly 32 bytes, or an old public sample key, the app stops.
In `development`, `local`, `test` and `testing` it only prints a warning.

- Keep `APP_KEY` in `.env` or in the secrets of your host. Never put it in code or in git.
- If you change `APP_KEY` with no `previousKeys`, old encrypted cookies and sessions can not be read any more, so every user is logged out. JWT tokens signed with it stop working too. See [Change the key](#change-the-key-key-rotation).

## Change the key (key rotation)

Change `APP_KEY` from time to time, or when someone who knew it leaves the team.
With `previousKeys`, users stay logged in while you change it.

### Steps

1. Copy the current `APP_KEY` to `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS`.
2. Run `dox key:generate`. It writes a new `APP_KEY`. Now `.env` has both:

    ```bash title=".env"
    APP_KEY=<the new key from dox key:generate>
    APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=<the old APP_KEY>
    ```

3. Read it in the env class, and give it to `AppConfig`:

    ```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
    List<String> get appPreviousKeys => <String>[]; // APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=a,b
    ```

    ```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
    AppConfig(
      appKey: env.appKey,
      previousKeys: env.appPreviousKeys,
    )
    ```

4. Deploy. Every instance must get the new env at the same time.
5. Wait until the old cookies have expired: the session `lifetime`, and the `maxAge` of your own cookies.
6. Remove the old key from `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS` and deploy again.

`APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS` can hold more than one key, comma separated. Dox tries them in order.

### What reads the old keys

| Value | With an old key |
| --- | --- |
| encrypted cookies (`req.cookie`) | read |
| `cookie` session driver | read |
| CSRF token | read (it is in the session) |
| JWT tokens of `JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey))` | checked. A JWT secret that is not `APP_KEY` needs its own `previousSecrets` option, see [Authentication](authentication.md#change-the-jwt-secret). |
| `Crypt.decryptString` and `Crypt.decrypt` | read |
| `AESEncryptor.decode` in your code | read only when you pass `previousSecrets: Dox().config.previousKeys` |
| anything new | made with `APP_KEY` only |

Dox writes a cookie with the new key the next time it sends that cookie.
So a user who comes back during step 5 moves to the new key without noticing.

### When the key leaked

Do **not** put a leaked key in `previousKeys`.
Anyone who has it can still make cookies and JWT tokens that Dox accepts.
Change `APP_KEY` with no `previousKeys`. Every user is logged out, and that is what you want.

## Cookies

`DoxCookie` encrypts its value with `APP_KEY` by default.
`req.cookie(key)` decrypts it.
To decrypt a raw cookie value yourself, call `DoxCookie.decrypt(name, value)`. It returns `null` when the value was changed, was made with another key, or was made for another cookie name.

```dart
return response().cookie(DoxCookie('theme', 'dark'));  // encrypted
DoxCookie('theme', 'dark', encrypt: false);             // plain text

String? theme = req.cookie('theme');                    // decrypted
String? raw = req.cookie('theme', decrypt: false);      // as sent
```

`req.cookie(key)` returns `null` when the cookie was changed, was made with another `APP_KEY`, or was made for another cookie name.
The cookie name is bound to the encrypted value, so a value can not be copied from one cookie to another.

## How it works

`AESEncryptor` uses AES-256-GCM. The work runs in Rust (in `dox_http_native`), with the AES instructions of the CPU. One cookie takes about 1–2 µs.

- Each message gets a new random 12-byte nonce.
- The output is base64 of `nonce + encrypted text + tag`.
- The 16-byte tag checks the message. If someone changes one byte, `decode` throws.
- `encode` and `decode` also take `associatedData`, a text like a cookie name. It is not in the output, but `decode` needs the same value. Cookies use the cookie name here.

To store passwords, do not encrypt them. Hash them. See [Hashing](hashing.md).


---

# Hashing

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/hashing/

# Hashing

This page shows how to hash passwords with `Hash` and check them later.

A hash is one-way. You can not turn it back into the password.
`Hash` uses bcrypt with a new random salt each time. It is in `package:dox_core/dox_core.dart`.

## Hash a password

Hash the password before you save it.

```dart
user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
await user.save();
```

`makeAsync` runs bcrypt in another isolate. See [Without blocking the server](#without-blocking-the-server).

The result looks like `$2a$10$...`. It holds the salt, so you only store this one string.
The same password gives a different hash each time.

## Check a password

```dart
bool ok = Hash.verify('secret', user.password!);
```

`Hash.verify(password, hashedPassword)` returns `true` when the password matches. `Hash.check` does the same.
It returns `false` when the password does not match, or when `hashedPassword` is not a valid bcrypt hash (for example an empty string).

## Without blocking the server

`Hash.make` and `Hash.verify` block the request isolate while bcrypt runs.
In a request handler, use the async versions. They run bcrypt in another isolate.

```dart
user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
bool ok = await Hash.verifyAsync('secret', user.password!);
```

## Cost

`Hash.rounds` is the bcrypt cost for new hashes. The default is `10`. Each step up doubles the time.
The cost must be from 4 to 31. Do not go below 10.

```dart
Hash.rounds = 12;
String hash = Hash.make('secret', rounds: 12); // or per call
```

Old hashes keep their own cost, so they still verify.
If you change it, also set `hashRounds` on `JwtAuthDriver` or `SessionAuthDriver` to the same value.
Then a login with an unknown email takes as long as a wrong password. See [Authentication](authentication.md).

## Long passwords

bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes.
`Hash.make` and `Hash.makeAsync` throw an `ArgumentError` when the password is longer than 72 bytes (UTF-8).
The error text does not hold the password, so it is safe in logs.
`Hash.verify` returns `false` for such a password.

So limit the length in your DTO, like `@Length(min: 8, max: 72)`.
`@Length` counts characters, and a letter outside ASCII can use up to 4 bytes.
So a password with such letters can still be too long. Catch the error and answer `422`, or use a smaller `max`.

## Compare secrets

To check an API key or a token, use `Hash.equals(given, expected)`, not `==`.
`==` stops at the first wrong character, so the time can tell how much of the key was right.
`Hash.equals` takes the same time for every value of the same length.

```dart
bool ok = Hash.equals(req.header('X-Api-Key') ?? '', Env.get<String>('API_KEY'));
```

## Store tokens

For a long random secret that you keep in the database (an API key, an access token), store only `Hash.sha256(token)`.
Find the row by the hash of what the client sends.
SHA-256 is fast and gives the same hash for the same input, so a unique index works on it.

```dart
String stored = Hash.sha256(token);          // save this, never the token
Token? row = await Token().where('hash', Hash.sha256(given)).getFirst();
```

Never use `Hash.sha256` for passwords. A password is short and can be guessed, so use `Hash.make` (bcrypt).

## With login

You do not need `Hash.verify` for normal login.
`Auth().attempt()` from `dox_auth` finds the user and checks the password with bcrypt.
See [Authentication](authentication.md).

## Things to know

- Never store or encrypt a plain password. Hash it.
- Never send the hash to the client. Put the column in the model `hidden` list.
- bcrypt is slow on purpose, so guessing is slow too. Do not hash in a loop on hot paths.


---

# Rate limiting

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/rate-limiting/

# Rate limiting

`RateLimit` is a middleware that stops a client that sends too many requests.

Use it on login, sign up and other routes that bots like to hammer.

## Limit a route

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, per: Duration(minutes: 1)),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);
```

Each client (by ip) can now send 5 login requests per minute. The 6th request gets:

```text
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 42
X-RateLimit-Limit: 5
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0

{"code":"too_many_requests","message":"Too Many Requests"}
```

- `Retry-After` is the number of seconds until the client can try again.
- Every answer, also a normal one, has `X-RateLimit-Limit` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining`.
- The error goes through your `exceptionHandler` and `responseHandler`, like any other error. So it has the same JSON shape as your other errors.

The defaults are `max: 60` and `per: Duration(minutes: 1)`.

## Limit every route

Put it in `globalMiddleware`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    RateLimit(max: 120),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

## Count by user, not by ip

`key` picks who is counted. The default is `req.ip()`.
The key is any `String`. For example, count by user id after `AuthMiddleware`:

```dart
Route.get('/reports', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  RateLimit(
    max: 100,
    key: (DoxRequest req) => '${req.auth?.user<User>()?.id ?? req.ip()}',
  ),
  (ReportController c) => c.index,
]);
```

!!! warning "Use a key the client can not choose"
    Do not count by a raw header, like `req.header('X-Api-Key')`.
    A client can send a new value with each request and get a new count each time.
    Count by a value that you checked first, like the id of the logged in user.

!!! warning "Behind a proxy"
    Behind Caddy, nginx or a load balancer, every request comes from the proxy ip.
    Then all clients share one count. Add the proxy to `AppConfig.trustedProxies`, so `req.ip()` is the real client ip.
    See [App config](../reference/app-config.md).

## Two limits on the same key

Two `RateLimit` with the same `max` and `per` share one counter for the same key. Give each one a `name` to keep them apart:

```dart
Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);
Route.post('/auth/register', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
  (AuthController c) => c.register,
]);
```

## Where the counts live

Where the counts are kept depends on the default [cache](../digging-deeper/cache.md) store:

- When the default cache store is **Redis**, the counts are in Redis. All isolates and all servers share them. Use this when you run more than one server.
- Else the counts are in the **main isolate**. All isolates of the server share them, so `max` holds for the whole server.
  The other isolates send each count to the main isolate and wait for the answer. This is one small message per limited request.
  Each server has its own counts, so with 3 servers a client can send up to 3 x `max` requests.
  This is also true for the default `file` store of a new app.

To use one store by name, pass `store`:

```dart
RateLimit(max: 10, store: 'redis')
```

A `memory` store named in `store` counts in the main isolate too. A store passed in `cacheStore` is used as it is.

## How it counts

By default it is a fixed window. With `per: Duration(minutes: 1)` the count starts at 0 at the start of each minute.
So a client can send `max` requests at the end of one minute and `max` more at the start of the next.
That is fine for most apps.

A blocked request still counts. A client that keeps sending while it is blocked stays blocked.

## Sliding window

Set `sliding: true` to stop the burst at the edge of a window:

```dart
RateLimit(max: 5, per: Duration(minutes: 1), sliding: true)
```

The count is then a guess of the requests in the last minute.
It is the count of this minute, plus a part of the count of the minute before.
That part gets smaller as the minute goes on.

For example, the client sent 4 requests last minute and 1 this minute. We are 15 seconds into this minute.
The count is `4 x 45/60 + 1 = 4`.

- `X-RateLimit-Remaining` is `max` minus this count, rounded up.
- `Retry-After` is the time until one more request fits, if the client sends nothing in between.
- It costs one more read per request. Each count is kept for 2 windows.

## See also

- [Middleware](../the-basic/middleware.md)
- [Security headers](security-headers.md)
- [Production checklist](../reference/production-checklist.md)

# Security headers

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/security-headers/

# Security headers

`SecurityHeaders` is a middleware that adds safe HTTP headers to every answer.

The browser reads them and blocks some common attacks, like showing your page in a frame on another site.

## Turn it on

Put it in `globalMiddleware`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SecurityHeaders(),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

Every answer now has these headers:

| Header | Default value | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` | The browser does not guess the file type. |
| `X-Frame-Options` | `DENY` | No site can show your page in a frame. |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` | Other sites only see your domain, not the full url. |
| `Permissions-Policy` | `camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()` | The page can not use the camera, the microphone or the location. |
| `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` | `same-origin` | A page of another site that opens yours can not reach it. |
| `Strict-Transport-Security` | `max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` | The browser uses only https for one year. Sent only on https requests. |

`Content-Security-Policy` is off by default. A good policy depends on your pages.

Without this middleware, the server already sends three headers on every answer, also on a `404`:
`X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `X-XSS-Protection: 0`.
`SecurityHeaders` replaces them with its own values.
`X-XSS-Protection: 0` turns the old XSS filter of browsers off, like OWASP says. The filter is gone from new browsers, and in old ones it can make holes. Use `Content-Security-Policy` instead.

## Change or turn off a header

Each header has an option. Give a new value to change it, or `null` to turn it off.
`null` removes the header, also one the server sends by default (like `frameOptions: null` for `X-Frame-Options`).
The option for `X-XSS-Protection` is `xssProtection` (default `'0'`).
In `extra`, a `null` value removes that header too.

```dart
const SecurityHeaders(
  frameOptions: 'SAMEORIGIN', // allow frames from your own site
  permissionsPolicy: null, // do not send this header
  contentSecurityPolicy: "frame-ancestors 'none'",
  extra: <String, String>{'Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy': 'same-origin'},
)
```

| Option | Header |
| --- | --- |
| `contentTypeOptions` | `X-Content-Type-Options` |
| `frameOptions` | `X-Frame-Options` |
| `referrerPolicy` | `Referrer-Policy` |
| `permissionsPolicy` | `Permissions-Policy` |
| `crossOriginOpenerPolicy` | `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` |
| `strictTransportSecurity` | `Strict-Transport-Security` |
| `contentSecurityPolicy` | `Content-Security-Policy` |
| `extra` | any other headers, name to value |

## HSTS behind a proxy

Dox serves plain http. The https part is done by a proxy (Caddy, nginx, a load balancer).
Dox sends `Strict-Transport-Security` only when the request came in over https.
It knows that from the `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` header, and it only believes this header from a trusted proxy.
So add your proxy to `AppConfig.trustedProxies`:

```dart
AppConfig(trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1']);
```

Without it, Dox never sends HSTS. See [App config](../reference/app-config.md).

!!! note
    Middleware runs only for routes that exist. A `404` for an unknown url gets only the three server headers.
    A preflight `OPTIONS` answer gets only them too.
    Put `SecurityHeaders` first in `globalMiddleware`. Then an error from a later middleware, like a `419` or a `429`, also gets the headers.

## See also

- [Middleware](../the-basic/middleware.md)
- [CORS](cors.md)
- [Rate limiting](rate-limiting.md)

# Signed URLs

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/signed-urls/

# Signed URLs

A signed url has a `signature` in its query.

Nobody can change the url without the `APP_KEY`.
Use it for links in emails, like "unsubscribe" or "download your file", where the user is not logged in.

## Make a signed url

Give the route a name and add the `ValidateSignature` middleware:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
Route.get('/unsubscribe/{user}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(),
  (UserController c) => c.unsubscribe,
]).name('unsubscribe');
```

Then make the url with `Route.signedUrl`:

```dart
String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'unsubscribe',
  params: <String, Object>{'user': 5},
);
// https://example.com/unsubscribe/5?signature=3f9a...
```

A url with no `signature`, a wrong one, or a changed path or query gets `403 Forbidden`.

## A url that expires

Give `expires`. The url gets an `expires` query param (unix seconds), and it is signed too.
After that time the url gets `403`.

```dart
String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'download',
  params: <String, Object>{'file': 12},
  expires: Duration(hours: 1),
);
```

## Absolute and relative urls

By default the url is absolute. Dox puts `APP_URL` from the env in front, like `https://example.com`. The scheme and host are signed too.
Give `baseUrl:` to use another one.

- The `Host` of the request must be the host of `APP_URL`, with the same port.
- The scheme must match too. Behind a proxy that ends TLS, add the proxy to `AppConfig.trustedProxies`, so Dox reads `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`.

With `absolute: false`, only the path and the query are signed. Check it with `ValidateSignature(absolute: false)`:

```dart
Route.get('/files/{id}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(absolute: false),
  (FileController c) => c.show,
]).name('files.show');

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'files.show',
  params: <String, Object>{'id': 3},
  absolute: false,
);
// /files/3?signature=...
```

## Check in a controller

`ValidateSignature.hasValidSignature(req)` gives `true` or `false`, so you can answer in your own way:

```dart
if (!ValidateSignature.hasValidSignature(req)) {
  return redirect('/link-expired');
}
```

## How it works

- The signature is HMAC-SHA256 of the url, with a key made from `APP_KEY` (`KeyDerivation.signedUrl`).
- Dox compares it in constant time.
- After you change `APP_KEY`, urls made with an old key still work when the old key is in `AppConfig.previousKeys`.
- `signature` is a reserved query param. Any other param added to a signed url makes it invalid.


---

# Validation

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/packages/validation/

# Validation

`dox_validation` checks input and gives you typed Dart objects.

It has two parts:

1. **DTOs**: a class with `@Dto()` and rule annotations. A generator writes the checks. Use this for almost everything.
2. **Fluent schemas**: `v.object(...)`, like [Zod](https://zod.dev). Use it only when the shape is known at runtime.

Both give all errors at once, and a JSON Schema for [OpenAPI](openapi.md).

## In a Dox app

`dox_core` uses `dox_validation` and exports it. There is nothing to install: `import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart'` is all you need.

1. Make a DTO with `dox make:dto CreateUser`. It writes `lib/app/dtos/create_user/create_user.dto.dart`.
2. Run the generator: `dox build_runner:build`.
3. Give the list of DTOs to the app, once:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  dtos: dtos, // from lib/generated/dtos.g.dart
);
```

Then ask for the DTO in a controller. Dox checks the body before the method runs. Bad input gets `422` with the errors:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart"
class UserController {
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> store(CreateUser body) async {
    // body is already checked and typed
    return <String, dynamic>{'name': body.name};
  }
}
```

The full guide is at [Validation](../the-basic/validation.md). Every rule is in the [rules reference](../the-basic/validation-rules.md).
The rest of this page is about the package itself.

## Without Dox

```bash
dart pub add dox_validation
dart pub add dev:dox_builder dev:build_runner
```

```dart
import 'package:dox_validation/dox_validation.dart';
```

The DTO generator is in `dox_builder`. Run it with `dart run build_runner build`.
`@Unique` and `@Exists` are in `dox_orm`, not here.

## DTOs

```dart
import 'package:dox_validation/dox_validation.dart';

part 'create_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class CreateUser {
  @Length(min: 3, max: 50)
  @Trim()
  final String name;

  @Email()
  final String email;

  const CreateUser({required this.name, required this.email});

  static const DtoSchema<CreateUser> schema = $CreateUserDto;
}
```

The generator makes, for each `@Dto` class:

| Name | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `$CreateUserDto` | a `const` `DtoSchema<CreateUser>`: the checks, the converter and the JSON Schema |
| `lib/generated/dtos.g.dart` | `const List<DtoSchema<Object>> dtos`: every DTO in `lib/`. Dox uses it to find DTOs by type. An app with no DTO gets an empty `final` list. |

The `static const ... schema = $CreateUserDto;` line is how you reach the schema: `CreateUser.schema`.

## `DtoSchema<T>`

`DtoSchema<T>` is also a `Schema<T>`. So it works everywhere a schema works:
inside `v.object(...)`, `v.list(...)`, with OpenAPI, and as a `StandardSchema`.

| Member | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `Future<T> validateMap(Map<String, dynamic> input, {Source source = Source.body, Map<String, String> params = const {}, MessageResolver? messages, String? locale})` | all checks, then the object. Throws `ValidationException` with the errors. |
| `Future<ParseResult<T>> safeValidateMap(input, {source, params, messages, locale})` | the same, but never throws for bad input. `result.success`, `result.value`, `result.errors`. |
| `T fromMap(Map<String, dynamic> input)` | builds the object with **no checks**. Reads keys, converts JSON types, uses defaults. A wrong type throws a `TypeError`. Only for data you trust. |
| `Map<String, dynamic> toMap(T value)` | the object as a map with the input keys (snake_case). `DateTime` becomes an ISO 8601 string, an enum its name. |
| `Map<String, dynamic> toJsonSchema()` | JSON Schema (draft 2020-12). |
| `parse`, `safeParse`, `parseAsync`, `safeParseAsync` | the normal `Schema` methods, with `Source.body`. `parse` throws a `StateError` when the DTO has async rules. |
| `Type get type`, `String get name` | `CreateUser` and `'CreateUser'`. |

`source: Source.query` reads the map like a query string: text is converted to the field type.
`params` are path params, used by `@Unique(ignoreParam: ...)`.
`messages` and `locale` change the error text for this call. See [Messages](#messages).

```dart
ParseResult<CreateUser> result = await CreateUser.schema.safeValidateMap(input);
if (!result.success) {
  print(result.errors); // {'email': 'The email is not a valid email'}
}
```

| `ParseResult` member | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `success` | `true` when there are no errors |
| `value` | the result. `null` when `success` is `false` |
| `errors` | the first message for each field, like `{'user.email': '...'}` |
| `fieldErrors` | all messages for each field |
| `issues` | the full list of `ValidationIssue` objects, with code and path |

!!! note
    `dox_core` has its own `ValidationException` (the HTTP 422 one), so it does not export the one from `dox_validation`.
    In a Dox app, both answer `422` when thrown in a controller. In tests, prefer `safeValidateMap`.

### JSON Schema of a DTO

For the `CreateUser` from the [Validation guide](../the-basic/validation.md) (with `age` and `role`):

```dart
CreateUser.schema.toJsonSchema();
```

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "title": "CreateUser",
  "properties": {
    "name": { "type": "string", "minLength": 3, "maxLength": 50 },
    "email": { "type": "string", "format": "email" },
    "age": { "type": ["integer", "null"], "minimum": 18 },
    "role": { "type": "string", "enum": ["admin", "user"], "default": "user" }
  },
  "required": ["name", "email"]
}
```

- `required` lists the required fields only.
- A nullable field has `"type": [..., "null"]`. A default becomes `default`.
- A nested DTO goes in `$defs` under its class name, with a `$ref`. OpenAPI moves it to `components/schemas`.
- `@Dto(strict: true)` adds `"additionalProperties": false`.
- A `///` doc comment on a field becomes `description`. `@Describe('...')` on a field sets it too, and wins over the comment. It does not change the checks.
- Each rule adds its keys. See the [rules reference](../the-basic/validation-rules.md).

## Fluent schemas (for dynamic input)

Use these when you only know the fields at runtime. The output is a `Map`, not a class.

```dart
final ObjectSchema createUser = v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
  'name': v.string().trim().min(3).max(50),
  'email': v.string().email(),
  'age': v.coerce.int().min(18).optional(),
  'role': v.enumOf<String>(<String>['admin', 'user']).defaultTo('user'),
  'tags': v.list(v.string()).max(5),
  'address': Address.schema, // a DTO inside a fluent schema
});

// throws ValidationException when the input is not valid
Map<String, dynamic> data = createUser.parse(input);

// never throws for bad input
ParseResult<Map<String, dynamic>> result = createUser.safeParse(input);
```

In a controller: `Map<String, dynamic> data = await req.validateSchema(createUser);`

!!! warning "Different defaults"
    Fluent schemas do not follow the DTO rules. A key is required unless you add `optional()`.
    `""` is a value, not "missing". Text is not converted, unless you use `v.coerce`.

### Schemas

| Schema | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| `v.string()` | `min`, `max`, `length`, `nonEmpty`, `email`, `url`, `uuid`, `ip`, `datetime`, `regex`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `includes`, `alpha`, `alphaDash`, `alphaNumeric`, `json`, `digits`, `digitsBetween`, `dateFormat`, `password`, `exists`, `unique`, `trim`, `toLowerCase`, `toUpperCase` |
| `v.int()`, `v.num()` | `min`, `max`, `between`, `gt`, `lt`, `positive`, `nonNegative`, `multipleOf`, `exists`, `unique` |
| `v.bool()` | |
| `v.date()` | `DateTime` only. `min`, `max` |
| `v.enumOf([...])`, `v.literal(x)` | |
| `v.list(item)` | `min`, `max`, `nonEmpty` |
| `v.object({...})` | `strict`, `passthrough`, `strip`, `pick`, `omit`, `extend`, `partial` |
| `v.map(values, keys: ...)` | any keys |
| `v.union([...])` | the first match wins |
| `v.any()`, `v.file()` | `file()` has `maxSize`, `minSize`, `mimes`, `mimeTypes`, `dimensions`, `image` and `extensions` |

On every schema:

- `optional()`: the key may be missing. `null` is still an error.
  After it: `requiredIf(other, value)` and `requiredWith([others])`.
- `nullable()`: the value may be `null`. The key must be there.
- `nullish()`: both.
- `defaultTo(x)`: the value when the key is missing. (`default` is a reserved word in Dart.)
- `transform(fn)`, `refine(fn)`, `refineAsync(fn)`, `superRefine(fn)`, `superRefineAsync(fn)`, `use(rule)`.
- `same(other)`, `confirmed()`: compare with another key of the same object.
- `bail()`: stop at the first failed rule. See [Stop at the first error](#stop-at-the-first-error).
- `excludeIf(other, value)`, `excludeUnless(other, value)`: leave a key out. See [Skip a field](#skip-a-field).
- `describe(text)`, `example(x)`: only used in the JSON Schema.

### Coercion

Query strings and form data are text. `v.coerce` turns text into the right type first.

```dart
v.coerce.int().parse('42');       // 42
v.coerce.num().parse('4.5');      // 4.5
v.coerce.bool().parse('on');      // true (true/1/yes/on, false/0/no/off)
v.coerce.date().parse('2024-01-31');
v.coerce.string().parse(5);       // '5'
```

### Checks across fields

```dart
final ObjectSchema signUp = v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
  'password': v.string().min(8),
  'confirm': v.string(),
}).refine((Map<String, dynamic> data) {
  return data['password'] == data['confirm'];
}, message: 'Passwords do not match', path: <Object>['confirm']);
```

### More rules

```dart
final ObjectSchema signUp = v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
  // needs password_confirmation with the same value
  'password': v.string().password(min: 8, mixedCase: true, numbers: true).confirmed(),
  'email': v.string().email().unique('users', column: 'email'),
  'team_id': v.int().exists('teams'),
  'type': v.enumOf<String>(<String>['person', 'company']),
  'company': v.string().optional().requiredIf('type', 'company'),
  'phone': v.string().digitsBetween(8, 12).optional(),
  'country_code': v.string().optional().requiredWith(<String>['phone']),
  'birthday': v.string().dateFormat('Y-m-d').optional(),
  'settings': v.string().json().optional(),
  'age': v.int().between(18, 120).optional(),
});

Map<String, dynamic> data = await signUp.parseAsync(input);
```

They use the same codes and messages as the DTO annotations. See the [rules reference](../the-basic/validation-rules.md#more-text-rules).

- `requiredIf` and `requiredWith` come after `optional()` or `nullish()`.
  Then a missing, `null` or blank value is an error when the condition is true.

More rules:

```dart
final ObjectSchema order = v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
  'type': v.string(),
  'email': v.string().optional().requiredWithout(<String>['phone']),
  'phone': v.string().optional(),
  'fax': v.string().optional().requiredWithoutAll(<String>['email', 'phone']),
  'company': v.string().optional().requiredUnless('type', 'person'),
  'nick': v.string().optional().filled(),
  'note': v.string().optional().present().nullable(),
  'coupon': v.string().optional().prohibitedIf('type', 'guest'),
  'debug': v.any().optional().prohibited(),
  'terms': v.coerce.bool().accepted(),
  'new_password': v.string().different('old_password'),
  'id': v.string().ulid(),
  'min_price': v.int(),
  'max_price': v.int().gtField('min_price'),
});
```

- `requiredUnless`, `requiredWithout`, `requiredWithoutAll`, `filled` and `present` come after `optional()`, like `requiredIf`.
- `present()` needs the key. Add `.nullable()` to allow `null`.
- `prohibited()` and `prohibitedIf()` come after `optional()`. They treat empty values in different ways:
    - `prohibited()`: a missing key or blank text passes. Any other sent value fails, also `null`, `[]`, `0` and `false`.
    - `prohibitedIf()`: when the condition matches, a missing key, `null`, blank text and an empty list or map pass. `0`, `false` and any other value fail.
- `accepted()` and `declined()` check the value after the type check. `v.bool()` takes only `true` and `false`, so `"yes"` is a `boolean` error there. Use `v.coerce.bool().accepted()` for form words like `yes` and `on` (any case), or `v.string()` or `v.any()` to check the exact words: `true`, `1`, `"1"`, `"true"`, `"yes"` and `"on"` for `accepted()`, and `false`, `0`, `"0"`, `"false"`, `"no"` and `"off"` for `declined()`. The text is case sensitive.
- `gtField`, `gteField`, `ltField` and `lteField` compare with another key. A missing other key fails.
- The rules are explained in the [rules reference](../the-basic/validation-rules.md#present-or-missing).
- `exists` and `unique` are async. Use `parseAsync()` or `safeParseAsync()`.
- For one value, the database decides what matches. On MySQL `TAKEN@dox.dev` is taken when `taken@dox.dev` is there.
- `exists(table, column: 'id')`: the column default is `id`. For a number id column, use `v.int().exists('teams')`, not `v.string()`. Then text like `abc` is a type error, before any query.
- `unique(table, column: 'email', ignore: id)`: `column` is required. It is never taken from the input key, because a key in `v.map()` comes from the user. `ignore` skips the row where `ignoreColumn` (default `id`) has this value. Use it for updates.

#### Stop at the first error

A fluent schema runs all rules of a value, and gives one error for each failed rule. Add `.bail()` to stop at the first failed rule. A DTO always does this.

```dart
v.string().min(8).email().bail().safeParse('ab');
// one error: min_length. Without bail(): min_length and email.
```

- It counts for all rules of that schema, wherever you put `.bail()` in the chain.
- Async rules after a failed rule do not run. So no database query is made for a value that is already wrong.
- Put it before `.optional()`, `.nullable()` or `.transform()`. A rule after one of them belongs to the wrapper, so it does not count. `.bail()` after a wrapper, like `.optional().bail()`, does nothing for the rules inside it.
- On `v.object()` or `v.list()`, it counts for the rules of the object or list only. Each field and each item keeps its own setting.
- A type error already stops the rules of a value, with or without `.bail()`.

#### Skip a field

`excludeIf(other, value)` and `excludeUnless(other, value)` skip a field of `v.object()`. When they match, the field is not checked, and its key is not in the output.

```dart
final ObjectSchema account = v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
  'type': v.string(),
  'vat_number': v.string().min(5).excludeIf('type', 'person'),
  'company': v.string().excludeUnless('type', 'company'),
});

account.parse(<String, dynamic>{'type': 'person', 'vat_number': 'x'});
// {type: person}
```

- They work like the DTO `@ExcludeIf` and `@ExcludeUnless`. They read the raw input of the other key, and match like `requiredIf` (also with a list of values).
- `other` is a key of the same object. A dotted path like `user.type` does not work.
- `excludeIf`: a missing other key does not skip. `excludeUnless`: a missing other key counts as `null`, so the field is skipped.
- The key is left out also with `.optional()`, `.nullable()` or `.defaultTo()`, in any order. A skipped field never gets its default.
- In a `v.list()` of objects, each item is checked on its own.
- A skipped key is not an unknown key for `strict()`, and `passthrough()` does not add it back.
- In the JSON Schema, the field is not in `required`.
- The rules of other fields that read this key (like `same`, `requiredIf` or `gtField`) still see its raw input, also when it is skipped.
- They work only on a field of `v.object()`. On a top-level value, a list item or a value of `v.map()`, they do nothing.

#### The presence verifier

`exists` and `unique` ask a `PresenceVerifier`. `dox_orm` sets one when the database starts, so in a Dox app they just work.
Outside Dox, or with another database layer, set your own. Each isolate has its own value, so set it in a provider's `setup()`, which runs in every isolate:

```dart
class MyVerifier extends PresenceVerifier {
  @override
  Future<Set<String>> found(
    String table,
    String column,
    List<Object?> values, {
    String? exceptColumn,
    Object? exceptValue,
    String? connection,
  }) async {
    // Return the values that are in the column, as text.
    // Bind the values as query parameters, never put them into the SQL.
    return <String>{};
  }
}

class VerifierProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    PresenceVerifier.instance = MyVerifier();
  }
}
```

Table and column names are checked when the schema is built. They take the same names as the dox_orm query builder: letters, digits, `_` and `$`, with `.` between parts, like `2fa_codes` or `public.users`. Other names throw an `ArgumentError`.

### Async checks

`refineAsync` runs a check that needs the database. Then use `parseAsync()` or `safeParseAsync()`.
`parse()` throws a `StateError` when a schema has async checks.

### Custom rules in a fluent schema

A `Rule<T>` class works in both worlds: as an annotation on a DTO, and with `use()` here.

```dart
v.string().min(3).use(const Slug());
```

See [Custom rules](../the-basic/validation.md#custom-rules) for how to write one.

## Messages

Each error has a code, like `required` or `min_length`.
Placeholders: `{field}`, `{value}`, and rule values like `{min}` and `{max}`.

```dart
// for the whole app (outside Dox; in Dox use AppConfig(validationMessages: ...))
MessageResolver.global = MessageResolver(messages: <String, String>{
  'required': 'Please fill in {field}',
});

// for one call
createUser.safeParse(input, messages: MessageResolver(messages: <String, String>{
  'email.required': 'We need your email',
}));
```

A resolver for one call is used in place of the global one.
Codes that it does not have get the built-in text, not the global text.

With the flag `laravelMessageKeys`, a key can use the Laravel rule name too, like `name.min` for the `min_length` error. See the [list of names](../the-basic/validation.md#laravel-rule-names-in-message-keys).

To show a name for `{field}` in place of the key, give `attributes`:

```dart
MessageResolver.global = MessageResolver(
  attributes: <String, String>{'first_name': 'first name'},
);
// The first name is required
```

A DTO can give its own names with `@Dto(attributes:)`. See [Names for `{field}`](../the-basic/validation.md#names-for-field).

For other languages, extend `MessageResolver` and override `resolve()`.
See [Messages](../the-basic/validation.md#messages).

## Opt-in flags

`ValidationFlags` turns on behaviors that are off by default.
Set it in `Validator.flags`.

```dart
// turn on one flag
Validator.flags = const ValidationFlags(unicodeAlpha: true);

// turn on every flag
Validator.flags = const ValidationFlags.all();
```

| Flag | What it does when on |
| --- | --- |
| `emptyStringsToNull` | Fluent schemas turn each `""` in the input into `null` before they check it. This also happens in nested maps and lists. So `""` fails a required field, and `.nullable()` gives `null`. |
| `unicodeAlpha` | `alpha`, `alphaNumeric` and `alphaDash` accept Unicode letters and marks, like `José`. `alphaNumeric` and `alphaDash` also accept Unicode digits. This works for fluent schemas and DTOs. |
| `shortInMessage` | The default `in` message is `The selected {field} is invalid`. It does not list the allowed values. |
| `dtoAllErrors` | A DTO runs the rules of each field that has the right type, also when another field is missing or has the wrong type. So one request gets all its errors at once. The type and `required` errors come first (a nested DTO's errors at its field), then the rule errors. A list or map with a bad item skips its rules. |
| `dtoRejectEmptyList` | A required `List` field of a DTO fails `required` on `[]`, and its other rules do not run. It does not apply to a nullable list, a list with a default, or a `Maybe<List>`. |
| `dtoMaybeRejectsEmpty` | A `Maybe<T>` field of a DTO (with `T` not nullable) fails `required` when the key is sent with an empty value, like `""`. A missing key still gives `Maybe.missing()`. It does not apply to `Maybe<T?>`. A text of only spaces is a value and passes. With `@Trim` it becomes `""` and fails. |
| `laravelMessageKeys` | A custom message key can use the Laravel rule name of a code, like `name.min` for the `min_length` error. It works in `@Dto(messages:)` and in a `MessageResolver`. At each step of the lookup the Dox code wins. The error code does not change. See the [list of names](../the-basic/validation.md#laravel-rule-names-in-message-keys). |

With a flag off, the check works as described in the rest of this page:
`""` is text, the alpha rules take only `a-z`, `A-Z` and `0-9`, the `in` message lists the allowed values, and a message key matches only the Dox code.
For DTOs: a missing field or a type error stops the rules of the other fields, `[]` passes a required list, and `""` in a `Maybe` field counts as not sent.

The three DTO flags are read when the check runs.
They need the DTO code from a `dox_builder` that knows them.
Run `dart run build_runner build` once to make it.

`emptyStringsToNull` is for fluent schemas.
A DTO checked on its own keeps `""`; use `@Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true)` there.
A DTO inside a fluent schema gets the changed input.

Each isolate has its own `Validator.flags`.
In a Dox app, set it in a provider's `setup()`, so every isolate runs it:

```dart
class ValidationProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Validator.flags = const ValidationFlags.all();
  }
}
```

## Standard Schema

Every schema, and every `DtoSchema`, implements the [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev) interface (`StandardSchema`).
Code that only needs to validate can accept any `StandardSchema`, from Dox or from another library.

# OpenAPI

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/packages/openapi/

# OpenAPI

This page shows how to make OpenAPI 3.1 docs for your Dox API, how to describe each route, and how to change the result.

You get three things:

- `/docs`: a [Scalar](https://github.com/scalar/scalar) page with every route and "Try it" buttons.
- `/openapi.json`: the OpenAPI document as JSON.
- `/openapi.yaml`: the same document as YAML.

The docs come from three places:

- **the routes**: method, path, path params, middleware (login),
- **the request classes**: a `@Dto` class,
- **the controllers**: the annotations (`@Summary`, `@Response` and more), the arguments and the return type of each method.

## Setup (optional)

!!! note "Made with `dox create`?"
    Your app already serves `/docs`, `/openapi.json` and `/openapi.yaml` while `APP_ENV` is `development`. The template `.env` sets this. You need no setup for that.
    But the config does not have `openApiRegistry` yet. So each route shows only its path and method.
    Do the steps below when you want the full docs from your code (annotations, request and response schemas), or when you want to change the title or other options.

1. Write the config. Pass the generated `openApiRegistry` to it:

    ```dart title="lib/config/openapi.dart"
    import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
    import 'package:my_app/generated/openapi.g.dart';

    OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
      info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
      registry: openApiRegistry,
    );
    ```

    The import of `generated/openapi.g.dart` shows an error until the builder runs in step 3.

2. Add it to `AppConfig`:

    ```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
    import 'package:my_app/config/openapi.dart';

    AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
      openApi: openApi,
      // ...
    );
    ```

3. Run the builder:

    ```bash
    dart run build_runner build      # or: dox build_runner:build
    ```

    `dox_builder` reads your code and writes `lib/generated/openapi.g.dart`.
    Run it again after you change routes, controllers, request classes or models.
    `dox build_runner:watch` does it for you while you work.

4. Make sure `.env` has `APP_ENV=development`. Then start the app and open `http://localhost:3000/docs`.
    Without `APP_ENV=development`, `/docs` gives 404.
    The document is built on the first `/docs` request, then kept.

!!! note
    The docs are on only when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`.
    If `APP_ENV` is not set, Dox treats the app as production: `/docs` is off and error details are hidden.
    Set `APP_ENV=development` in your `.env` and in CI.
    To turn the docs on in production, see [Turn the docs on in production](#turn-the-docs-on-in-production).

## Describe a route

Put annotations on a controller method. They are all in `dox_core`.

```dart
class BlogController {
  @Summary('Get one blog')
  @Description('Deleted blogs are not found.')
  @Tags(<String>['Blogs'])
  Future<Blog?> show(DoxRequest req, String id) async {
    return Blog().find(id);
  }

  @Summary('Create a blog')
  @Response(201, Blog, description: 'The new blog')
  Future<DoxResponse> store(CreateBlog body) async { ... }
}

// routes
Route.get('/blogs/{id}', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (BlogController c) => c.show]);
```

Here is what you get. The generated docs for `GET /blogs/{id}`:

```yaml
get:
  tags: [Blogs]
  summary: Get one blog
  description: Deleted blogs are not found.
  operationId: BlogController.show
  parameters:
    - {name: id, in: path, required: true, schema: {type: string}}
  responses:
    "200":
      content:
        application/json:
          schema: {$ref: "#/components/schemas/Blog"}
    "401": {description: Not logged in}
    "404": {description: Not found}
    "500": {description: Server error}
  security:
    - bearerAuth: []
```

`Blog` is in `components/schemas`, made from the model:

```yaml
Blog:
  type: object
  properties:
    id: {type: integer}
    title: {type: [string, "null"]}
    user: {anyOf: [{$ref: "#/components/schemas/User"}, {type: "null"}]}
    created_at: {type: [string, "null"], format: date-time}
```

Annotations are all optional. Without them, Dox fills in the docs for you, see [What Dox fills in for you](#what-dox-fills-in-for-you).

Another example, with a request and more than one answer:

```dart
@Summary('Log in')
@Description('Gives a bearer token for the Authorization header.')
@Tags(<String>['Auth'])
@Request(LoginUser)
@Response(200, LoginResult)
@Response(401, null, description: 'Wrong email or password')
Future<dynamic> login(DoxRequest req) async { ... }
```

| Annotation | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `@Summary('text')` | short title. Default: the first line of the `///` comment |
| `@Description('text')` | longer text. Default: the rest of the `///` comment |
| `@Tags(['Users'])` | groups. On a method or on the class |
| `@Request(T)` | the request class. Body or query by the HTTP method |
| `@Body(T)` | the request class, always the body |
| `@Query(T)` | the request class, always the query |
| `@Response(status, Type, description: '')` | one answer. Add more than one for more codes. With a `2xx` one, the return type is not used |
| `@ApiDeprecated()` | marks the route as deprecated. Dart `@Deprecated` works too |
| `@ApiIgnore()` | leaves the method (or the whole class) out of the docs. To leave out routes by path, use `include` and `exclude` in `OpenApiConfig` |
| `@DoxController(tag: 'Users')` | for a class that the builder can not see in a `Route.get(...)` call |

The `Type` of `@Response` can be a model, `List<User>`, a `@Dto`, a `Serializer` or a basic type like `String`.

Each annotation also has a lower case name, like `@summary('Log in')`.
Only `@Response` has none, because `response()` is already a `dox_core` helper.

## Request

The builder looks in this order. The first one wins.

1. `@Body(T)`, `@Query(T)` or `@Request(T)` on the method.
2. An argument whose type is a `@Dto` class: `store(CreateBlog body)`.
3. A `req.validate<T>()` call in the method, where `T` is a `@Dto` class.

For `POST`, `PUT` and `PATCH` the request is the JSON body.
For other methods each field is one query parameter.
`@Dto(source: Source.query)` or `Source.body` chooses the place by hand.
The route `body:` option still works, and it wins over all of these.

A `@Dto` class:

```dart
@Dto()
class CreateBlog {
  @Length(min: 3, max: 200)
  final String title;

  /// Text of the blog.
  final String? description;   // nullable: optional

  final int views;             // default: optional, `default: 0`

  final Status status;         // enum: only `draft` or `published`

  final List<Tag> tags;        // a list of another @Dto class

  const CreateBlog({required this.title, this.description, this.views = 0,
      required this.status, required this.tags});
}
```

The keys are the same as the keys the DTO reads: snake_case by default (`postCode` is `post_code`),
or `@Name('key')`, or `@Dto(keyCase: KeyCase.field)`.
Each rule annotation adds its JSON Schema keys. See the [rules reference](../the-basic/validation-rules.md).

## Response

The return type of the method gives the `200` answer. `Future<T>` counts as `T`.

| Return type | Schema |
| --- | --- |
| a model (`@DoxModel`) | `$ref` to the model. Keys in `hidden` are left out |
| `List<Model>` | an array of the model |
| a `@Dto` class | `$ref` to the class |
| a `Serializer<Model>` | the map that `convert()` returns, else the model |
| `Pagination` | `total`, `per_page`, `last_page`, `current_page`, `data` |
| `String`, `int`, `bool`, `Map`, `List` | the basic JSON type |
| `dynamic` | the types of the `return` values. A map literal gives its keys. Exceptions are left out |
| `DoxResponse`, `void` | no schema |

A model schema has the primary key, the `@Column` fields, `created_at`, `updated_at`,
the relations (only there when loaded) and the `@Computed` getters.

## Login schemes

Put `@Security` above a middleware class. Every route with this middleware gets the scheme in the docs.
Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add it.

```dart
/// `Authorization: Bearer <api key>`. Not a JWT.
@Security.bearer(format: 'API key')
class ApiKeyAuthMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware { ... }

/// `X-API-Key: <key>`
@Security.apiKey(header: 'X-API-Key')
class HeaderKeyMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware { ... }
```

| Annotation | Scheme in the docs |
| --- | --- |
| `@Security.bearer()` | `type: http`, `scheme: bearer`, no format |
| `@Security.bearer(format: 'JWT')` | the same, with `bearerFormat: JWT` |
| `@Security.apiKey(header: 'X-API-Key')` | `type: apiKey`, `in: header`, `name: X-API-Key`. The default header is `X-API-Key` |

The scheme name is the class name without `Middleware`, with a small first letter: `ApiKeyAuthMiddleware` gives `apiKeyAuth`.
Use `scheme: 'myName'` to pick another name.

A middleware without `@Security` whose class name ends with `AuthMiddleware` gets `bearerAuth`: a bearer token with no format, because Dox can not know if it is a JWT.

For a key in the query or a cookie, or to change a scheme without the builder, set it in the config.
The config wins over `@Security`:

```dart
OpenApiConfig(
  registry: openApiRegistry,
  securitySchemes: <String, SecurityScheme>{
    'apiKey': SecurityScheme.apiKey(name: 'X-API-Key'),
  },
  securityByMiddleware: <String, List<Map<String, List<String>>>>{
    'ApiKeyMiddleware': <Map<String, List<String>>>[
      <String, List<String>>{'apiKey': <String>[]},
    ],
  },
);
```

## What Dox fills in for you

You do not have to write all of the above. A normal controller already gets docs. Annotations only change the result.

| Part of the docs | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- |
| path, method | the live route table |
| path param types | the controller arguments after the first one, in order. `int id` gives `integer` |
| tags | the controller class name without `Controller` (`BlogController` gives `Blog`) |
| operationId | `Class.method`, for example `BlogController.show` |
| summary | `@Summary`. Else the first line of the `///` comment |
| description | `@Description`. Else the rest of the `///` comment |
| request | see [Request](#request) |
| 200 answer | the return type, see [Response](#response) |
| `401` and a login scheme | `@Security` on a middleware class, or a middleware whose class name ends with `AuthMiddleware`. See [Login schemes](#login-schemes) |
| `401` and `403` | the `Can` middleware on the route, or a `req.authorize(...)` call in the controller method |
| `403` | the `GuestMiddleware` or `ValidateSignature` middleware on the route, or a `Gate.authorize(...)` call in the controller method |
| `404` | the path has a `{param}`. The short path of an optional param, like `/blog`, has no `404` |
| `422` | the route has a request class, or the controller method calls `req.validate<T>()` or `req.validateSchema(...)`. The body is `{field: message}` |
| `500` | every route |

`Can`, `GuestMiddleware` and `ValidateSignature` are found by their class name. `req.authorize(...)` is found when it is called on the request (`DoxRequest` or `IDoxRequest`) in the controller method. `Gate.authorize(...)` is found when `Gate` is the class of `dox_auth`. A `@Response` with the same status wins over an automatic answer.

`GuestMiddleware(redirectTo: ...)` also shows a `403`, but the app sends a redirect. Put `@Response(403, ...)` on the method to replace it.

Routes that the builder does not know (for example inline closures) still get a basic entry.

An optional param shows as two paths. The route `/blog/{id?}` gives `/blog/{id}` and `/blog`. OpenAPI path params must always be required.
An optional param in the middle, like `/a/{x?}/b`, also gives the path without it: `/a/{x}/b` and `/a/b`.
Optional params next to each other are dropped from the right, the same way the Dox router matches them.
When the summary and operation id are made from the path, the short path gets its own, like `GET /blog` and `getBlog`.

### `///` comments (optional)

A `///` comment on a method also sets the summary and the description.
The first line is the summary. The rest is the description.

```dart
/// Get one blog
///
/// Deleted blogs are not found.
Future<Blog?> show(DoxRequest req, String id) async {
  return Blog().find(id);
}
```

When a method has both, the annotation wins. `@Summary` replaces the first line of the comment, and `@Description` replaces the rest.

## Config options

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `null` | `true` or `false` turns the docs routes on or off. `null`: on only when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`. See [Turn the docs on in production](#turn-the-docs-on-in-production) |
| `info` | `Info(title: 'Dox API', version: '1.0.0')` | title and version of the API |
| `servers` | `[]` | base URLs, like `[Server('https://api.my.app')]` |
| `registry` | empty | `openApiRegistry` from `lib/generated/openapi.g.dart` |
| `securitySchemes`, `securityByMiddleware` | `{}` | see [Login schemes](#login-schemes) |
| `ui` | `DocsUi.scalar` | the docs page: `DocsUi.scalar` or `DocsUi.swagger` |
| `scalar` | `ScalarOptions()` | see [The docs page](#the-docs-page) |
| `pageTitle` | `info.title` | title of the `/docs` page |
| `include` | `[]` (all routes) | only these paths go in the docs, like `['/api/*']` |
| `exclude` | `[]` | these paths are left out, like `['/api/internal/*']` |

In production the docs are off, unless you set `enabled: true`. See [Turn the docs on in production](#turn-the-docs-on-in-production).

### Turn the docs on in production

By default `enabled` is `null`. Then Dox looks at `APP_ENV`:

| `APP_ENV` value | Are the docs on? |
| --- | --- |
| `development` | yes |
| `local` | yes |
| `production` | no. `/docs`, `/openapi.json` and `/openapi.yaml` give 404 |
| not set | no. Dox treats the app as production |

To turn the docs on in every environment, also production, set `enabled: true`:

```dart title="lib/config/openapi.dart"
OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  enabled: true,
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);
```

!!! warning
    `/docs` has no login. In production, anyone can see every route of your API.
    Only do this for a public API.

`enabled: false` turns the docs off in every environment.

### The docs page

The page loads Scalar from the jsDelivr CDN, at a fixed version, and reads `/openapi.json`.
Change the look with `scalar:`:

```dart
OpenApiConfig(
  registry: openApiRegistry,
  pageTitle: 'Blog API docs',
  scalar: ScalarOptions(theme: ScalarTheme.purple, darkMode: true),
);
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `theme` | `ScalarTheme.default_` | Color theme. Same names as Scalar: `moon`, `purple`, `deepSpace`, `saturn`, `kepler`, `mars` and more. |
| `darkMode` | `false` | Start in dark mode. The user can still switch. |
| `showDownloadButton` | `true` | Show the button that downloads the document. |
| `proxyUrl` | `null` | Send "Try it" requests through this proxy. Off by default, so requests go from the browser straight to your API. |

`pageTitle` and all options are escaped, so a value can not break the page.

To use Swagger UI instead, set `ui:`:

```dart
OpenApiConfig(registry: openApiRegistry, ui: DocsUi.swagger);
```

## Write the files

Use `dox openapi:generate` to write the document to files.

```bash
dox openapi:generate              # storage/openapi/openapi.json and openapi.yaml
dox openapi:generate docs/api     # another folder
```

It runs `bin/openapi.dart` of your app.
A new app does not have this file. Make it with this code:

```dart title="bin/openapi.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
  await Dox().writeOpenApi(args.isEmpty ? 'storage/openapi' : args.first);
  exit(0);
}
```

`writeOpenApi` runs your providers and registers the routes. It does not start the server.

To serve these files in production, see [Production setup](#production-setup).

## Production setup

By default the docs are off in production. `enabled: true` is the quick way to turn them on, see [Turn the docs on in production](#turn-the-docs-on-in-production).
This section is the other way: make the document at build time, put the files in the image, and serve the files.
The URLs stay the same: `/docs`, `/openapi.json` and `/openapi.yaml`.

You need two files first: `lib/config/openapi.dart` (see [Setup](#setup-optional)) and `bin/openapi.dart` (see [Write the files](#write-the-files)). An app made with `dox create` has neither file.

1. Make both files, if you do not have them yet.

2. Add a controller that serves the files:

    ```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/docs.controller.dart"
    import 'dart:io';

    import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
    import 'package:dox_openapi/dox_openapi.dart'
        show OpenApiConstants, OpenApiServer;
    import 'package:my_app/config/openapi.dart';

    @Inject()
    class DocsController {
      /// The same Scalar page as the live docs. It loads `/openapi.json`.
      final String _page = OpenApiServer(
        OpenApi(info: openApi.info),
        pageTitle: openApi.pageTitle,
        ui: openApi.ui,
        scalar: openApi.scalar,
      ).docsPage().body;

      DoxResponse page() {
        return response(_page)
            .contentType(ContentType.parse(OpenApiConstants.htmlContentType));
      }

      DoxResponse json() {
        return _file('openapi.json', OpenApiConstants.jsonContentType);
      }

      DoxResponse yaml() {
        return _file('openapi.yaml', OpenApiConstants.yamlContentType);
      }

      DoxResponse _file(String name, String contentType) {
        File file = File('docs/openapi/$name');
        if (!file.existsSync()) throw NotFoundHttpException();
        return response(file.readAsStringSync())
            .contentType(ContentType.parse(contentType));
      }
    }
    ```

    A new app has `dox_openapi` in its `pubspec.yaml`. If yours does not, run `dart pub add dox_openapi`.
    Run the builder again after you add the controller.

3. Add the routes. Add them only when the live docs are off, so the routes do not clash in development:

    ```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
    @override
    void register() {
      if (!openApi.isEnabled) {
        Route.get('/docs', (DocsController c) => c.page);
        Route.get('/openapi.json', (DocsController c) => c.json);
        Route.get('/openapi.yaml', (DocsController c) => c.yaml);
      }
      // ...
    }
    ```

    `openApi` is the config of `lib/config/openapi.dart`. Import it, and the controller, in this file.

4. Make the files in the Docker build, and copy them into the image. Change the `Dockerfile` in two places.
    First, in the build stage, right after `RUN /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build`, add:

    ```dockerfile title="Dockerfile"
    RUN APP_KEY=only-for-the-build-not-a-key /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox openapi:generate docs/openapi
    ```

    Second, in the `RUN` step that lays out `/out`, add `/out/app/docs` to the `mkdir -p` list. Add one line to the `&&` chain after the `cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/` line:

    ```dockerfile title="Dockerfile"
    RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/app/docs /out/tmp \
      && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
      && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
      && cp -r docs/openapi /out/app/docs/openapi \
      # ... the lines that follow stay as they are
    ```

    `bin/openapi.dart` starts your app config, so it needs `APP_KEY`. The dummy key is only for this step. It is not in the image.
    If a provider of your app connects to a database in `setup()`, that database must be reachable in the build step.
    The server runs in `/app`, so the controller reads `/app/docs/openapi/`.

5. Start the image with `APP_ENV=production` and open `/docs`.

!!! warning
    The route has no login. Anyone can open `/docs` and see every route of your API.
    To protect it, put a middleware on the three routes.

To test it on your machine, run `dox openapi:generate docs/openapi`, then start the app with `APP_ENV=production`.

## How a route finds its docs

The builder saves the docs of each controller method, and each `Route.get(...)` / `Route.resource(...)` call it finds.
At runtime, Dox matches each route handler by its method name, HTTP method and the end of its path.
If there is no match, it picks the only method with that name and the same argument types.
Group prefixes (like `api/`) do not matter.

!!! tip
    Two controllers can have a method with the same name, like `index`.
    When the route names the class, like `(LinkController c) => c.index` or `Route.get<LinkController>(...)`,
    only methods of that class match. With a plain `links.index`, the path of the route call decides.

## Without Dox

`dox_openapi` also works on its own. Describe routes by hand with `ApiDoc`:

```dart
import 'package:dox_openapi/dox_openapi.dart';

ApiDoc docs = ApiDoc();
Map<String, dynamic> user = docs.schema('User', userSchema); // returns a $ref

docs.route('GET', '/users/{id}',
    summary: 'Get one user',
    tags: <String>['users'],
    params: <String, Object>{'id': <String, dynamic>{'type': 'integer'}},
    responses: <int, ResponseDoc>{
      200: ResponseDoc(schema: user, description: 'The user'),
      404: const ResponseDoc(description: 'Not found'),
    });

OpenApi api = OpenApi(info: const Info(title: 'My API', version: '1.0.0'), docs: docs);

api.toJson();                              // Map
api.toJsonString();                        // pretty JSON
api.toYaml();                              // YAML
await api.writeFiles('storage/openapi');   // openapi.json + openapi.yaml

// Serve the docs from your own server
OpenApiServer server = OpenApiServer(api); // Swagger UI: OpenApiServer(api, ui: DocsUi.swagger)
OpenApiResponse? page = server.handle('/docs'); // also '/openapi.json' and '/openapi.yaml'
if (page != null) {
  // send page.body with the header Content-Type: page.contentType
}
```

A schema can be a JSON Schema `Map`, a [`dox_validation`](validation.md) schema, or any object with `toJsonSchema()`.
Paths can use `{id}` or `:id`. Both become `{id}`.
`responses` takes status codes as `int` keys. To use a text key like `default` or `2XX`, pass `namedResponses`:

```dart
docs.route('GET', '/users/{id}',
    responses: <int, ResponseDoc>{
      200: ResponseDoc(schema: user, description: 'The user'),
    },
    namedResponses: <String, ResponseDoc>{
      'default': const ResponseDoc(description: 'Any other error'),
    });
```

`namedResponses` come after `responses`. When the same key is in both, the one in `namedResponses` wins.
`DoxRouteAdapter().addTo(docs, routes)` adds a basic entry for each route you did not describe.
